Xulin Hu and four co-authors trace how a language model's refusal to comply is built up inside the network, and use that trace to detect jailbreak attempts. Standard analysis reads refusal from a single static direction in the final layers. Attacks can suppress that end signal, which raises the question of whether the refusal process leaves earlier marks that survive.

Causal tracing finds a sparse upstream activation pattern, a refusal trajectory, that often persists even when the final signal is suppressed. Their detector works on raw hidden states from a chosen layer window, with no heavy machinery. Across three model families it improved detection on several attack types at a fixed operating point. Tests against adaptive attacks and encoded inputs map where the method holds and where it thins. Trajectory monitoring is promising, not settled.
arxiv-2605-03158:
Benjamin M. Ampel and Sagar Samtani release HackerSignal, a large dataset linking hacker forum talk to the full life cycle of software vulnerabilities. Threat analysts need to connect early chatter, exploits, advisories, and fixes, but those records usually sit in separate silos.

The set holds millions of deduplicated documents from dozens of sources across eight layers and more than three decades, linked by shared CVE identifiers. Three benchmark tasks are shown: cross-source linkage, exploit type classification, and forward-in-time generalization with disjoint vulnerabilities. Leakage checks, audit packets, and governance notes ship with the release for careful use.
arxiv-2605-03758:
Zihong Cheng and Fa Peng Huang study whether dark matter could have been produced by bubble collisions during a first-order phase transition at the end of inflation. The transition happens in a spectator scalar sector whose potential depends on the inflaton, so bubbles form faster as inflation ends. The authors first map where vacuum decay is led by the Coleman-De Luccia channel and the transition completes.

In the viable regime, elastic self-scatterings spread the spectator particles' momenta efficiently, while their decay into dark matter is the main channel moving the population into the dark sector. The final abundance combines direct production in bubble collisions with later decays of spectator particles. Competing number-changing processes stay too slow compared with cosmic expansion.
arxiv-2605-03858:
Jaeyun Lee and four co-authors introduce MCJudgeBench, a benchmark for judging language model judges on multi-constraint instructions, constraint by constraint. Judges are usually scored on whole responses, yet real instructions bundle several demands that can each pass, partly pass, or fail. Each benchmark instance pairs an instruction and a candidate response. It adds an explicit constraint list and per-constraint gold labels.

Controlled perturbations of responses and variants of the prompt let the protocol separate two kinds of inconsistency. One is intrinsic, under stochastic decoding. The other is procedural, under prompt changes. Across proprietary and open-source judges, strong overall scores did not guarantee sound detection of the rarer partial and negative cases, and higher correctness did not always mean lower inconsistency. Reasoning improved correctness but not stability across the board.
arxiv-2605-03958:
J. Sumaya-Martinez proposes a Fisher-informational reformulation of physical time, in which clock time is not a fundamental substance but an emergent calibration of how distinguishable physical states become along a causal order. Clocks, on this view, do not measure time itself; they are reproducible processes whose distinguishable states correlate with other events. The framework defines a causal-informational parameter as a summed Fisher-geometric distance along a trajectory in state space.

In classical systems the parameter comes from the Fisher information metric; in quantum systems it uses quantum Fisher information with the Bures and Fubini-Study geometries. The manuscript distinguishes model-dependent from quantum Fisher information. It clarifies how Schrödinger dynamics gets recast. It gives examples including a qubit clock and a decay process, and a Fisher-based measure of clock quality.
arxiv-2605-04158:
Rohit Ghosh and four co-authors show that analogue gravity effects in fluids that accrete are not an artifact of the linear theory. Analogue gravity uses fluid flows to mimic spacetime geometry. Here the system is spherical accretion onto compact objects. The fluid has a relativistic, mixed equation of state. Its adiabatic index varies with position. The authors extend the acoustic metric into the nonlinear, higher-order regime.

They show the perturbations obey a covariant wave equation. The equation lives in an effective acoustic spacetime with nonlinear corrections. That makes the analogue geometry move rather than stay fixed. So the acoustic horizon can shift inward or outward. The shift depends on how large the swings in density, temperature, and mass accretion rate are. The result gives a truer framework for studying such spacetimes in such flows.
arxiv-2605-04358:
Zhenhan Huang and three co-authors propose a search-based method for spotting images made by generative artificial intelligence. Photorealistic fakes raise misuse concerns, yet trained detectors are costly and often fail on new kinds of data, while training-free methods have been weaker.

Their method looks inside a model's intermediate layers and compares how an image's internal representation changes when the image is slightly perturbed. Real and generated images react differently, and that gap drives the detection. On two broad benchmarks the method beat both trained and training-free rivals, with the largest average gain on the harder forensic set.
arxiv-2605-04458:
Bryan Li and eight co-authors automate a tedious step in evaluating long, citation-backed reports produced by retrieval-augmented systems. Evaluators break a topic into small nuggets of required information, often written as question-answer pairs, but building those sets by hand scales poorly, especially across languages.

Their pipeline generates nugget sets in three stages, grounding each question in the source documents so the answer is attested in the collection. Separating the question from its possible answers allows finer scoring of what a report covers. The work aims to make report evaluation reusable for new topics and multilingual collections.
arxiv-2605-04658:
Wei Cheng and Jiahui Hong survey a framework that unifies gradient flow ideas with Hamiltonian dynamics. It is used to study Hamilton-Jacobi equations. Those equations are central to mechanics and control. The survey emphasises how singularities travel through solutions and connects the theory to weak KAM theory, optimal transport, and mean field control.

Beyond reviewing known results, the authors construct generalised special curves. They use a minimising movement scheme. They then pass to a weak limit using Young measures. They also lift the dynamics of strict singular curves to a flow on trajectory space. They prove its only steady measures at the critical value are exactly the projected Mather measures. That is a new dynamical description.
arxiv-2605-04958:
Federica Fieramosca and four co-authors test fast computer simulation of indoor Wi-Fi signals as a way to locate people without asking them to carry a device. Human bodies disturb radio waves, and those disturbances can reveal position. Measuring real rooms for every design is costly, so a trustworthy simulation baseline would help planning.

Their compact full-wave setup produces maps of received signal strength and checks the patterns against controlled settings. The maps reproduced the main spatial features and interference structure, though simple material descriptions left some gaps. The authors propose diffraction-aware refinements and present the approach as a pre-measurement reference for designing device-free sensing systems.
arxiv-2605-05158:
P Taylor-Burdett and five co-authors present a device for switching a permanent magnet's field on and off with very low power and very low noise. Many experiments need magnetic fields that are both ultra-stable and switchable. Wires are switchable but noisy, while existing ways to switch permanent magnets need large pulses and waste power, especially at high switching rates.

Their Saturable Electronic Reluctance Switch routes the magnet's flux through a nonlinear ferromagnetic circuit. The field ramps smoothly with current up to a threshold, then holds constant, shielding stability from current noise and avoiding demagnetisation. The authors expect far lower power per switching cycle than existing approaches, plus robustness to fabrication errors.
arxiv-2605-05758:
Biomedical researchers lean on specialized tools daily; language models mostly cannot use them. Xin Gao and four co-authors build BioTool, a dataset for teaching models to call biomedical tools properly. Earlier efforts relied on prompting tricks and a handful of tools, which caps what an agent can actually do in a lab workflow.

BioTool covers 34 frequently used tools gathered from real research practice, with examples formatted for fine-tuning. Training on it should move models from describing procedures to executing them through the right tool with the right arguments. The dataset is meant to close the gap between general-purpose tool use and specialist biomedical practice.
arxiv-2605-05858:
Simulating how magnetization evolves carries a constraint: its length must never change. Changjian Xie compares two numerical schemes for the continuity-equation form, asking whether an extra projection step is needed at all. Its own structure keeps the length fixed, since the motion is always at right angles to the magnetization.

Xie discretizes the equation and tests an implicit Gauss-Seidel method against a semi-implicit backward scheme. The test checks accuracy and whether the constraint survives in practice. The study answers a practical coding question: enforce the constraint by projection, or trust its geometry.
arxiv-2605-05958:
Peilin Zhan and four co-authors work on knowledge tracing, the task of estimating what a student has mastered over time. Learning logs are not random samples, since exercises are recommended and chosen in biased ways. Most tracing methods ignore that bias, so their mastery estimates skew and errors feed into later recommendations.

The team build a doubly robust method that joins a propensity model with an error imputation model. It stays unbiased if either part is right, a classic strength of that design. They then show that estimator variance builds up over a learning sequence and destabilizes training. A temporal smoothness term controls that variance in their framework, and tests on real benchmarks show gains across several tracing backbones.
arxiv-2605-06158:
Zhengchunmin Dai and seven co-authors study backdoor attacks that stretch across many sessions of a language model agent. A multi step attack may need chances that appear in different sessions, such as access to target data or the right tool. To exploit them, the attack must keep state, store partial results, and branch on current conditions like a small program.

The authors model such attack programs as Mealy machines and build a sub backdoor for each transition. Training trajectories for the parts are combined so one fine tuned model learns all local behaviors, linked later through persistent memory. Across four models, complete programs succeeded at high rates in two agent environments. The results show end to end cross session attack programs are feasible, a risk defenders must plan for.
arxiv-2605-06658:
Weiqing Xiao and nine co-authors present Relit-LiVE, a framework that relights videos under new illumination without needing camera poses. Neural relighting usually decomposes a video into intrinsic scene parts first, but that decomposition is unreliable on real footage and errors pile up as distorted materials and flicker. Their key move is feeding raw reference images directly into the rendering process.

A single diffusion process jointly generates the relit video and per-frame environment maps aligned to each viewpoint, enforcing consistency between geometry and lighting. That supports moving lights and cameras naturally. Experiments beat leading relighting and neural rendering methods on synthetic and real benchmarks, with uses in material editing and object insertion.
arxiv-2605-06858:
Jose Falla and Ilya Safro add counterdiabatic driving to quantum portfolio optimization. The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm searches for good portfolios, but real budget and risk constraints tangle the search. Their constrained variant builds its ansatz from approximate gauge potentials. These come from nested commutators between the portfolio problem Hamiltonian and a mixer that preserves total weight.

Tests compare the approach against standard mixer, Grover mixer, and penalty-based versions of the algorithm. At fixed circuit depth, the counterdiabatic version steadily achieves better ratios under the constraints. The work suggests shortcut ideas from adiabatic control can buy optimization quality without deeper quantum circuits.
arxiv-2605-07158:
Junseon Yoo audits a core assumption behind scientific search tools: that embedding similarity reflects real relatedness. He built an expanded citation graph over millions of papers and split it into sub-fields and finer research agendas. Four leading embedding models were then tested on whether their nearest neighbors share those groupings.

The models did reasonably at the broad sub-field level but failed at the agenda level, where most retrieved papers were off-agenda. The failure appeared across eight domains and all models. A simple citation-count reranking recovered much of the missed signal, suggesting embeddings miss agenda-level structure that citation graphs carry, a concrete warning for scientific retrieval systems.
arxiv-2605-07258:
M. Kohno and H. Kamada calculate low-energy scattering between a Xi particle and a deuteron using the Faddeev three-body equations. Three candidate descriptions of the Xi-nucleon interaction are tested, one from chiral theory and two from lattice-based HAL-QCD calculations. Phase shifts are reported for two spin states of the combined system.

From the three-body wave functions, the authors compute momentum correlation functions that experiments can measure. Deuteron breakup matters strongly in one spin channel, which earlier treatments could miss. Differences between the calculated correlation functions reveal how strongly the candidate interactions differ, so future experimental data could help pin down the true Xi-nucleon force.
arxiv-2605-07758:
Tiago Ferreira and two co-authors learn weighted automata, using an SMT solver as the engine. Weighted automata assign weights from a semiring to strings, and classic learning algorithms in the Hankel or L-star style are fragile in practice. Their algorithm is built around the semiring and, when it terminates, is certain to return a minimal one.

They prove partial correctness and give a termination condition that covers all finite semirings in particular. In many experiments the learner recovered many minimal machines over finite and infinite semirings. It vastly outperformed a naive baseline. It also stayed competitive with a state-of-the-art algorithm while producing much smaller automata and asking the teacher fewer queries.
arxiv-2605-07858:
Jad Koleilat gives differential linear logic, a proof system that builds in differentiation through links between linear and non-linear formulas, a new categorical semantics. Models of the logic are stated as a pair of Grothendieck fibrations with a tangent functor. They draw methods from the categorical semantics of type theory and fit them to linear-non-linear adjunctions.

The paper is clear about its scope: this fibrational view is a first step toward joining differential linear logic with dependent types. Framing it through tangent structure on fibrations is what makes that joining plausible.
arxiv-2605-07958:
Aaron Gobeyn and two co-authors extend the standard model for superconducting layered coatings used in radio-frequency cavities. The established Kubo model covered superconductor-insulator-superconductor stacks; accelerator builders now stack arbitrary sequences of superconducting, normal, and insulating layers, with losses and dielectric effects that the old model omitted.

The extended model handles any layer sequence and counts all parts, including ohmic losses and dielectric effects. For repeated two-layer structures, the single-repeat setup gives the highest usable field, though those layers can be thinned below the depth fields reach at minor cost. Transition regions between layers are modeled with virtual blended layers, and thicker transitions degrade the peak field. A surface impedance form plugs the model into finite element simulations.
arxiv-2605-08158:
Haopeng Jin, Wenlong Zhao, Tao Yu, Tiankun Yang, and coauthors present HIMMEL, a framework for understanding long videos with multimodal language models. Long video is expensive three ways: decoding dense frames costs heavily, token counts grow with frames, and sparse keyframes miss motion.

HIMMEL splits the work. A few semantic anchor frames go to the costly vision transformer to fix identity and layout. The dense intervals between them are handled by a light adapter that reads compressed-domain signals directly: motion-vector maps, residual maps, and an intra-frame context branch. Motion evidence is gathered without decoding every frame, so long videos become cheaper to process while keeping their movement information.
arxiv-2605-08258:
John deVadoss lays out a design-first architecture for intelligent agents in large firms. Enterprise interest has moved on from generic software agents. It now centers on language model agents that plan and call tools. They keep memory, check their own work, and sometimes write into systems of record. Governance matters, he argues. But it cannot be the organizing idea.

The CEAD reference architecture starts from agent design itself. It covers capability boundaries and how autonomy is split. It covers interaction protocols and authority over tools and data. It also covers memory design, verification, and the human interface. It borrows contracts and registries from service-oriented design. It rejects governance as the primary abstraction.
arxiv-2605-08458:
Jakeb Chouinard examines which radial basis kernels a brain-like representation can build. Spatial semantic pointers encode continuous space in distributed neural activity. Radial basis functions respond by distance from a center. They are the natural currency for merging physical and perceptual information into one space.

Chouinard characterizes the common radial basis kernels that fit the pointer framework. He checks earlier work based on grid cell-like codes. Those codes are the periodic neurons known from navigation research. The analysis shows grid-style representations can realize radial basis kernels. More than that, they are optimal for the job. The result links a neuroscience motif to a machine learning staple.
arxiv-2605-08558:
Muyun Lu, Haoyang Hong, Huazheng Wang, and Ying Lin study decision problems where cheap rough tests can improve with use. Classic multi fidelity bandits assume the gap between rough and exact feedback stays fixed, yet simulators and language model judges get better when calibrated. Their work focuses on two feedback levels where the cheap source grows more informative over time.

Their algorithm, TACC, uses an optimistic rule to decide when cheap sampling still pays and when to switch to exact checks. Theory shows real savings for middling options, and tests on synthetic tasks plus a model judging task probe when continuing cheap trials helps. Experiment design gains guidance for budgets that mix practice runs with costly truth.
arxiv-2605-08658:
Jiang and two colleagues ask how a practitioner stuck with a small, cheap code model should spend extra test time. Their answer, SketchVerify, is a cost performance rule for one model tier, not a universal accuracy improvement. The model lists distinct algorithmic strategies, drafts a partial program sketch for each strategy, and fills each sketch several times.

That yields diverse candidates checked by running them and grouped by fingerprint clustering. Each new sketch explores a different algorithm by design, while each new flat sample likely repeats an existing one. On the hard subset where Lite greedy fails, Lite Sketch with two sketches and five fills recovers 11 of 19 problems, against 5 of 19 for flat sampling. Flat sampling still loses even at roughly triple the budget, while sketching still wins. Across tiers, upgrading still beats sketching: Pro greedy dominates Lite Sketch on pass rate and dollar cost.
arxiv-2605-08758:
Jiaxin Liu, Peng Yang, Yuping Li, and Xinyue Xie coordinate warehouse robots that shuttle totes instead of pallets, a shift driven by online shopping and small batch production. Orders, totes, and robots must be decided in sequence, yet past methods fit one system only. Their OLSF-TRS framework joins structured combinatorial optimization with multi agent reinforcement learning into one general, scalable decision scheme.

On small systems it lands within a few percent of optimal across two layouts. At large scale it beats heuristic rivals, cutting tote movements clearly against strong rule based methods while answering in real time. Warehouse operators gain lower cost, energy use, and steadier throughput from one transferable framework.
arxiv-2605-08858:
Piotr Borycki and four coauthors explain image classifier decisions with prototypes, the this looks like that style of explanation, without needing any of the original data. Prototype methods normally mine example patches from a held out dataset, blocking use where data is private or gone, while post hoc explainers avoid retraining but still needed that data access. ProDG instead synthesizes clean, high fidelity prototypes directly from the frozen model's own weights using generative models.

No external data enters at any point. The authors frame the result as a new frontier in data free explainability, aimed at privacy sensitive domains like medicine where original images are restricted or fundamentally unavailable. Model auditing gains explanations that respect the same privacy walls as deployment.
arxiv-2605-09358:
Raeisi and four colleagues present a new 6G radio part: beyond-diagonal reconfigurable intelligent surfaces built into the transceiver opening as a wave-domain analog processing unit. 6G networks must handle fast data, sensing everywhere, and sub-meter location, plus sustainability and inclusiveness. Old-style radios lean on digital baseband processing whose cost, power, and complexity grow badly with array size and carrier frequency.

Beyond-diagonal surfaces shape electromagnetic waves right in the analog domain, and shifting linear signal work off the digital baseband into the wave domain cuts compute load and energy use. That allows scalable, sustainable work for extra-large antenna arrays. Joint flexibility, modularity, and energy-saving analog processing make these surfaces a strong pick for next-generation wireless radios.
arxiv-2605-09458:
Corradetti studies shell polytopes from integral systems in real composition algebras. Each shell is the convex hull of integral elements sharing one norm. The opening shells recover the familiar root-polytopal shapes of the classical Hurwitz systems. The Okubo algebra behaves quite differently. Its integral closure does not reach the Gosset polytope directly.

Instead it picks a two-adic ladder whose opening layers include a cross-polytope and a D8 root polytope. Corradetti further shows the natural intermediate lattice matches the rescaled cubic lattice up to isometry. Every shell then splits into clear orbits under the hyperoctahedral group W(B8). The higher Okubo shells admit a full combinatorial account in cubic-lattice coordinates. The full E8 Gosset polytope is then recovered by maximal-isotropic gluing along (Z/2)^4.
arxiv-2605-09658:
Ganguly and Menzies argue that search based software engineering should zoom, not wander. Traditional practice treats global search and full Pareto exploration as essential, but under tight evaluation budgets the authors find regional search far more effective. Their minimal greedy zoom method, EZR, runs about a thousand times faster than Pareto and global Bayesian methods. Across more than 100 software engineering optimization tasks, it ranks higher and wins or ties on 84 to 89 percent of data sets at equal budget.

Even at one fifth of the budget, EZR wins or ties on 79 to 81 percent of data sets. Surprisingly, it matches or beats Pareto methods on their own coverage metrics despite never seeking a frontier. The explanation is structural: Pareto optimal solutions form a tiny, tight cluster in a compact region of decision space, so wandering wastes budget outside it. Zooming also yields small, interpretable models, making optimization more accessible.
arxiv-2605-09958:
Li and four co-authors make nonlinear quantum measurements far cheaper. Nonlinear properties of quantum states, like higher-order average values, matter for quantum information and many-body physics, but measuring them usually needs multi-copy steps or many measurement settings. Their universal system, collision-based nonlinear estimation, uses single-copy randomised readings instead.

Oddly, the method needs only one measurement setting, given the system is large enough or a few extra qubits are on hand. That defies the usual expectation that nonlinear measuring needs multiple bases. The method is also free of device choice during the test, so many nonlinear functions can be estimated at once. It extends to main-component traits and partial-transpose moments, giving a scalable route for near-term quantum devices.
arxiv-2605-10358:
Catrin Mair extends the study of the condensed Galois category of a scheme. That category was introduced by Barwick, Glasman, and Haine in their work on Exodromy. Condensed math refines classical topology by tracking how spaces vary over profinite sets. The Galois category extends the absolute Galois groups of residue fields at points of a scheme. Her 2026 paper elaborates its link to Lurie's work on ultracategories and describes it via w-contractible rings.

Mair classifies schemes whose Galois category has an initial or a terminal object. Such schemes have trivial condensed homotopy type. She also computes a formula for the core group of the condensed fundamental group of a general Dedekind domain. She shows it is non-trivial for Spec(Z), the spectrum of the integers. Spec(Z) is therefore not condensed trivial in that sense. That sharpens the line between classical étale contractibility and its condensed refinement.
arxiv-2605-10458:
Pablo Martínez Crespo and eight colleagues rethink how AI models are tested in atomic chemical space. Atomic properties inform downstream molecular property prediction. But testing them as machine-learning targets lacked a sound atomic-level protocol. Their 2026 paper proposes a held-out protocol clustering atomic environments by SOAP descriptors and scoring only cluster labels unseen during training.

Using 5-by-5 cross-validation and Tukey's HSD test, the authors compare E(3)-equivariant models against non-equivariant, rotation-augmented models. Targets are electron populations and moments of hydrogen, carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen atoms. They introduce QT-Net, a rotation-augmented graph neural network. QT-Net infers properties of atoms in molecules from QM9 outside its training set. Those properties improve downstream prediction. Dipole moments worked out from QT-Net's per-atom outputs match QM9 ground-truth values, and all code and data are released.
arxiv-2605-10658:
Yao Shu, Jian Mu, and Zhongxiang Dai give a random gradient-shaping theory explaining why zeroth-order tuning may lose less than first-order descent in ongoing learning. Their analysis shows finite differences expose a raw shape mean-aligned with first-order gradients, while a norm-matched benchmark fixes the mean squared tuning norm. Loss is thus controlled by how the tuning shape exposes memory bend.

For norm-matched zeroth-order updates, the mean shaped memory bend obeys an exact rule preserving the even memory floor while contracting only the uneven component. Projecting this rule onto the incoming gradient yields the seen loss gap. Zeroth-order improves mean loss exactly when the first-order direction has above-average memory bend, by a query-dependent fraction of that excess. The mechanism also transfers in code: RISE applies the calibrated zeroth-order shape to exact first-order gradients inside parameter blocks.
arxiv-2605-10758:
Can Yin, Bo Fan, and Antonio M. García-García show that no measurement-led phase shift takes place in the entanglement moves of watched non-interacting one-dimensional fermions in messy or quasiperiodic fields. The entanglement entropy of such fermions with U(1) symmetry, with jobs watched by homodyne or projective rules, always stays in an area-law phase.

By growing the set size to eighteen thousand sites with graphics processors and finite-size scaling study, the authors find the key watching strength fits with zero, so no shift takes place. For the messy case, a math proof mapping the task onto a nonlinear sigma model backs the shift's lack for any watching or mess strength. Mess's mark is caught by a symmetry flip from BDI to AIII, giving a longer link length in the weak mess edge. A true watching strength grows in line with mess.
arxiv-2605-10958: Md Abdullah Al Mazid and Naphtali Rishe build a physics-guided stand-in for atmospheric correction coefficients, the numbers that clean satellite images of air effects. Their pKANrtm network takes the state of the air plus low-fidelity 6S coefficients. It predicts the gap to high-fidelity libRadtran results, and rebuilds the high-fidelity values. Trained with a physics-consistency penalty, it beats leading regression stand-ins in standard and shifted tests while running far faster than libRadtran.
arxiv-2605-11058:
Niayesh Afshordi, Phil Halper, Matteo Rini, and Michael Schirber report the Big Mysteries Survey, a large poll of physicists' views on cosmology, black holes, quantum mechanics, quantum gravity, and anthropic coincidences. Run through Physics Magazine, it polled 1,675 people, following a smaller 2024 Copenhagen survey.

The top finding upends public talk: several views billed as field-wide consensus hold slim majorities or just the largest share. The broad magazine sample and the focused conference sample also differ, showing how group makeup shifts views. Writers and physicists get a snapshot that swaps consensus talk for counted dissent.
arxiv-2605-11258: Andrew Shen, Shaul Druckmann and James Zou test whether language models can invent varied new solutions to open science problems. Left alone, the models collapse into low-diversity repeats. Analogical reasoning, their new method, draws analogies to problems in other fields that share relational structure, then searches through those analogies. It raises diversity sharply, invents new solutions over half the time, and gains on four biomedical tasks in real tests.
arxiv-2605-11558: Park and five colleagues propose the Heavy Tailed Activation Function, HTAF, for learning stable binary representations. Binary activations aid compute, memory and interpretability, but Heaviside activations block gradient training because they cannot be differentiated. HTAF smooths the Heaviside function as a sigmoid hyperbolic tangent composite, keeping large gradient mass near zero with slower tail decay. Spiking, binary and deep Heaviside networks all train stably with HTAF. The authors also build Implicit Concept Bottleneck Models, interpretable image models using HTAF for discrete features with performance matching or beating standard models.
arxiv-2605-11758: Rezkellah Noureddine Khiati, Pierre-Yves Brillet, and Catalin Fetita segment lung disease in CT scans without any labeled cases. Their DiffSegLung system uses hand-made radiomic measures as a teacher. The teacher shapes a 3D diffusion network through a contrast goal, then core features are grouped at run time with Hounsfield-unit guidance. On 190 expert-labeled slices from four CT cohorts, it beat label-free rivals on all four disease classes.
arxiv-2605-11858: Saqib Hussain, Gabrijela Zaharijas, and Klaus Dolag model high-energy gamma-ray and neutrino glow from three galaxy clusters: Virgo, Perseus, and Coma. Combining magnetohydrodynamic simulations with Monte Carlo cosmic-ray propagation, and assuming cosmic-ray injection scales with gas density, they predict gamma-ray fluxes well below current LHAASO limits. Their diffuse flux also sits below Fermi-LAT reports while remaining consistent with IceCube neutrino limits.
arxiv-2605-12058: Yuxiang Chen and ten colleagues widen group relative policy optimization with the Hölder mean. GRPO scores gains across groups of sampled paths, but fixed ways of pooling token odds limit it: some pooling modes crash training, others give weak results. HölderPO pools token odds by the Hölder mean, where a bigger p sharpens gradients on rare signals and a smaller p caps gradient spread. A slow annealing plan for p through training beats the trade-off, reaching 54.9 percent mean accuracy on math tests and 93.8 percent on ALFWorld.
arxiv-2605-12158: Thiago Santos de Moura and three colleagues build ReproBreak, a dataset of reproducible web locator breaks. Test tools like Cypress and Playwright find page elements through locators. A break happens when a site change stops a locator finding its target, breaking tests even though the feature still works. No prior dataset measured locator fragility at scale, so the authors mined 359 open-source codebases for locator-change commits. They reproduced breaks in the four projects with the most locator changes, yielding 449 confirmed breaks with scripts to replay them.
arxiv-2605-12258: Runhe Lai and five colleagues show that instruction tokens can power object hallucination detection in multi-mode language models. Token embeddings quietly encode visual information while sifting errors from false visual codes. Their Instruction Lens Score joins two scores: a Calibrated Local Score, and a Context Consistency Score gauging match of object tokens. The method works plug-and-play, needing no extra models or extra training. Tests across benchmarks and model designs show it always beats past detection methods.
arxiv-2605-12358: Mathys and three colleagues recast graph learning as sequence modelling, borrowing the rapid progress of sequence architectures. Their Linearized Graph Sequence Models separate how deep the computation runs from how far information travels across the graph, turning core graph design choices into sequence design choices. The paper studies, in theory and in tests, which sequence properties preserve the graph's built-in bias toward local structure. Results show improved handling of long-range information tasks, offering a principled bridge between graph and sequence methods.
arxiv-2605-12658: Nagy, Nesterov and Rigó develop a new algorithm for multiconic optimisation using the parabolic target approach. The cone is a direct product of many small cones. Their approach rests on hyperbolic coupling, giving linked primal-dual pairs whose conduct is much more tame. They justify all main steps in the cost analysis and prove overall cost like the best known cost for linear programs of the same size.
arxiv-2605-12858: Schiebelbein-Zwack and Fishbach test which histories of black-hole formation fit the observed merger rate across cosmic time. The merger rate combines the birth rate of progenitor binaries with the delay before they merge. They show some delay distributions are forbidden outright, since their long-delay tails predict too many nearby mergers. Using population models and gravitational-wave data, they find the data disfavour long delays and channels like stable mass transfer.
arxiv-2605-13358: Hakan Sahin, Mustafa Aslantas and Ishak Altun introduce a shrinking rule for mappings that send each point to a set of points. Instead of comparing pairs, their rule compares triangles of three points and asks whether their perimeters shrink by a fixed factor. They show this triangle rule extends Nadler's older contraction idea. Yet they give a counterexample proving it does not imply that older rule. From the new rule they derive results guaranteeing fixed points, where a mapping leaves a point unchanged.
arxiv-2605-13858: Eslam Reda and Sara El-Metwally introduce HormoneT5, a shifter word model boosted with a Hormone Emotion Block copying the human gland system's role in feeling handling. These hormone values transform into a feeling code tuning encoder hidden states, enabling feeling-fitting response making. Tests on a picked emotion-tagged data show HormoneT5 reaches over 85 percent per-hormone hits within a 0.15 slack threshold. Hormone spread ranges exceed 0.85 across all six hormones between opposed feeling tones.
arxiv-2605-14258: Fernando and Guitchounts map how computation moves through layers of three large language models using full Jacobian eigendecomposition. Depth is treated as discrete time and the stream as a dynamic system, with each layer's nonlinear update locally linear. Prior work used scalar sums or rough linear fits, leaving the spectral shape of trained models unknown. Training installs a steady spectral slope through depth, from rotation-heavy early layers to near-symmetric late layers. A growing low-rank choke point funnels nudges into a small share of the stream's widths.
arxiv-2605-14358: Chowdhury and Manocha measure how much of a language model's long chain-of-thought trace is actually needed to keep its answer. The minimal core is the smallest step subset preserving the answer or prediction distribution. On average, about 46 percent of steps prove removable while keeping the original answer in 86 percent of cases. Support is concentrated in the top three steps, carrying 65 percent of measured necessity. Minimal cores separate right from wrong traces better. They also transfer across model families, suggesting much trace text is verbose padding.
arxiv-2605-14458: Park and colleagues, in work published in 2026, propose OmniDrop, a layer-wise pruning framework for omni-modal models. Token explosion from audio and video bottlenecks live use and long reasoning. Existing methods prune at input on similarity proxies, which often fail. OmniDrop prunes audiovisual tokens in decoder layers, letting early layers fuse information before deeper layers remove tokens. Text queries guide task-adaptive pruning, and a diversity score balances survival. Across benchmarks, OmniDrop beats baselines by up to 3.58 points, cutting latency by 40 percent and memory use by 14.7 percent.
arxiv-2605-14558: He, Zhu, Zhou, Gu, Liu, Huang, Zou, Wipf, Yu and Wu argue that standard policy-gradient training misallocates credit in agentic reinforcement learning, where long reasoning traces surround short actions. Their energy-based analysis finds training signal concentrates on action tokens, a pattern they call the action bottleneck. Their ActFocus reweighting downweights reasoning tokens and boosts uncertain action tokens, with claimed final-step gains over PPO and GRPO across four environments.
arxiv-2605-14658: Giacchini, Kolar, Pravda and Pravdova study static spherically symmetric Kundt vacuum solutions. They work in quadratic gravity with a cosmological constant, plus six-derivative models. In quadratic gravity, all cases are found when alpha differs from three beta. The equal case is treated by the Frobenius method, which gives a power series. Curvature singularities and their reach for geodesic viewers are analysed. Exact waves on these backgrounds are built. In higher-order gravity, globally smooth waves exist with singular ones.
arxiv-2605-14758: Marzari and Marchesini propose RNN-ProVe, a probabilistic framework for verifying recurrent neural network policies. Such policies act where only part of the state is seen, and hidden state dynamics make checks hard. Existing tools lean on narrow assumptions or coarse over-approximations of hidden states. Policy-driven sampling instead maps the feasible hidden states under a trained policy. Error bounds then yield high-confidence estimates of violations. Tests on single-agent and team tasks claim stronger guarantees than rivals.
arxiv-2605-14958: Francisco M. Blanco, Eanna E. Flanagan, and Abraham I. Harte split the self-force on an object into conservative and dissipative parts, one that saves energy and one that drains it, within a nonlinear scalar toy model. Such splits agree at first order but can diverge at higher orders. Demanding that any sensible energy-saving sector be Hamiltonian, the authors identify several possible second-order definitions and derive their Hamiltonians. The results cover unbound scattering orbits only, since bound orbits bring infrared divergences.
arxiv-2605-15058: Alessio Caviglia and four others survey how spiking neural networks are trained, a field split across surrogate gradients, local and three-factor rules, brain-like plasticity, conversion pipelines, and other optimizers. They sort these methods into a fine-grained taxonomy. It groups by working principle, learning signal, and locality. With the survey they release NeuroTrain, an open snnTorch-based toolkit that runs a sample of these methods in one modular system. The goal is steady testing across datasets, model designs, and training regimes.
arxiv-2605-15158: Daniel Zhou and Erwin Frey establish a duality between chemical-potential dynamics and mass-conserving reaction-diffusion systems for patterns. Such theories sit as slow motion on an attracting manifold of such a system. Every such system with an attractive nullcline admits an exact form of that kind in the fast-switching limit. The build fixes non-invertibility of that potential in phase-splitting regimes. It yields a dictionary for phase coexistence.
arxiv-2605-15958: Bram van Duinen and three colleagues propose simulated annealing for selecting representative climate years. Energy models need representative input, but climate science uses hundreds of years while power models process a handful, and current picks lack validation. Representativeness is scored with the seasonal sliced Wasserstein distance, capturing marginals, correlations and seasonal structure. Against random search and K-Medoids clustering on three European cases with 180 climate years, annealing gives the best picks, with effective sample size four to five times larger, roughly 2.5 to 3.5 times more representative than ENTSO-E practice.
arxiv-2605-16058: Hussain and five colleagues build a shared-memory parallel version of the star-M SVD, a tensor tool that shrinks big data with optimality guarantees. Earlier code lived mostly in languages built for ease of use, not speed. Their fast implementation aims to make optimal shrinkage practical for huge scientific data sets. It should also sharpen later analysis.
arxiv-2605-16158: Bisht and Kolb propose smart target point control for Gaussian splatting, where the Gaussian count strongly affects quality and runtime. Naive caps on densification bias training, since methods hit the cap at different times. Their quota-governor preserves the standard densification window and cadence but tunes densification and opacity-culling hyperparameters to track a quadratic target trajectory. It reaches the desired count by 15,000 iterations without abrupt cutoffs, enabling fairer capacity-matched comparisons.
arxiv-2605-16658: Baldi, Farb, Javanpeykar and Stover study the moduli space of smooth complex cubic surfaces and its orbifold fundamental group. They prove the divisor subgroup, tied to nodal cubic surfaces, is characteristic, meaning the group itself remembers that divisor. From this group fact plus basic complex analysis, they deduce the space has no nontrivial biholomorphic automorphisms as a complex analytic orbifold.
arxiv-2605-16758: Mita and colleagues test whether pre-pretraining on a language inspired by the Language Acquisition Device hypothesis can close the data-efficiency gap between language models and humans. Their MP-STRUCT language encodes layered structure, feature-based links, and long-distance movement through MERGE, AGREE, and MOVE. A brief 500-step run matches strong formal-language baselines in token use and adds human-like pushback against languages with impossible structures. Useful landmarks that reduce link doubt emerge as a key driver of the effect.
arxiv-2605-17058: Vivienne Wang, Tinghuai Wang and Pajarinen tackle planning problems where choices explode in number, outcomes are random, and horizons run long. Their layered method pairs a tree-search planner with a world model that handles actions of varied length. A multi-timescale goal shapes the model's inner dynamics so lookahead matches each action's true time span, and a budget rule steers limited resources. The method tops strong baselines across hard test problems.
arxiv-2605-17258: Sazaki and colleagues track a WZ Sge-type dwarf nova catalogued as TCP J23580961+5502508, through its 2022 superoutburst with the Kanata telescope. They catch early superhumps on three straight nights, including the rise to peak. Rebuilding the accretion disk from multiband light curves reveals a flaring arm on the leading side. On day three a second arm joins on the far side, forming a two-armed pattern tied to 2:1 resonance.
arxiv-2605-17358: Jeonghyun Woo and colleagues propose PrISM, a probabilistic RowHammer defense that fixes the non-selection problem at low thresholds without per-row counters. It samples a few activation slots per window, keeps sampled-but-unmitigated rows in a history queue, and triggers extra mitigation when a sampled row reappears. At a threshold of 500 it slows memory by just 0.2 percent against 14 percent for PRAC, using only 625 bytes of SRAM per bank.
arxiv-2606-00058:
Sangal and co-authors survey the tangled ties between quantum computing and cybersecurity in this 2026 arXiv review. Quantum machines promise to solve problems beyond classical reach, yet today's noisy devices suffer decoherence, gate drift, and readout errors that hurt accuracy and may open security holes. The survey organizes the field into three parts: security problems inside quantum computers, threats they pose to others, and defenses built using quantum tech.

Coverage includes flaws in quantum hardware and software stacks, plus the danger quantum algorithms pose to current cryptography. Countermeasures reviewed include post-quantum crypto, quantum-safe communication methods, and quantum intrusion detection systems. The authors also survey quantum tools applied to malware hunting, network defense, and Internet of Things security. Error mitigation and fault tolerance receive attention as foundations for trustworthy machines. The paper closes with open challenges and future directions, offered as a reference for building quantum-ready secure systems.

arxiv-2606-04358:
Yuancheng Luo speeds up in 2026 the simulation of room acoustics by the image-source model. The model mirrors a sound source across a room's walls again and again. The mirrors build the room's impulse response.

For rectangular rooms, the count of image sources grows fast with response length. The growth caps practical work at three dimensions. Luo ties the counting to the classic Gauss circle problem, the count of lattice points inside a circle. He extends the bookkeeping to sources with frequency-dependent weights, and links dimensions through convolution. The new bound grows far more gently. Two constructions realize the responses, with time-frequency controls, error and runtime analysis, and response statistics.
arxiv-2606-04958:
Weerda, Syljuåsen, Rizzi, and Burrello hunt numerical fingerprints of an exotic superconducting phase where charge moves in fours, in a 2026 arXiv condensed matter paper. Superconductivity mediated by Cooper quartets matters for understanding exotic superconductors and for engineering quantum memories. Josephson junction arrays shaped as the dice lattice are a leading candidate platform. The authors frustrate the arrays by inserting one third of a flux quantum per rhombic plaquette and simulate Monte Carlo, and tensor networks.

They find the peaks of critical current and temperature correspond to a superconductor-insulator transition compatible with the deconfinement of half-vortices, while low-temperature correlation functions confirm the onset of quartet-mediated superconductivity. They also address Josephson energy and flux disorder. The multi-method agreement strengthens the case that dice arrays really can host quartet superconductivity.
arxiv-2606-05058:
Jingyuan Chen and colleagues introduce UniCAD in this 2026 arXiv paper, a unified benchmark and universal model for computer-aided design learning. CAD software underpins engineering and manufacturing by producing precise, editable 3D models, but research usually treats each CAD task in isolation, and no shared benchmark covered multi-modal, multi-task learning. UniCAD fills that gap.

The benchmark spans point cloud to CAD reconstruction, text and image to CAD generation, and CAD question answering across varied input types. Alongside it, UniCAD-MLLM is a single multi-modal large language model that accepts text, images, sketches, and point clouds and handles all these tasks end to end in one framework. Experiments on the UniCAD and Fusion 360 benchmarks show it reaching state-of-the-art results on every task, ahead of both task-specific and multi-task baselines. The team plans to release the dataset, code, and pretrained models.
arxiv-2606-05358:
Michael Turner and Dragan Huterer examine how the DESI results shift the locally measured Hubble constant in this 2026 arXiv paper. DESI's baryon acoustic oscillation measurements have produced evidence that dark energy evolves over time rather than staying a cosmological constant. The Hubble constant inferred from the distance ladder is analyzed under the constant-dark-energy model, and that assumption is not innocent.

If distance measurements are analyzed with the evolving-dark-energy models that DESI prefers, the Hubble constant can be as much as 2.5 kilometers per second per megaparsec smaller than the standard-model value. Constraining those models with cosmic microwave background data shrinks the shift to 1.1, and adding type Ia supernova data shrinks it to 0.5, in the same units. Local determinations depend on the background cosmology, and the low-redshift cosmology is not well constrained, so part of the discrepancy may live in the modeling rather than the measurements.
arxiv-2606-05458:
João Alves and colleagues automate the detection of eye blinks in horses in this 2026 arXiv paper, aiming at objective pain and welfare assessment. Half and full blinks are recognized indicators of pain and stress, but as micro-expressions they are easily missed by the naked eye and require frame-by-frame video inspection.

The team developed and evaluated three methods on a publicly available dataset. They are a frame-based YOLOv12 object detector, an optical-flow thresholding approach that tracks motion between frames, and a fine-tuned VideoMAE model that reads video clips directly. Their best results reached a macro-F1 score of 0.898 on the harder task of classifying blink type and 0.926 on binary blink detection. A human baseline study underlined why automation matters: even human observers agreed only 73 percent of the time on half-blink labels.
arxiv-2606-05658:
Maharjan, Kaur, and Molyet compare agent-style search pipelines on two contrasting tasks in a 2026 arXiv paper. Search-augmented generation grounds model answers in fetched documents. Standard pipelines fetch once with the raw query, which falters on tangled questions. Their framework splits queries into parts, fetches in rounds, and reflects on results within a bounded loop. Two testbeds check the design: a DevOps knowledge base and a multi-hop reasoning set.

Query splitting gave steady gains on the structured DevOps data, lifting both overall score and ranking quality. On the multi-hop benchmark the same move hurt ranking precision instead. The reflection loop improved citation accuracy but cost substantial response time. Gains in one setting became losses in the other. The authors argue for cost-aware control that turns agentic steps on only where they pay. Uniformly aggressive pipelines, they conclude, waste effort and can even backfire.
arxiv-2606-06058:
Salmani-Zarchi, Rahimi, Faili, and Dousti diagnose why a reinforcement learning method wobbles on instructions in a 2026 arXiv paper. Multi-constraint requests, exact endings, casing rules, word counts, suit verifiable rewards. Yet group-relative policy optimization destabilizes when rewards are discrete and groups score alike. The authors formalize three pathologies of z-score normalization: zero-variance collapse, mean-centering blindness, and low-variance amplification.

MDP-GRPO answers with four stabilizers. Multi-temperature sampling spreads rewards out. Dual-anchor advantages restore gradients when a group is homogeneous. Prospect-theoretic shaping, borrowed from Kahneman and Tversky, bounds updates and punishes violations asymmetrically. An asymmetric KL term completes the package. On FollowBench, IFEval, and a curated set, strict constraint satisfaction improved by up to five points on a Llama model. Training stayed stable with small groups, and abilities held on standard benchmarks. Careful advantage bookkeeping, not bigger models, fixed the instability.
arxiv-2606-06158:
Kevin Dave and co-authors present a cheaper way to compress video for machine use in this 2026 arXiv paper. Video tokenisation turns frames into tokens, compact units that later models process. Adaptive methods spend tokens where a scene changes and save them where it stays still, but many need extra decoder passes or learned estimators to decide. The authors show the needed signal is already visible inside a frozen continuous tokeniser.

Positions whose internal representation barely changes between frames carry almost no new information, so a fixed threshold on that change drops them with no learned allocation network at all. Static scenes then compress steeply while busy scenes keep more tokens, and the rate follows the content itself. A small transformer, LIT, paints the dropped positions back in from those kept. On TokenBench and DAVIS, the method matched continuous-regime rivals at equal keep rates with much lower inference cost.
arxiv-2606-06258:
Shenwei Huang, Yiao Ju, and Yidong Zhou push a famous graph conjecture to two new cases in this 2026 arXiv paper. The Erdős Hajnal conjecture says that any graph avoiding one fixed pattern as an induced subgraph must contain a large clique or independent set. A clique is a set of vertices all joined to each other, while an independent set has no edges at all. The conjecture was recently proved for the five vertex path.

They prove it for two larger patterns built from that path and from the bull graph. One adds a pendant edge to the middle of the path, forming the E graph. The other adds a pendant edge to one horn of the bull. Their proof generalizes the iterative sparsification framework behind the path result, and extends the older Chudnovsky and Safra theorem on the bull.
arxiv-2606-06458:
Alexander Möllers and co-authors teach a model to learn classification tasks from a handful of examples in this 2026 arXiv paper. Multiple instance learning trains on bags of items with only a bag level label, common in pathology slides and satellite images. Labels are scarce in exactly those fields, and ordinary models either overfit or cannot adapt. Their answer is in context learning: pretrain once, then solve new tasks in a single forward pass.

The learner, built on a Perceiver style architecture, was pretrained entirely on synthetic bag data. The team designed several data generators, each encoding a different bias about how bags relate to labels. A model trained on a mixture of the generators inherited their separate strengths. Across twelve multiple instance benchmarks in the low label regime, it achieved the best average ranking, beating supervised baselines that needed task specific training for every problem.
arxiv-2606-06658:
Bhargav Sriram Siddani and co-authors give coarse grained physics a memory in this 2026 arXiv paper. Simulating every particle in a fluid is costly. Modelers instead use stochastic equations for the density, like the Dean Kawasaki equation. Those equations are Markovian, memoryless, and Gaussian. They miss short time behavior and sparse regimes where real systems remember their recent past. The authors learn the distribution of fluxes directly from particle data with flow matching, a generative technique.

Their test case is the Kramers first passage problem, timing how long Brownian particles take to escape. The learned model captured the short time dynamics accurately. It predicted the density's statistical moments better than the Markovian baseline, including higher order statistics at early times. Predictions drift at later times, a limitation the authors state plainly.
arxiv-2606-06958:
Before birth, doctors watch the fluid spaces inside a baby's brain for dangerous swelling. Sayem automates one key measurement in this 2026 arXiv paper. The condition is fetal ventriculomegaly, enlargement of the lateral ventricle. Clinicians judge it by atrial width, measured from ultrasound images.

His network, MVSegNet, first outlines the ventricle, then estimates that width. Manual measurement varies between observers, so consistency matters. Ultrasound also fights back with shadowing, speckle, and weak contrast. The model pairs multi scale feature extraction with boundary aware refinement. It trained on five hundred eighty four expert labeled frames. Against six rival segmenters, it won on boundary and measurement scores. Its overlap score reached about eighty one percent. Width error averaged about three point four millimeters. The model is small, with about two point three million parameters, and runs very fast.
arxiv-2606-07158:
Defenders name attacker groups by their habits, but AI attackers may not keep steady habits. Francesco Balassone and a large team test that idea in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their AI agents posed as five famous state linked hacking groups, including APT28 and Lazarus. They attacked two defended test networks, one business style and one military.

A binary pattern emerged across twenty experiments. All ten enterprise attacks ended in compromise. All ten military experiments were defended or stalled, whatever the persona. In eight enterprise cases, attackers independently turned the defender's own endpoint platform into their control channel. That trick appeared in no threat intelligence profile. Yet checks against official profiles still matched the fake attack chains with fifty five to eighty percent precision. The personas mimicked state tradecraft well enough to fool attribution. If machines can wear any group's fingerprint, habit based attribution collapses.
arxiv-2606-07458:
Israeli and co-authors observe collective light emission from disordered solid-state atom arrays, against expectations, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Quantum metasurfaces made of subwavelength atomic arrays promise strong light-matter interaction for quantum devices. Solid-state emitters were thought unfit here because inhomogeneous broadening, the spread of emitters' frequencies, exceeds their natural linewidth hugely and should destroy the photon-mediated cooperation behind emission. The team used silicon-vacancy centers in diamond, whose broadening is about 100 times the natural linewidth.

Collective effects survived: resonance shifts, changed decay rates, and coherent emission all appeared. The trick was placing many silicon ions at each array site, creating superatoms, local groups where some emitters match across the array and amplify the response. Theory explains how cooperation survives the disorder. The authors argue the result opens subwavelength emitter arrays to any solid-state platform, easing use with nanophotonic devices.
arxiv-2606-07658:
Cepeda and co-authors tackle brain shift, the movement of brain tissue during surgery that makes pre-operative scans misleading, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their setting is glioma surgery, where removing as much tumour as safely possible improves survival, yet navigation maps drift once the skull is opened. Operating-room MRI can correct the drift but is rare and costly, while ultrasound is cheap and repeatable.

The pipeline turns intra-operative ultrasound into a synthetic MRI, then uses that image to anchor a deformable registration, a warping that aligns the old scan with the patient's current anatomy. In fourteen patients scored against two hundred fifteen expert landmarks, the anchored warping cut mean alignment error from about six point three millimetres to about five point nine. The real gain is the updated whole-brain volume itself, which shows the resection cavity that registration alone cannot represent.
arxiv-2606-07958:
Xin Peng and co-authors rank three candidate shapes for early-universe inflation energy, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Inflation models give the inflaton field a potential energy curve. The simplest family is monomial, rising as a power of the field: quadratic, cubic, or quartic. In cold inflation these are squeezed by the observed limit on gravitational waves. Warm inflation, where the inflaton leaks energy into radiation, relaxes that squeeze differently per power.

The team computes a Bayesian evidence score for each power. They solve the warm background equations with radiation back-reaction and integrate over the parameter ranges. With fifty-five e-folds, the quartic potential wins clearly. The quadratic branch is disfavoured by about thirty-two log-evidence units, a crushing margin, and the cubic by about seven. If low-temperature warm inflation with this dissipation law is right, the data already point strongly to the quartic shape.
arxiv-2606-08458:
Gonzalez, Shovo, and Ayub design a household robot that predicts what its human needs next, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Proactive assistance requires predicting human activities and object usage under noisy conditions. People move things, pets wander through, toddlers rearrange the home. Existing approaches often rely on complex spatio-temporal models that are expensive and sensitive to this noise. Their framework, GLOBE, instead pairs a lightweight statistical predictor with a large language model consulted only when needed.

The predictor is an n-gram Markov model, which forecasts the next activity from recent activity sequences, running efficiently on the robot. Uncertainty guides the language model's involvement. When confidence is low, the model reasons about the situation. When high, the cheap predictor acts alone. To test robustness, the authors introduce HOMER-Noise, a noisy extension of a household dataset simulating disturbances such as objects moved by humans, pets, and toddlers.
arxiv-2606-08558:
Yingcheng Li and Zou construct a universal theory of an exotic phase of matter from measurable ingredients, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Symmetry-enriched topological quantum spin liquids are phases where spins refuse to order conventionally. They form a liquid with topological order, patterns of long-range entanglement, enriched by symmetries.  The authors present exactly that: a microscopic universal theory for these phases in two spatial dimensions.

The theory is deliberately general. It covers Abelian and non-Abelian phases, chiral and non-chiral ones, internal and lattice symmetries, unitary and anti-unitary symmetries, discrete and continuous ones, with or without spin-orbit coupling. The input is concrete: microscopic states containing anyons, the exotic quasiparticles of the phase, plus operators and symmetry actions. The output is a set of data characterizing the universal properties.
arxiv-2606-08658:
Hila surveys how formal knowledge structures meet neural embeddings, and proposes a hybrid future, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Ontologies and knowledge graphs model knowledge explicitly, with named concepts and relations that support crisp logical inference, but they are brittle and hand-built. Dense embeddings, the vector representations behind large language models, capture similarity and context probabilistically but lack explicit, inspectable structure. The paper reviews the ways ontologies and knowledge graphs have been integrated with dense embedding algorithms.

Hila proposes a new frontier: knowledge representation systems that accommodate both kinds of inference in the same representation. The proposal is neuro-quantum-fuzzy systems, which combine neural learning, fuzzy logic's graded truth values, and quantum-neural networks whose contextual behavior models how meaning shifts with context. The paper is a position and survey piece, arguing that the probabilistic-crisp trade-off is a limitation of current representation choices.
arxiv-2606-08758:
Dentelski tests whether a neural quantum decoder's confidence can be trusted like a classical score, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Quantum error correction requires a decoder to infer the logical state of protected information from error syndromes. Beyond a hard decision, some decoders give soft information estimating reliability of the call. For the standard matching decoder, a common confidence measure is the complementary gap, the cost difference between the chosen correction and the best alternative. Dentelski asks whether a graph neural network decoder's output logit can serve as a learned proxy for that gap.

Using a pretrained graph network for the rotated surface code under circuit-level noise, the study compares the network's output with the matching decoder's gap. Post-selection on the network's confidence yields a lower logical error rate than post-selection on the classical gap here. The network assigns higher confidence to many correctly decoded shots.
arxiv-2606-09158:
Junnila, Laihonen, Lehtilä, and Padavu Devaraj count exactly how many strings lie in several error balls at once, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A Hamming ball collects strings within a set number of substitutions of a center, over an alphabet of size q. Intersecting balls matters for DNA data storage and the Levenshtein reconstruction problem, recovering a stored string from noisy copies. Center distances alone were known not to determine the size.

They derive an exact formula for the intersection size of any number of Hamming balls, any radii. It reveals which center properties determine the size. Asymptotics for long strings follow. For 3 balls they give necessary and sufficient conditions, every alphabet size at least 2 except 6, long strings, for the maximum intersection size at a given minimum center distance. The maximum is computable from the formula. The q equals 6 exception is a real arithmetic obstruction: the 3-ball characterization is complete.
arxiv-2606-09558:
Mikele Milia and his co-authors build known gene regulation into a Transformer model for single-cell data in this 2026 arXiv paper. Single-cell RNA sequencing records which genes are active in each cell. Most models treat genes as lone features, so the model must learn all links from data alone. Known biology says which regulator genes switch which target genes on or off.

Their model, scTransformer, limits attention flow to paths that match those known links. Attention is the step where the model weighs links between features. The team tested it on disease-linked single-nucleus data, sorting cells by type. Accuracy reached about ninety-one percent, close to the ninety-two percent of a free-form model. With just one percent of the training data, the guided model won clearly. Its chosen gene sets also stayed far more stable across repeat runs.
arxiv-2606-09658:
Tianyu Ruan and his co-authors ask whether the Muon optimizer teaches models better internal features than Adam in this 2026 arXiv paper. Optimizers steer training by setting each update step. Muon, which reshapes gradient matrices, trains big models fast. Its speed edge is known, but whether its features are better was not.

The team tested models trained each way on bent inputs: smudged images and warped text. Muon-trained models held up best across image nets and transformers alike. Probes on each layer showed wider logit margins, a sign of firmer class splits. When the features were reused on fresh tasks, Muon again won, by direct transfer and by full fine-tuning. Hidden states from Muon models also spanned more directions, a trait called effective rank. A toy proof in a clean setting backs both edges.
arxiv-2606-09758:
Quinn Pfeifer and his co-authors fix a weak spot of learning by copying, without new data or expert help in this 2026 arXiv paper. Behavior cloning trains a robot policy on expert demos, then drops the data at run time. Small slips then pile up, pushing the robot into states the demos never showed. Their DARP method keeps the data in play.

At each step, DARP fetches the nearest demo states to the live one. It feeds the model those states, their actions, and the gap vectors between them and the live state. The policy thus reads local structure, not a blunt global map. No fresh demos, feedback, or task tricks are needed. Gains over plain cloning ran from fifteen to forty-six percent. The wins spanned control tasks and arm work, and held for rich image inputs as well.
arxiv-2606-10158:
Balloli and colleagues explore what different stakeholders need before trusting AI tools for pregnancy-related information, in a 2026 arXiv paper on human-computer interaction and health. AI systems increasingly promise to fill information gaps in maternal health, where timely, accurate guidance matters and preventable deaths show stark racial disparities in the United States. The study centers those social questions instead.

The team ran four synchronous focus groups with twenty-four participants spanning birthing people, clinicians, and health workers such as doulas, social workers, and community health workers. Discussions covered information seeking, experiences with current clinical infrastructure, misinformation, and reactions to an AI factual answering tool used as a design probe. The title question, asking where an answer comes from, captures the trustworthiness ideals participants voiced. Findings aim to guide AI peripartum tools that respect how trust is actually built among the groups who support pregnancy care.
arxiv-2606-10258:
Wang and his team extend a background-removal technique so researchers can test whether tiny collision systems create quark-gluon plasma, in a 2026 arXiv paper on nuclear physics. In particle correlations, collective flow signals the plasma, while nonflow, links from other sources, contaminate the signal. Their method extends the subtraction to multi-particle cumulants, built on how nonflow scales with multiplicity in a many-source picture.

Correlators with the dipolar flow component serve as clean nonflow estimators, since its total value nearly vanishes. Using a nonflow-only test setting as ground truth, they test the subtraction on three targets in oxygen-oxygen and deuteron-gold collisions at two energies. Most nonflow is removed, with residual fractions usually within twenty to thirty percent when mapped to the two-particle level, though the best measure differs by target. The method pushes genuine collectivity tests into the smallest collision systems.
arxiv-2606-10458:
Xu studies a design question in signal processing in this 2026 arXiv paper: how should a quantizer be built when its output must follow a distribution chosen in advance? Quantization squeezes a continuous value into one of a few allowed labels, how signals are stored and sent digitally. Designers usually only minimise distortion, the average error between a value and its label. Here the labels must also appear with specified frequencies, for compression, channels, and privacy.

Xu derives the optimal quantizer and shows it has an explicit form built from cumulative distribution functions, curves tracking how probability accumulates. The best labelling is found by choosing a permutation of the output labels, and the proof leans on majorization, a way of comparing how spread out distributions are. When either the input or the required output is uniform, the optimal rule simplifies to one direct mapping, a closed answer where search is usual.
arxiv-2606-10758:
Cristian-Teodor Neamtu and colleagues trace synthetic speech back to its maker in this 2026 arXiv paper on audio forensics. Detecting fake audio is half the forensic problem; investigators want to know which text-to-speech system made it, including systems never seen in training. The framework learns an embedding space with proxy-anchor metric learning over Wav2Vec2-BERT representations, so samples from one system cluster tightly while unknown systems fall away from every cluster. An architecture-merging step groups system versions into unified classes, cutting confusion between near-identical generators.

On the MLAAD v9 benchmark, spanning 140 systems in 51 languages, attribution accuracy reaches 99.76 percent across 110 classes, and unknown systems are flagged with a false positive rate of 2.04 percent. On the MLAAD v5 splits it doubles the best prior out-of-distribution accuracy and cuts the false alarm rate. Well-clustered embeddings serve attribution and rejection at once.
arxiv-2606-10858:
Fjeldstad, Bueie, and de Wijn rework kinetic theory for dense fluids in this 2026 arXiv paper. Chapman-Enskog theory predicts transport properties such as shear viscosity, but its extensions lean on effective hard-sphere diameters that fit poorly for soft, long-range forces. The authors build a framework around an exchange function tied to the fluid's thermodynamics, and show two existing extensions fit inside it.

Their alternative adds the potential interaction energy that modified Enskog theory omits. Tested on simulated Weeks-Chandler-Anderson and Lennard-Jones fluids across wide density and temperature ranges, mean prediction errors stay between 2 and 4 percent at low and middle densities. The worst cases reach 4.4 percent and 8.1 percent for the two fluids.
arxiv-2606-10958:
Khalatbari investigates the hidden life of graphics cards in this 2026 arXiv paper. Over four years the author combined social science with hands-on research-creation: dismantling, dissolving, rebuilding, and remixing some fifty acquired graphics cards. Fieldwork reached liquid-nitrogen overclockers in Taiwan and urban miners in Ghana, two ends of the same device's world.

Miniaturization, the paper argues, is what lets AI look abstract and placeless, hiding rare metals, assembly labor, and the communities that inherit the waste. Taking cards apart made those material ties tangible in ways reading could not. The work presents making itself as a rigorous way of knowing, aimed at ICT sustainability.
arxiv-2606-11358:
Pandit and Koranga expose a hidden systematic error in neutrino physics in a 2026 arXiv paper. Long-baseline analyses often treat Earth matter effects with a constant-density approximation. Using exact propagation through realistic PREM density profiles, they show this mismodeling does not merely shift the standard appearance probability. It generates correlated biases across all oscillation channels at once, as PMNS unitarity dictates.

Their stochastic analysis finds the muon-to-tau neutrino channel is the most volatile carrier of the geophysical error. At baselines like 5,000 and 7,000 kilometers, the tau channel always carries larger mean bias and variance than the electron appearance channel. Below roughly 4,000 kilometers the CP bias is negligible, under one degree, but grows sharply beyond. A multi-channel joint fit does not help, since the coherent errors favor the same wrong CP minimum. They conclude spatially resolved density treatments are a necessity for future precision facilities.
arxiv-2606-11858:
Yiwen Zhang and four colleagues speed up control of virtually coupled trains in this 2026 arXiv paper. Virtual coupling lets trains run close together, coordinated by radio rather than physical links, raising line capacity. The controller must track a target speed profile while respecting comfort limits and guaranteeing no collisions, all in real time, which makes ordinary predictive control expensive.

Their approach lifts the curved train dynamics into a Koopman space, a transformed space where the dynamics become nearly linear, using closed-form observable functions. Freezing the lifted predictor along the predicted path turns each control step into a quadratic program, a fast standard problem. Safety terms involving squared speed are lifted along with the dynamics. In a simulated two-train metro scenario, the desired gap is nine metres on a line just over two kilometres long. There the method matches a conventional controller's tracking while cutting online computation time substantially.
arxiv-2606-11958:
Di Yang, Jiayi Zhao and Jian Zhou revisit classical formulas for random matrices in this 2026 arXiv paper. Hermitian matrix models are a backbone of random matrix theory, used from nuclear physics to combinatorics. Their connected correlation functions, which describe how eigenvalues at several points fluctuate together, admit determinantal formulas built from a kernel. The authors give a direct proof of those determinantal formulas for connected multi-point functions.

They also supply a new proof that these functions are integrable in the sense of the KP hierarchy. From that viewpoint they re-derive the explicit formula for the affine coordinates encoding the model. Duality for certain hermitian matrix models is proved as well. A concrete dividend appears in the examples: generating functions match classical path-counting sequences, including Dyck, Motzkin and Schröder paths and Catalan numbers. Conjectures in earlier literature about those identifications are now theorems.
arxiv-2606-12058:
Itay Lavie leads a six-author team explaining why attention circuits appear suddenly during training in this 2026 arXiv paper. Induction heads, the transformer circuits that copy patterns from context, underpin in-context learning, and their key component emerges abruptly. The authors build a Bayesian theory of this feature learning.

They study a single-layer softmax attention network trained on a copy task and derive a closed-form posterior over the attention matrix. Reducing it to a low-dimensional order parameter space reveals a genuine phase transition in the amount of training data. Both Bayesian sampling and standard training with the Adam optimiser confirm the transition. The comparison with linear attention is sharp. Softmax attention shows a first-order transition, an abrupt jump, while linear attention crosses a second-order transition and then evolves smoothly. The work gives a first-principles account of abrupt circuit emergence in language models.
arxiv-2606-12158:
