He also had mild intellectual disability and a similarly tall younger brother. Gene sequencing found a stop-making variant in GPC3, confirming Simpson-Golabi-Behmel syndrome, with his mother a carrier. The authors urge clinicians to consider overgrowth syndromes behind acromegaloid features.
pmc-13218158:
Helga Birgit Bjørnarå, Gerd Monika Flodgren, and Arnfinn Helleve describe a 2026 protocol for a scoping review of policy monitoring indexes for non-communicable diseases. Proven, affordable policy actions against these diseases exist, such as the World Health Organization's Best Buys, but governments need ways to track whether the policies are being put in place. Several composite indexes have been built for that monitoring job.

The review will search eight databases for work published from 2013 onward, in any language, plus grey literature and reference lists. Eligible studies must describe a composite index that monitors implementation of government policies aimed at non-communicable diseases or their risk factors, within the World Health Organization's European region. Screening and data extraction will proceed in duplicate, and results will be summarized with descriptive statistics and visuals. The review sits inside the Joint Action PreventNCD project, a European Commission-funded effort across 25 countries.
pmc-13219158:
Kyle Tuohy and colleagues search for pre-treatment clues to who will suffer brain and hormone damage after radiation in a 2026 cohort study. Radiation remains central to treating primary and metastatic brain tumors, but thinking problems and hormone failure can surface afterward, and doctors cannot forecast them. Better prediction would let clinicians warn patients and design preventive studies.

Eighty patients treated at one institution with radiation as part of tumor therapy were assessed across five toxicity measures, with change on a mental status exam as the main outcome. Two findings stood out in adjusted models as the strongest predictors of decline: elevated homocysteine, an amino acid linked to vascular injury, and carrying the ApoE4 variant, tied to Alzheimer's risk. Homocysteine tracked with white matter change on MRI, and ApoE4 with new hormone deficiencies. The team built a nomogram estimating patient risk across all five outcomes and calls for validation.
pmc-13219958:
Jelle P. van der List and colleagues isolate the outcomes of restorative treatment for kneecap lesions in a 2026 review and meta-analysis. Cartilage damage on the patella causes disability, but reviews mixed it with damage to the groove it slides in, blurring the results. It admitted only studies of isolated lesions, with at least ten patients and a year of follow-up.

Thirty-six studies covering 1,058 patients, average age thirty-two and follow-up over five years, met the bar. Implantation was the commonest operation, then osteochondral autograft transfer, then a scaffold, AMIC. Failure risk ran lowest for the autograft at 1.7 percent, with the two near nine percent, though the autograft also treated the smallest lesions. Scores favored the autograft and scaffold on scales. When the analysis was restricted to lesions under three and a half square centimeters, failure rates equalized across three, a nuance they emphasize for planning.
pmc-13222558:
Yan Zhao and co-authors survey nanoparticle drug delivery systems for cancer treatment, in a 2026 review. Most cancer drugs poison the whole body while chasing tumors, and metastasis drives most cancer deaths. Carriers covered range from metal particles to liposomes and polymer micelles, including products already approved for patients.

Loading drugs into nanoparticles can dissolve stubborn compounds, keep them circulating longer, and steer them toward tumors. Those traits promise stronger effect with less collateral toxicity. The review explains carrier composition, targeting strategies reaching even subcellular compartments, and approved examples. The authors present the field as the future direction for tumor therapy and a base for faster clinical translation.
pmc-13223658:
Bill Berners-Lee and co-authors explore why eating the DASH way is hard on Montserrat, in a 2026 interview study of sixteen adults with hypertension. The diet, rich in produce, whole grains, and pulses and low in salt and fatty meats, is promoted in local primary care. Interviews held in mid-2025 ran through a behavior lens to sort the obstacles.

Five themes shaped adherence: understanding of hypertension and the diet, access to healthy food, skills and confidence, cultural practices, and readiness to change. Cost, availability, and seasonality of fruit, vegetables, and fish bit hardest. Cooking and growing skills helped, while label reading lagged. Suggested fixes included nutrition education and financial support.
pmc-13224758:
Joud S Makki and colleagues survey a 2026 cross-sectional study of pregnant women in Saudi Arabia about the Tdap vaccine, which guards mothers and newborns against tetanus, diphtheria, and whooping cough. Uptake in pregnancy there remains low, at roughly a quarter to a third of women. Questionnaires from 398 women aged eighteen to forty mapped what they knew and felt.

Knowledge showed wide gaps: only about a third correctly identified whooping cough as highly contagious yet vaccine-preventable, and fewer still recognised its danger to newborns. Higher education tracked with better knowledge. Most women held positive views of vaccination overall, but about seventy-one percent worried about side effects, pointing to safety-focused education as the lever most likely to raise uptake.
pmc-13225158:
Ziwei Huang and colleagues run a 2026 questionnaire study of orthodontic patients who wear removable braces, asking whether believing masks hide unattractive appliances changes how faithfully patients wear them. The survey covered 214 patients, mostly women aged nineteen to thirty, and recorded recommended versus actual wear time, split between daytime and total hours.

Just over half agreed that masks made unaesthetic appliances easier to accept. Surprisingly, holding that belief came with lower daytime and overall compliance. Patients with neutral feelings about masks wore their appliances more during the day than those with strong views either way. Daytime wear strongly predicted total compliance, and men reported more mask-related acceptance than women.
pmc-13229358:
Winsy Wing Sze Wong and colleagues set out a 2026 trial protocol testing whether immersive virtual reality strengthens a computerised speech therapy for Cantonese speakers living with chronic aphasia after stroke. Script training has patients rehearse personalised everyday dialogues, and about a fifth of stroke survivors face lasting language difficulty. The trial will recruit 120 participants into three groups.

One group will practise scripts inside virtual scenes of daily life, a second will use the same training with still photographs, and a third will receive no training. Assessors who do not know group assignments will score aphasia severity, functional communication, and quality of life before and after. The comparison isolates what immersion itself adds to an established therapy format.
pmc-13229458:
Bianca Thakkar and colleagues describe in 2026 a sixty-one-year-old woman with neurofibromatosis type 1 who had several small bowel tumors at once. Scans showed multiple masses in the jejunum plus a separate lesion near the duodenum. Such stromal tumors in this condition often appear in many places and respond poorly to drug therapy.

Surgeons removed thirty-three centimeters of jejunum that held three masses felt by hand, and testing found four stromal tumors in total. Care continued for the duodenal lesion, which proved to be a neuroendocrine tumor alongside the stromal tumors. The pairing is described as exceptionally uncommon. Careful mapping of each lesion before surgery helped the team choose how much bowel to remove.
pmc-13231158:
Zeynep Yagmur Yilmaz and Raihan El-Naas report in 2026 a teenager whose overactive thyroid came from eating raw cow thyroid bought online. The nineteen-year-old showed the classic lab pattern of too much thyroid hormone paired with a suppressed control hormone. Antibody tests were negative and the gland looked normal on ultrasound, which pointed away from usual causes.

Supportive care alone settled the illness, and hormone levels fell steadily during the hospital stay. A careful history about diet, supplements, and online health trends proved central to solving the case. Unusual sources like animal organs can hide behind a common hormone picture. Clinicians who ask early about such products may spare patients needless scans and wrong long-term treatment.
pmc-13231558:
Josephine T V Greenbrook and colleagues explore in 2026 how senior doctors keep patients visible as persons while teaching juniors. Hospital work prizes speed and measured output, which can push the human side of care out of view. Seventeen physicians at two Swedish university hospitals gave long interviews about supervising students and trainees.

Supervisors described making personhood a named part of clinical reasoning, not a soft extra. They modeled humility inside steep hierarchies and defended humane values against organizational pressure. Keeping their own ethical focus took steady inner work, fresh reminders, and energy drawn from contact with patients and learners. Teaching renewed their own commitments in return, so formation flowed both ways.
pmc-13232558:
Nicole Novaresi and colleagues target in 2026 a surface protein that helps KRAS-driven lung cancers grow and hide. The protein PCDH7 appears at high levels in lung adenocarcinoma and tracks with poor outcomes for patients. Removing it in mouse models shrank tumors and extended survival, marking it as a drug target.

Antibodies built against the protein blocked a key growth pathway inside tumor cells and slowed tumors across several models. One lead antibody made tumors respond better to two approved pathway drugs given alongside it. A human-ready version also helped immune cells kill tumor cells directly. Treated tumors drew in more active killer immune cells, which strengthened the overall attack.
pmc-13232758:
Mohamed Sarsari and colleagues recount in 2026 a rescue where a heart stent poking far into the aorta was pulled back out with a snare. A sixty-year-old man with diabetes arrived with a heart attack pattern from a tight narrowing at the very start of the left main artery. During the emergency procedure, patient movement pushed the fresh stent too far out, and balloon work bent it.

Leaving the metal jutting out risked clots, loose debris, and valve trouble, so the team chose removal while the stent was still fresh. A loop snare caught and extracted it cleanly, and a new stent was placed in the ideal spot. He recovered without complications, a rare bail-out that worked because it happened early.
pmc-13232858:
Sunny L Jardine and colleagues test in 2026 whether the simple rules managers use to pick fish-passage projects waste restoration money. Agencies often rank barriers by how much upstream habitat they block, sometimes weighting habitat quality by nearby natural land. Western Washington salmon rivers served as the case, with rule-based picks benchmarked against fully optimized portfolios.

Judged on habitat quantity alone, the plain upstream-habitat rule captured nearly all the gain an optimizer could reach. Adding the popular natural-cover quality proxy cut performance almost in half, because it steered picks away from connected habitat. Better rules would score quality in ways tied to actual fish gains. With billions flowing into river repair, rule design is money design.
pmc-13233658:
Lauren Cunniff and Johannes Weickenmeier published a 2026 imaging study on how the brain's fluid-filled ventricles change shape with age. Ventricles enlarge steadily in normal ageing and faster in Alzheimer's disease, yet the mechanical strain this places on surrounding tissue is barely understood. Using Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative scans, the team followed fifty cognitively normal adults aged seventy to seventy-five across four to five years.

Image registration measured how each person's ventricles deformed between scans. Expansion was mostly uniform, averaging just under a millimeter of outward movement, yet strain concentrated sharply along the ventricle edges and the rear chamber called the atrium. About twenty-nine percent of the wall stretched while only a small share shrank, and no sex differences appeared. The maps show where ageing brains bear the greatest mechanical load.
pmc-13233758:
Liisa Hakaste and colleagues published a 2026 pooled analysis tracing metabolic changes in the years before diabetes appears. Adult-onset diabetes splits into subgroups with different causes, from autoimmune and insulin-deficient forms to insulin-resistant, obesity-related, and age-related types. Nine European cohorts contributed 3,309 people who later developed diabetes and 13,963 matched controls, with measurements grouped into three windows before diagnosis.

The subgroups already differed more than a decade ahead. The obesity-related group carried body mass far above controls early and stayed there, while weight climbed progressively in the insulin-resistant group. Insulin responses to glucose also split the groups, running high in insulin-resistant and obesity-related cases but low in insulin-deficient and age-related ones. Even the autoimmune group showed metabolic syndrome features. The findings suggest prevention could start earlier and differ by subgroup.
pmc-13233958:
Chen Wu and colleagues published a 2026 engineering review of silicon carbide pressure sensors built for extreme heat. Jets, geothermal wells, nuclear plants, and even Venus probes need pressure readings where ordinary silicon sensors fail through electrical leakage or warping. Silicon carbide, a wide-bandgap semiconductor, resists heat, radiation, and corrosion, making it the leading replacement material.

The review traces how these heat-proof pressure sensors have evolved. It then walks through the craft of building them from this stubborn stock: chip layout, making the parts, contacts that survive heat, packaging, and strength testing. Laboratory prototypes still fall short on operating temperature range, sensitivity, and long-term stability. The authors close by mapping the technical problems that must be solved before such sensors move from prototypes into routine extreme-environment service.
pmc-13234258:
Haifang Mao and co-authors reported in 2026 on tiny capsules designed to protect citronellal, a fragrant plant compound with antibacterial action. The capsules were built from black bean protein and gum Arabic joined through a process called complex coacervation. Strawberries were the test fruit, because they spoil quickly from microbes, water loss, and softening. The team searched for the best ingredient ratio and acidity for forming the capsules.

A ratio of four to one worked best under mildly acidic conditions, and the capsules trapped the compound efficiently. Encapsulated citronellal stayed more stable during storage and heat, then released slowly over time. Treated strawberries resisted spoilage microbes better and lost less weight and firmness. The findings support plant-based capsules as a preservation aid for delicate fruit.
pmc-13234458:
Haozhou Shen and co-authors reviewed in 2026 tools for measuring frailty before and around surgery. Frailty means reduced physical reserve across body systems, and it raises the risk of complications, slow recovery, and death. Older surgical patients are increasingly likely to be frail, yet standard preoperative checks often miss the condition. The review covered recent advances from 2019 to 2025 plus older foundational studies.

Different tools are compared for how well they predict outcomes and how practical they are in clinics. Strengths, limits, and fit within enhanced recovery pathways receive close attention. The authors note problems with timing, standardization, and adaptation to surgical settings. Their aim is to help clinicians choose a tool and interpret its result for a given patient. Better selection could support safer anaesthesia and recovery planning.
pmc-13235658:
Daina Baublyte and colleagues built in 2026 machine learning models to flag people at risk of gut and digestive organ cancers in South Korea. Cancers were rare in their long-followed cohort, which makes prediction models favour the healthy majority. Their new undersampling method trims the majority class while preserving the population's structure, mimicking matched study designs. Several common resampling tricks served as comparisons across six classifier types.

Only about two percent of more than seven thousand cohort members developed these cancers over fourteen years. Models trained with the new sampling method showed better sensitivity, especially among more complex classifiers. The best model caught roughly three quarters of future cases in the test group. Simpler logistic regression performed in a balanced way even without any resampling in their results. The authors used behavioural and metabolic predictors that patients can plausibly change.
pmc-13236658:
Sayna Norouzi and co-authors interviewed in 2026 doctors, patients, and caregivers across six countries about two rare progressive kidney diseases. Twenty-one clinicians, thirteen patients, and eight caregivers shared experiences of diagnosis, burden, and management between mid-2024 and early 2025. Mild early symptoms often delayed recognition of the diseases in patient accounts. Specialists also cited poor disease awareness and reluctance toward kidney biopsy as barriers.

Exhaustion and deep fatigue ranked as the most burdensome symptoms for patients and caregivers alike. Keeping the disease stable was the treatment goal patients named most often in interviews. Available options at the time were limited, and dialysis weighed mainly heavily on daily life. Caregivers described heavy physical and emotional support roles that strained their own mental wellbeing. Clinicians expressed hope about new drugs then approaching approval for these conditions.
pmc-13236758:
Sergio N. Galarce and colleagues published a modeling study in 2026 on how animals tell familiar objects from new ones. Their work uses Allan Wagner's Standard Operating Procedures model, called SOP, which explains recognition through priming. A primed stimulus draws less exploration because its mental representation is already active.

The authors built a numerical version of SOP and simulated three standard tasks: spontaneous object recognition, relative recency, and object-in-place. The simulations matched the usual preferences for new, earlier-seen, and moved objects. The paper also suggests new experiments that vary spacing, location, and distraction. Such tests could help separate memory effects that come from the object itself from effects carried by context.
pmc-13237258:
Zhaoyi Lu and co-authors applied Mendelian randomization in 2026 to ask whether gut microbes causally change the risk of head and neck cancer. Observational links between gut composition and cancers outside the gut are easy to confound, so the team used inherited gene variants tied to microbe levels as instruments. Public genome-wide study data supplied both sides of the analysis.

Sixteen candidate links appeared at first pass, and ten survived sensitivity checks for bias and consistency. The surviving signals covered two bacterial classes and a list of families and genera, some raising risk and others lowering it. Direction tests supported the assumed causal arrow. The authors propose gut composition as a source of biomarkers for prevention and treatment strategies, pending confirmation.
pmc-13238258:
Cian P. Murray and co-authors pooled ten studies covering more than 270,000 people in a 2026 meta-analysis of artificial intelligence applied to electrocardiograms for detecting heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. This stiff-heart form of failure accounts for about half of all heart failure and is notoriously hard to confirm. Seven studies supplied enough data for the main pooling.

The combined discrimination score was 0.84, a good level, though the studies disagreed with each other almost completely. Most evidence was retrospective, reference standards varied, and several studies carried moderate to high bias risk. No prospective study has yet shown that AI heart tracings improve patient outcomes. The authors see promise, but call real-world testing the missing step.
pmc-13238358:
Antigona Aliu and colleagues presented a German-language case series in 2026 of ten adults with dermatomyositis, an inflammatory muscle disease, marked by striking violet-red swelling around the eyes. Adult dermatomyositis can be driven by a hidden cancer, especially when certain antibodies are present. The team checked how often the dramatic eye sign coincided with malignancy in their patients.

In nine of the ten cases, work-up confirmed an underlying cancer. Drawing on their cases plus published markers and clinical features, the authors propose a simple criteria list to judge whether a patient's dermatomyositis is likely cancer-linked. They argue the eye sign should trigger a careful cancer search. The series is small, so the list is offered as practical guidance rather than proof.
pmc-13239058:
Jordan S. Nunnelee and colleagues reported in 2026 a previously healthy 34-year-old woman whose paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria announced itself through clots inside both sides of her heart. She arrived with right-sided chest pain three weeks after a viral illness, and blood tests showed anemia, low platelets, and intense red cell destruction. Imaging found a large clot in her left ventricle, and heart MRI suggested inflamed heart tissue plus a second clot on the right.

Flow cytometry confirmed the diagnosis: large shares of her blood cells lacked the protective proteins this disorder strips away. Urgent vaccination, the complement-blocking drug eculizumab, and preventive antibiotics followed, alongside anticoagulation. Later imaging showed the clots nearly gone and blood values normalized. The authors call it the first such intracardiac presentation in a healthy new patient and urge early recognition.
pmc-13240358:
Edita Islami and colleagues profile cell recycling markers in fat tissue across weight and sugar conditions in a 2026 study. Autophagy, the process that clears worn cell parts, has been reported both raised and lowered in obesity, and the team measured seven of its markers to find a consistent pattern.

Fat from forty patients with severe obesity differed from lean controls, with some markers reduced and others increased rather than a single direction. One marker also ran lower in the deeper belly fat and in patients who had type 2 diabetes. In cultured fat cells, markers shifted with cell maturation, insulin, glucose level, and the diabetes drug metformin, helping explain earlier contradictions.
pmc-13240558:
Alexis L. Levengood and co-authors publish a 2026 methods comparison for preserving fecal DNA from wildlife. Their test material came from fresh koala droppings. Good preservation matters because field samples often travel far before lab work begins.

Seven storage approaches were tested for how much genetic data went missing during targeted sequencing. Every method yielded usable DNA. A lysis buffer method with a washing step performed best, nearly matching results from high-quality tissue samples. The authors argue that careful field handling protects later analysis. Their optimized approach can support population studies, conservation genetics, and wildlife management decisions that depend on samples collected without handling animals.
pmc-13241458:
Kim at Bonn tackles the counting rules behind Whittaker functionals for the general linear group. These functionals anchor the wave analysis of principal series representations. Kim supplies a plain formula for a two-way map on each Schubert cell. Matrix splittings grow markedly simpler under the new map.

Using it yields a fresh proof that Whittaker functionals exist for principal series of real groups. Step-by-step integrating does the heavy lifting. This first part proves the map's counting traits and helper lemmas. The groundwork is laid plainly for the sequel's group-theory arguments.
pmc-13241658:
Tom G Jacobs and co-authors report a 2026 comparison of large language models reading handwritten medication lists. Handwritten bedside lists remain common, especially where resources are limited. Reading them wrongly can cause medication errors.

Volunteers handwrote a standard list of ten medicines with dosing instructions, in Dutch. Three GPT-based models transcribed the lists, and scoring covered drug name, dose, frequency, and route. The largest model scored highest, and accuracy rose with human-rated legibility. Printed writing and blue ink were easier for the models than cursive writing and black ink. Complex dosing instructions caused the most errors. The authors see promise for digitization, provided a human still checks the output.
pmc-13241758:
Michal Ziga and co-authors report a 2026 prospective study of epidural steroid injections for sciatica from worn lumbar discs. Patients often must choose between injections and surgery, yet objective measures of injection benefit are scarce. The team tracked pain and walking capacity with a phone-based test.

Forty-five patients were assessed before injection and at one day, one week, and one month after. Walking distance rose sharply by the first day and then held steady. Pain scores improved along a similar path. Reaching a meaningful improvement within the first week predicted success at one month very reliably. The authors recommend the short walking test as an early, objective check on whether the injection worked.
pmc-13241958:
Vargas-Fernández and Hernández-Vásquez in Lima give Peru its first national portrait of teenage vaping. The 2024 national school survey covered over forty-five thousand urban secondary students. Ever use, recent use, current use, and dual use with cigarettes were weighted. Access routes and motivations for use were tallied too.

Sixteen percent had tried e-cigarettes; about seven percent currently used them. Girls started earlier than boys and reported higher ever use. Corner stores sold to nearly a third of users despite regulations. Flavor led the stated motivations, ahead of curiosity and stress relief.
pmc-13242358:
Cronin's team across four lands built a reflection framework for nurses crossing menopause. It collides with care loads, shifting family roles, and workplace demands. Many women describe feeling alone and threats to who they are. The team blended known thoughtful practice models with studies of the change.

Their MIRROR Cycle packages diaries, reflective guidance, Schwartz rounds, structured debriefs, and calm focus. Stigma, silence, split services, and workplace ageism compound distress in the change. Placing this practice in schools, clinics, and policy may help nurses cope and stay. The goal is workplaces that understand the change, not private silent struggle.
pmc-13242758:
Yang-Chuan Chen and co-authors publish a 2026 population study from Taiwan comparing two anthracycline drugs in early breast cancer. These drugs anchor chemotherapy after surgery but can damage the heart over time. The liposome-wrapped form of doxorubicin was compared with epirubicin using national insurance records.

Matching produced two balanced groups of patients with hormone-insensitive, early-stage disease. The wrapped drug group lived longer overall, with benefits visible at three years, five years, and across full follow-up. Higher cumulative dose tracked with stronger benefit. Disease-free survival and diagnosed heart events did not differ significantly. The authors suggest the wrapped form as a favorable option, particularly for patients with heart risk factors.
pmc-13242858:
Lin Wang and a large team publish a 2026 mouse study of cornuside, a natural compound from a traditional medicinal fruit, in acute liver failure. The failure model combines a bacterial toxin with a sugar that sensitizes the liver. Timing mattered: the compound was given either before or after the injury challenge.

Treatment after injury gave no meaningful protection. Pretreatment, in contrast, sharply lowered liver enzyme leakage, tissue damage, and liver cell death. Immune activation inside the liver calmed, inflammatory signals fell, and oxidative stress eased. The compound also shifted markers of ferroptosis, an iron-driven cell death route, in a protective direction. The authors position cornuside as a preventive candidate rather than a rescue treatment.
pmc-13243358:
Yusuf Mohamed Salad and co-authors frame consent delays in emergency birth care as a safety event in a 2026 commentary from Somalia. When a mother needs urgent escalation, family doubt or refusal can stall care while her condition worsens. The authors treat that stall as a governance problem, not just a hard conversation.

They propose a clear definition for when consent delay counts as a sentinel event that demands review. Their framework calls for fast recognition of disputed consent, set steps for escalation, and careful records. Lawful emergency action stays allowed when delay risks grave harm. Folding these cases into near-miss reviews could make a hidden source of harm visible and fixable.
pmc-13243758:
Ruonan Li and colleagues asked whether body weight predicts the headache that can follow a lumbar puncture. Their cross-sectional study appeared in the Journal of International Medical Research in 2026. They reviewed 499 Chinese adults who had the procedure in a neurology department between 2022 and 2024. Sixty-five patients, about one in eight, developed the characteristic headache, and nearly two-thirds of them were women.

Those with headaches were younger and, on average, leaner than those without. They also ran lower blood pressure and lower spinal fluid protein, and had more fluid withdrawn. Statistical models confirmed that lower body mass index raised the odds of headache on its own. The link held steady across sex, age, and fluid subgroups. The authors advise weighing body mass in risk checks before the procedure and in care afterward. A cross-sectional snapshot cannot prove cause, they note.
pmc-13245058:
Felix Jimenez-Rondan, Courtney Ruggiero, Robert Cousins, and co-authors trace how losing a zinc transporter floods the mouse gut with mucus and a mucus-eating microbe. Their study appeared in Gut Microbes in 2026. Zip14 normally rises during inflammation and pulls zinc into gut lining cells. Mice lacking it entirely accumulated excess intestinal mucus and excreted strikingly more Akkermansia muciniphila, a bacterium that feeds on mucus.

Gene and chromatin studies explained why. Two mucus-building genes, including the main mucin Muc2, were switched up because their DNA sat in an open, readable state tied to the inflammatory factor NF-κB. The whole picture proved reversible. Either pasteurized Akkermansia or a single zinc feeding calmed the microbe surge, the inflammation, and the mucus genes. The authors conclude that zinc delivery through Zip14 keeps mucus production in check. The work ties a metal transporter to the gut's microbial balance.
pmc-13245558:
Emma Braun and Amanda Proch examine health literacy in Delaware community health needs assessments in a 2026 article. Health literacy means being able to find, grasp, and use health information for sound choices. It shapes outcomes and fairness, so hospitals are starting to measure it.

Every Delaware system now folds some literacy check into its needs assessment. None yet uses the standard questions the state literacy council advises, so results vary in form. Residents with social disadvantage still struggle most with health information, owing to schooling, language, and culture gaps. The authors call wider use of shared questions the next step toward statewide action.
pmc-13248058:
Lin, Song, and Li updated the evidence on high-flow nasal oxygen after surgery in this 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Patients recovering from anesthesia often run low on oxygen, and high-flow nasal cannula, warm, fast oxygen through nasal prongs, is widely used, but earlier reviews disagreed on whether it prevents reintubation. The team pooled twenty-five randomized trials with over four thousand patients comparing it against conventional oxygen therapy.

Reintubation rates did not differ significantly overall. The high-flow approach did cut lung collapse and low-oxygen episodes clearly. Certainty of the evidence was graded low to moderate. The authors' practical warning stands out: high-flow oxygen is a comfort and oxygenation tool, not a rescue, and its use must never delay stepping up to stronger ventilation support.
pmc-13248758:
Kazuma Handa and co-authors deliver a five-gene mRNA cocktail to injured hearts in mice in a 2026 study. Heart attack damage unfolds through many routes at once, so single fixes fall short. Synthetic mRNA can carry several repair instructions in one dose.

Genes were picked from vesicles shed by stem-cell-grown heart cells that had restored heart function. Tiny polymer bubbles carried the mRNAs straight into heart muscle. Treated hearts grew new vessels, scarred less, and pumped better, and mice lived longer. Distinct signal paths drove each benefit in the analysis. The cocktail idea may suit other diseases with tangled damage.
pmc-13248958:
Sung-Jong Eun introduces a themed journal issue on technology frontiers in urology in a 2026 editorial. The issue gathers work on devices and intelligence that widen what clinics can do. Generative AI and large language models loom large in its pages.

Four papers use layered approaches to urinary and voiding problems, from body markers to implant stimulators. Daily feasibility gets its own stress through an automated collection device study. A family-centered paper reminds readers that care reaches past drugs into home life. Image and signal recognition studies round out the issue. Eun frames the set as proof that hardware and human context must advance together.
pmc-13249058:
Coskun and colleagues asked whether blood transfusions dull immunotherapy in melanoma, in a 2026 Turkish study. Fifty-seven patients with metastatic skin melanoma received nivolumab as second-line treatment between 2018 and 2023. Transfusions can calm the immune system, which might undercut a drug whose job is to unleash it, so the team compared survival by transfusion history.

Patients who received red cell transfusions during their metastatic phase lived shorter and progressed sooner than those who did not. Transfusion joined brain spread and shorter drug exposure among the markers of poorer outcome. The authors suggest viewing transfusion as a factor doctors can sometimes limit, while noting their small, backward-looking design.
pmc-13249758:
Karangeli and a Greek team mapped how the neck's great arteries sit beside the voice box cartilage, in a 2026 anatomy study. Surgeons use the thyroid cartilage as a landmark, and its upper horn lies close to the carotid arteries, sometimes uncomfortably so. The team measured two hundred fourteen CT angiograms, recording where the carotid fork falls relative to that horn and the gaps between vessel and cartilage.

The fork sat above the horn's level in nearly nine of ten sides. The common carotid artery hugged the cartilage closest, a few millimeters away on average, with the two branches progressively farther. Eleven relationship patterns were cataloged, led by one dominant layout. The authors propose the classification for clearer scan reporting and safer surgical planning.
pmc-13249858: Wang and colleagues issued this correction in Scientific Reports in 2026 for their randomized trial of pulsed radiofrequency treatment on the dorsal root ganglion for battered sensory nerve syndrome. A single word was misspelled throughout the original article: the syndrome's name appeared as battered sensory never syndrome, in the title, abstract, and text. The correction restores nerve in every place, and the journal has updated the article. No methods, results, or conclusions are affected.
pmc-13249958:
Hamed and an Egyptian team profiled the chemistry of three sage species, in a 2026 Scientific Reports study. Salvia plants are rich in compounds that fight inflammation, a process tied to most cancers. Using high-resolution mass spectrometry and molecular networking, the team cataloged the metabolite mix of each species, then docked two hundred eighteen compounds against two cancer-relevant protein targets in the computer.

Network analysis tied the chemistry to hub genes in inflammation and antioxidant pathways. One species, Salvia multicaulis, carried most of the promising compounds, and its extract switched on a protective enzyme in a liver cell cancer-prevention model while suppressing inflammatory nitric oxide in immune cells. The authors nominate it for drug development work.
pmc-13250258:
Rohman and colleagues fine-tune a method for pulling healthy plant compounds from green mango peel. Their 2026 Food Science and Nutrition study treats the peel, a common processing waste, as a source of phenolic compounds with antioxidant power. Ultrasound-assisted extraction was adjusted for time, temperature, and alcohol strength using a structured experimental design.

Seventeen test runs fed statistical models that predicted phenolic yield, free-radical scavenging, and reducing power with strong accuracy. All three settings mattered, and the best balance landed near thirty-six degrees, twelve minutes, and a little over half alcohol in the mix. Lab checks at those settings matched the predictions closely. The authors present the method as a green way to turn fruit waste into useful ingredients.
pmc-13250458:
Farhangiyan and co-authors compare pancreas attacks triggered by very high blood fats with attacks from other causes. Their 2026 Health Science Reports study reviews three hundred patients admitted to one Iranian hospital between 2020 and 2025. Half had pancreatitis driven by high triglycerides, and half formed the comparison group.

The fat-driven group was younger and heavier, scored worse on every severity scale used, and stayed in hospital nearly twice as long. Complications such as lung failure, sepsis, kidney failure, and dead pancreatic tissue all came more often in that group. No patient in either group died during the hospital stay. The authors urge early recognition of this subtype, while noting that their single-center design limits certainty.
pmc-13251158:
Lee and co-authors show that diabetes rewires the brain and blood long before injury, then sabotages repair. Their 2026 Molecular Brain study injures a deep brain region in diabetic mice and compares healing with healthy controls using high-field MRI scans. Diabetes is a known risk factor for poor recovery after brain injury.

Diabetic mice developed larger initial lesions and recovered more slowly, even when starting lesion size was matched. Gene readings from uninjured diabetic brains already showed weakened synapse and skeleton pathways. After injury, their blood immune cells and brain-infiltrating cells carried altered programs, and support-cell activation faltered. The authors argue this pre-set reprogramming explains much of the extra harm diabetes causes after injury.
pmc-13251758:
Feng, Luan, and Zhu measure a sugar-binding protein, galectin-1, in mothers whose babies grew too slowly in the womb. Their 2026 International Journal of Women's Health study compares thirty early-onset and thirty late-onset growth restriction cases with thirty normal deliveries at one Chinese hospital. Blood, placenta, and membrane samples were all tested.

Blood levels of galectin-1 ran higher in both growth restriction groups than in controls, highest in early-onset cases. Inside the placenta the pattern flipped: gene activity for the protein fell, while stained protein deposits rose. Routine traits like age and body mass did not differ between the groups. The authors propose galectin-1 as a candidate marker for this condition, especially its early form.
pmc-13251858:
Chrysovalantou Xirouchaki and a large team link a muscle enzyme to ageing in this 2026 study. Exercise switches on a protective stress-response system in muscle, steered by a master protein, and that protection fades with age.

The enzyme NOX4, which makes small amounts of reactive oxygen in working muscle, turned out to feed that protective switch. Its levels fell in aged mice and humans. Mice lacking it in muscle aged badly, with wasting, frailty, weight gain, and liver disease. Restoring the enzyme, or switching the downstream system on with a broccoli-derived compound, brought the exercise-like protection back. The findings frame one way exercise keeps ageing at bay.
pmc-13252758:
Jonathan Santana and a large team excavate an island fish-processing site in this 2026 archaeology paper. Playa Chica, on Gran Canaria in the Canary Islands, holds five layers of Indigenous occupation from the 6th to the 13th centuries, left by communities of North African origin.

Focusing on the last phase, the team combined shell, bone, seed, and charcoal evidence. Shellfish and sea urchins dominated, with fish remains, crustaceans, and crowds of fish scales pointing to heavy on-site processing. Goat horn tools and pig-tooth hooks, smoke-friendly fuels, and 29 hearths suggest drying or smoking fish for storage. The site likely fed exchange networks between coast and inland.
pmc-13253258:
Laith N. Al-Eitan and a large team test whether vitamin D pathway genes predict breast cancer risk in Jordanian women in a 2026 case-control study. Vitamin D helps restrain tumor growth, and inherited variants in the genes that activate, break down, and carry it change blood levels of the vitamin. The team genotyped four such genes in three hundred patients and three hundred healthy controls.

Two variants stood out as protective. Women carrying the GG genotype of a CYP2R1 variant, a gene involved in the first activation step, faced lower risk. A TG genotype in CYP27B1, the gene for the final activation step, was also linked with reduced risk. The remaining variants, in CYP2R1, CYP24A1, and the vitamin D binding protein gene, showed no clear association. The authors caution that the sample is modest and the findings need confirmation in larger cohorts.
pmc-13253658:
Led by Alessandra Giuliani, a 2026 study tests how well trauma memories can be read in young people. The team pooled data from 407 trauma-exposed youth aged 6 to 17 in South Africa and the United Kingdom. One month after the event, each youth told their story and rated their own memory and stress signs.

Self-ratings of memory quality linked clearly to post-traumatic stress signs in both countries. By contrast, scores drawn from the told stories, such as how ordered or sense-rich they were, did not match self-ratings. Those story scores also failed to predict stress signs, so the authors favor self-report for care.
pmc-13253758:
Supaporn Suwanchote and Phatcharawat Chirasuthat report a 2026 case of skin infection after cosmetic filler shots. A 27-year-old woman with no prior illness had firm red lumps along her jawline for 11 months. The lumps began one month after hyaluronic acid filler, a gel used to shape the face, plus other shots in the same session.

Common antibiotics and an enzyme shot did not help her. Tests pointed to Nocardia nova, a soil bacterium, which the authors call the first known case of this skin disease after filler. The paper also reviews other cosmetic cases to warn clinics about slow, odd infections.
pmc-13254758:
Sarah Bennett and a large team ask teens about a sleep app in a 2026 interview study. Sleep Solved was co-created with adolescents from underserved groups in the United Kingdom to improve sleep. Sixty-three participants aged 16 to 18 tried the app and then gave interviews.

Teens saw the app as useful, with clear advice on changeable habits. They praised its reward system, easy-read sleep hacks, and calm level of science, and rated it more trustworthy than social media advice. Many reported better routines, longer sleep, and improved mood and energy, though sleep was not measured by devices.
pmc-13254958:
Anran Dai and colleagues build a two-stage, web-based prediction tool for lung complications after surgery in a 2026 modeling study. The team developed models in 997 patients having non-heart-or-chest surgery under general anesthesia, then validated the winners in 286 patients from another institution.

A logistic regression model using preoperative variables alone discriminated well, reaching an accuracy-curve score of 0.828 on the test set, led by inflammation marker CRP, physical status class, age, and smoking. Adding intraoperative data let a gradient boosting model called CatBoost take over at 0.927, with operative duration and blood loss joining the dominant predictors. In external validation the boosting model held up best at 0.865 with the strongest overall error profile. The authors deployed the two stages as a web tool for early and post-surgery use.
pmc-13256358:
Nevena Lazarevic and a large team report a 2026 rat study of lemon balm extract against autoimmune myocarditis, heart inflammation that can progress to a stretched, failing heart. Fifty rats were immunized with heart myosin to trigger the disease, then split into healthy controls, untreated disease, and three extract dose groups treated for six weeks.

The extract lowered a panel of inflammatory signals and restored the calming cytokine IL-10. Oxidative stress markers fell while the rats' own antioxidant enzymes rose in activity and gene expression. At the highest dose, scarring of the heart was markedly reversed, with less collagen deposited, and fewer heart cells died by apoptosis. Heart structure and function measures backed the molecular story. The authors cast lemon balm as a multi-pathway heart protector worth further study.
pmc-13256758:

pmc-13257158:

pmc-13257358:

About a fourth of children got the drip, all of them in the lead virus group, and they were younger with more breath pauses on arrival. Most children came out well. Poor results sat only in the lead virus group and showed no link to the drip. Child doctors read a warning here: sicker children got the extra care, which hides any gain in raw counts.
pmc-13257458:
Thanh Sang Vo and colleagues test a plant fraction against allergic responses in cells and mice in a 2026 study. pmc-13257658:
Christopher Bock and colleagues map how printing settings shape large 3D-printed carbon-filled plastic in a 2026 study. pmc-13258158:

pmc-13258258:
Przemysław Smela and Bartosz Miller tune layered slabs for pitch while facing build scatter in a 2026 paper. A screen for key inputs and a robust stage built on low quantile aims dealt with factory scatter.

pmc-13258458:

pmc-13258558:

pmc-13258758:

pmc-13258958:

pmc-13259358:
Lingfeng Cheng and colleagues forecast satellite clock errors by mixing physics with sequence learning in a 2026 paper. Precise positioning depends on continuous clock corrections from the BeiDou system. Gaps in live products degrade positioning until predictions fill them.

Navigation services gain a fallback that keeps precise positioning alive during product gaps.
pmc-13259658:

pmc-13259758:
Weidi Wang and coauthors build a simple pre screening model for diabetic foot ulcers in a 2026 study. Training data covered over eighteen hundred hospitalized diabetes patients, with a separate outpatient group for validation. A ratio joining albumin nutrition status to long term sugar control anchored the design.

Four predictors survived selection, led by injury history and age. Foot ulcers affected about a fifth of the training group. Accuracy held up well in the separate validation group. Risk maps showed age and the ratio interacting, with injury history raising risk everywhere. Clinics with few resources gain a rule out tool from routine data.
pmc-13260158:

pmc-13260258: Martin Schlager and colleagues published a 2026 correction notice for their paper on the western corn rootworm, a beetle pest, and its attraction to floral scent compounds from oil pumpkin. The correction lists changes the published paper needs. They include capitalizing the title in a new form. They change the first sentences of the abstract and introduction to lower-case wording for the species name. They also fix a methods sentence about comparing mass spectra and retention data with published sources.
pmc-13260458:

pmc-13260858:

pmc-13262158:

pmc-13262958:

Short-acting forms can make blood levels surge soon after an injection and sag before the next, causing symptoms to cycle. pmc-13263358:

The leak sealed without complications in twenty-two of them, about sixty-three percent, taking about seven days on average. Thirteen patients needed further procedures. pmc-13263558:

pmc-13263758:

pmc-13264058:

pmc-13264258:

pmc-13264358:

pmc-13264558:

pmc-13264858:

pmc-13264958:

pmc-13265158:

pmc-13265258:

pmc-13266158:

pmc-13266258:

pmc-13266358:

pmc-13267158:

pmc-13267558:

pmc-13269358:

pmc-13270058:

pmc-13271058:

pmc-13271258:

pmc-13271558:

pmc-13271958:

pmc-13272158:

pmc-13272358:

pmc-13272858:

pmc-13273058:

pmc-13273258:

pmc-13273358:

pmc-13273858:

pmc-13274458:

pmc-13274858:
Siqi Zhang and co-authors report a 2026 journal article reviewing adverse events reported after HPV vaccination in the United States reporting system VAERS. Headache and fatigue were the most common complaints. Fainting was the most frequent statistical signal, while a racing-heart condition called POTS showed the strongest signal strength, meriting further study.
pmc-13275558:

pmc-13276458:

pmc-13276558:

pmc-13276758:
Barbora Lujka and colleagues study fat-like membrane molecules in colon cancer cells in a 2026 laboratory paper. pmc-13276858:

The authors suggest these markers could help flag children at risk of worsening, pending wider confirmation.
pmc-13279658:

pmc-13280058:

pmc-13280258:

pmc-13280458:

pmc-13280558:

pmc-13280658:

They also flag side effects such as nausea and a need to take the drug with food. The piece frames the drug as a precise tool, not a broad cure.
pmc-13280858:

pmc-13280958:

pmc-13281158:

pmc-13281358:

pmc-13281758:

pmc-13281858:

pmc-13282458:

pmc-13282858:

pmc-13283258:

pmc-13283458:

pmc-13283858:

pmc-13283958:

pmc-13284058:

pmc-13284458:

pmc-13284558:

pmc-13284758:

pmc-13285358:

pmc-13285558:

pmc-13285658:

pmc-13286158:

pmc-13286758:

pmc-13286958:

pmc-13287058:

pmc-13287158:

pmc-13287458:

pmc-13287758:

pmc-13287958:
