Nine patients relapsed during follow-up, and thirteen died of their disease. Spread of cancer at diagnosis and tumor left at the surgical edge both linked strongly to higher mortality. No measured factor predicted relapse in this small group. The authors call for earlier detection and stronger local tumor control in the region.
pmc-13288358:
Yawen Li and co-authors measured three calming immune signals in 2026 in eye fluid and blood from 96 people across the main glaucoma types, plus cataract controls. The question was whether signal levels match the nerve thinning that steals sight in this disease family.

One signal rose in eye fluid only in the chronic closed-angle group, marking that subtype. The other two ran high in both chronic groups. Eye fluid levels of all three fell as the nerve layer thinned. One signal, IL-38, tracked thinning most tightly in two chronic groups. The authors propose eye fluid signals as candidate markers of damage, pending mechanism work.
pmc-13288758:
Yuting Sun and colleagues review gut-derived fatty acids as a lever in sepsis-related lung failure in a 2026 article. When sepsis unbalances gut microbes, bacteria and their products can reach the lungs, drive body-wide inflammation, and scramble immune control, while the protective short-chain fatty acids those microbes normally make run short.

Acetate, propionate, and butyrate calm inflammation, tune immunity, and guard tissue barriers by blocking histone deacetylases and switching on certain cell receptors, the authors summarize. Yet the same molecules can push the other way depending on dose, type, and illness stage. Mapping that two-way behavior is presented as the key to precise dosing and gut-focused treatments for this often fatal complication.
pmc-13288858:
Sinead Purcell and colleagues issue a 2026 protocol for agreeing a standard outcome list for trials targeting thinking problems after stroke. Post-stroke cognitive impairment harms quality of life and independence, guidelines urge assessment for every survivor, yet trials measure wildly different outcomes, which blocks comparison and slows uptake into practice.

Their six-stage plan starts with a scoping review of trial outcomes and a quick synthesis of what stakeholders value, then focus groups with survivors, supporters, and clinicians. A candidate list follows, narrowed through a real-time online Delphi round and settled at international consensus meetings that also pick measurement tools. Patients and the public are woven through every stage.
pmc-13289058:
Joyce Oi Kwan Chung and colleagues plan a 2026 trial of laughter yoga in Hong Kong. The trial deals with children with autism. Such children face high rates of low mood and worry. Their parents face high stress too. Laughter yoga may lift mood for both.

The plan will enroll 66 child-parent pairs. Half will start classes at once. Half will wait for their turn. Classes run one hour, twelve in all. They span six months in total. Checks run before, after, and three months later. Join and stay rates lead the goals. Mood and stress scores come second. Talks will probe safety and fit.
pmc-13289158:
Clara Pons-Duran and colleagues study vaccine coverage in Ethiopian children in 2026. A local surveillance site supplied the records. It holds 7,417 children born from 2018 to 2021. Home visits ran every three months. Data came from vaccine cards and caregiver reports.

Full coverage ran from 26 to 31 percent by year counts. A survey-style count gave 32 to 42 percent. The gap shows how method shapes the picture. On-time dosing lagged across the board. Under half of infants got doses within four weeks of due dates. Measles timing fared better than most. The authors back the slow, home-based count as more true.
pmc-13289258:
Emmanuel Okiror Okello and colleagues analyzed a 2026 national dataset on acute flaccid paralysis in Uganda. Surveillance for sudden limb weakness in children under 15 helps catch poliovirus early and supports the global push to end polio by 2026. Records covered routine reporting from 2016 to 2023 across the country.

A total of 6409 cases were reported, and 5837 were confirmed as true cases after review. Median age was 3 years, most cases were under age 5, and boys made up 57.8 percent of cases overall. About 63 percent were notified within seven days, and stool samples were adequate in 88.6 percent of cases as reported. Rates of non-polio paralysis met the target in five of eight years, showing a system that works but still has timing gaps.
pmc-13289658:
Matthew E. Lowe and colleagues survey a 2026 perspective on breaking down PTFE plastic at low heat. PTFE, best known as Teflon, resists heat and chemicals so well that disposal is hard: landfill burial lasts, burning creates harmful small fluorinated chemicals, and full breakdown usually needs harsh force. Global output reached 309 000 tons in 2021 alone.

New methods aim to split the polymer at or below 100 °C, far gentler than older routes. In several cases, freed fluoride is captured and built into useful fluorinated fine chemicals instead of waste. The perspective weighs each cutting-edge route, its limits, and its upcycling value. Cleaner recycling of a near-indestructible plastic would cut a lasting waste stream.
pmc-13289958:
Kazuhiro Yamamoto and co-authors train an AI grader for duodenal tumors in a 2026 validation study. These surface tumors of the small intestine are found more often as scopes improve. Telling low-grade from high-grade growth guides how aggressively doctors remove them. No standard endoscopic grading method exists today. The team trained a deep learning classifier on white-light images from 85 cases at one university.

A test set of 69 lesions from three institutions checked the finished model. The classifier reached about 78 percent accuracy and 92 percent sensitivity for high-grade disease. Three expert endoscopists grading the same images scored near 58 percent accuracy and 50 percent sensitivity. The AI's advantage on both measures passed statistical testing. Its specificity was modest, so it overcalls some low-grade lesions. Still, the authors see a role in steering resection choices. High sensitivity fits a safety-first task where missing high-grade disease is costly.
pmc-13290458:
A single eye, sampled nine times, reveals how the chemical weather inside a lymphoma changes under treatment, in a 2026 case report by Maria Carmela Saturno and colleagues. The patient, in their 70s, had vitreoretinal lymphoma, a rare B-cell cancer of immune-privileged sites, treated with injections of methotrexate and dexamethasone into the eye.

Across 12 weeks, each 0.2 mL vitreous sample was screened for 58 cytokines, chemokines, and growth factors. Key signals such as IL-10 fell steadily, with IL-10 gone by day 22, while the homing chemokines CXCL12 and CXCL13 faded more slowly and HGF stayed high. Saturno and colleagues, reporting the first such longitudinal series, suggest these patterns could mark disease activity, guide how long treatment should run, and flag more aggressive cases.
pmc-13290958:
Four decades of clot care evolution get distilled by L. W. Greenspon and colleagues in a perspective from 2026 on high-risk pulmonary embolism. Their single center moved from whole-body clot-dissolving drugs to catheter-based therapies, and now to large-bore clot removal by catheter, with heart-lung machine backup.

The through-line is physiology first. Choices hinge on right ventricle function, lung artery pressures, and cardiac output, weighed against age, underlying heart and lung disease, and deep vein clots. A dedicated response team, and lately AI detection systems, sped up spotting and teamwork for high-risk cases. Greenspon and colleagues distill the lessons as early severity checks, selective use of aggressive clot removal, and a ready multi-team system. They present the account as hard-won practice where trial evidence still lags.
pmc-13291058:
Two ways to measure back movement are compared by Hongtao Li and colleagues in 2026. The work used sheep spines in a lab. Dynamic X-ray and optical tracking both record spine motion. How well they agree was not well known.

Six sheep lumbar segments were bent in set directions. Each bend was repeated three times. Both systems recorded the same bends at once. Error and agreement stats framed the comparison. Within-method scores looked high at first glance. Wide doubt ranges came with the small sample count. The numbers should guide lab design, the authors say. They do not settle the method contest yet.
pmc-13291258:
Immune cells in breast tumor tissue may warn against chemotherapy. Zak Kinsella leads a 2026 study of hormone-sensitive breast cancer. Such tumors often look safe for five to ten years. Late return of disease is still common. Mid-range risk scores leave hard calls for doctors.

Tissue from hundreds of patients was mapped in fine detail. Gene and protein maps showed stroma and tumor nests differ. Inflamed stroma carried signs of worn-out immune cells. More killer immune cells in stroma linked to worse outcome. That link held in a treated trial group. It also held in a second tissue set. The marker may help spare some women harsh drugs.
pmc-13291358:
A rare hernia after bladder surgery is repaired in a 2026 case from Yusuke Sato and colleagues. The patient was an 80-year-old man. Four years earlier, a robot had removed his bladder for cancer. A routine scan then found bowel slipping through his pelvic floor.

He felt no symptoms at first and was watched. Signs of a partial bowel blockage later forced surgery. Doctors worked through the perineum from below. They freed the bowel and closed the small defect with a cross-shaped mesh. The patch was fixed to pubic bone on both sides. No return of the hernia showed at six months.
pmc-13291458:
A simple blood ratio may predict arthritis drug success. Jingru Zhu leads a 2026 study of adalimumab in rheumatoid arthritis. The ratio compares neutrophils to lymphocytes in blood. High values mark stronger body inflammation.

The study followed 189 patients to week 24. Response was scored on a 28-joint disease scale. High starting ratios predicted a good response. Good responders saw their ratios fall after treatment. Patients reaching remission started with higher ratios. Far more high-ratio patients hit remission than low-ratio ones. A cheap blood test could thus guide drug choice. More work must confirm the cut point.
pmc-13291558:
A strong antibody against mpox is found and mapped in fine detail. Shimeng Bai leads a 2026 study targeting a surface protein, A35R. That protein helps the virus spread inside a host. Blocking it could curb severe illness.

Mice were primed with mRNA shots to raise antibodies. A light-based sorter fished out the best binders fast. One antibody, 17H1, neutralized real mpox virus well. Cryo imaging showed it gripping the protein’s far ends. A web of bonds locks that grip in place. Treated animals were fully protected from infection. Lung virus counts and tissue harm both fell. A fresh treatment candidate emerges here.
pmc-13291858:
Fulu Gao and colleagues report a 2026 genome-wide study of the ABC transporter gene family in sweet potato. These membrane proteins burn ATP to move substances such as metal ions and hormones across cell boundaries. The team catalogued the family's members, their chemistry, chromosome positions, and tissue activity, then measured gene responses under metal stress.

Seedlings faced iron, aluminum, zinc, and copper treatments, with expression checked by RT-qPCR. Most family genes changed activity under at least one metal. One gene, IbABCC14, switched on under all four metals and resembles known detox transporters in Arabidopsis and rice, hinting it locks metals away in vacuoles. The authors propose it as a lead candidate for breeding metal-tolerant sweet potato varieties.
pmc-13292058:
Jinhui Che, with co-authors, reports a 2026 study on why liver cancers that resist sorafenib stay aggressive, focusing on mitochondria and sugar metabolism. Resistant cells were checked for mitochondrial shape, oxygen use, glucose uptake, and lactate output. The team also tested drug combinations in orthotopic mouse tumors.

A protein called Drp1 drove mitochondrial splitting and a switch from oxygen-based energy to aerobic glycolysis in resistant cells, and that pattern tracked with poor prognosis. Blocking Drp1 curbed invasion and spread but sped cell growth by flipping metabolism back toward oxygen use. Pairing the Drp1 blocker mdivi-1 with the OXPHOS inhibitor IACS-010759 hit both sides of that trade-off and slowed tumors markedly. The authors frame the pair as a route around sorafenib resistance.
pmc-13292158:
Mingqiang Lin and colleagues compare treatment timing for advanced esophageal cancer in a 2026 matched study. Patients had resectable squamous tumors staged cT3 to cT4a. One path gives chemoradiation before surgery, the other after it. Records for 223 patients were balanced into fifty-nine matched pairs by propensity scores. Survival and side effects were then compared head to head.

The before-surgery group lived longer, with median survival near sixty-two months against forty-six. Five-year survival reached about sixty-seven percent against about forty-eight percent. Time without progression also favored the earlier treatment, though its five-year gap missed significance. Side effects looked alike between the paths. Treatment choice, body mass index, and nodal stage each predicted survival. A simple score from weight and nodal stage sorted patients into risk bands, except within the before-surgery group. The authors back chemoradiation first for this stage.
pmc-13292258:
Weixing Liu and co-authors trace a 2026 mechanism by which a circular RNA drives head and neck squamous cell carcinoma. The molecule, circ_0008777, runs high in these tumors and matches poorer patient outcomes. Most cases of this cancer, arising in the mouth, throat, and voice box, are caught late, so fresh targets matter.

Experiments in cells and animals show the circular RNA lifting levels of c-Myc, a powerful growth driver, through two routes at once. It binds the protein PC4 to boost c-Myc gene transcription directly. It also soaks up miR-185-3p, a small RNA that normally restrains c-Myc. With both brakes off, tumors grew and spread more readily. The authors propose blocking circ_0008777 as a possible treatment strategy for this cancer.
pmc-13292558:
Burak Ulkumen, Sabri Mutlu, and Onur Celik ask a 2026 question most nose surgeons never test: do spreader grafts protect the voice during rhinoplasty? Reshaping the nose can narrow the internal valve and shift the resonances that color speech and singing, especially the F3 and F4 formants. Their prospective randomized study, described as double-blind and the first of its kind, compared patients with and without the grafts.

Patients lacking spreader grafts showed significant acoustic deterioration after surgery, while grafted patients kept their essential formants intact. Voice handicap scores on the VHI-10 scale rose postoperatively only in the ungrafted group. The authors argue the grafts defend the singer's and speaker's formant clusters, not just breathing and looks. They recommend weighing voice outcomes when planning structural rhinoplasty.
pmc-13292658:
Mengfei Xu and co-authors develop a 2026 urine test angle for cervical cancer, hunting microRNAs that could triage women who test positive for high-risk HPV. Screening is shifting toward self-sampling, which rules out the usual cytology follow-up, so objective molecular triage is in demand. The team optimized a workflow, called IsoSeek in its profiling arm, for squeezing sensitive small-RNA sequencing out of whole urine.

Two microRNAs stood out as disturbed in cancer: miR-143-3p and miR-204-3p, detectable from urine rather than tissue. Their ratio separated cervical cancer cases with promising discrimination in the reported analysis. The authors frame urine microRNA profiling as a patient-friendly route, since samples can be collected at home without a clinic visit. They position the pair as candidate triage markers pending wider analytical validation.
pmc-13292758:
Shenao Wang and co-authors compare two chicken breeds in a 2026 study of egg laying and liver gene activity. White Leghorn hens lay many eggs, while Wenchang chickens lay far fewer, and the liver makes the yolk material that drives output.

Gene activity in Leghorn livers favored fat handling, with genes such as CPT1A and ACSL1 more active. The three-dimensional folding of DNA was mostly alike in both breeds, yet local switches differed. Some fat genes moved into active zones in Leghorns, domain borders were looser, and DNA loops linked more strongly to fat genes. The findings link genome folding to breed differences in laying.
pmc-13292858:
Zhanwei Zhu and co-authors build a gene-based risk score, reported in 2026, for liver cancer known as hepatocellular carcinoma. Blood vessel growth feeds this cancer, so genes tied to new vessels may help sort patients by outlook.

Using large cancer datasets, the team formed a score from four genes: APOH, SLCO2A1, SPP1, and VTN. High-score patients lived shorter lives in test groups from other cohorts. Single-cell data showed which cell types made each gene, with SPP1 coming mainly from macrophages and liver cells. Lowering SPP1 slowed vessel growth in lab and animal tests. High-score tumors also responded less to the drug sorafenib.
pmc-13293258:
Yingjie Zhang presents a 2026 case report on a hard hospital course after heart valve surgery in a woman aged 57 who had severe rheumatic mitral stenosis. She also had atrial fibrillation and class III heart failure before surgery.

Surgery replaced the mitral valve and fixed other heart issues, but the left ventricle tore during the operation and was repaired at once. Her heart then pumped very weakly and needed balloon pump support, followed by stomach bleeding and later a clot on the new valve. Stronger blood thinning and team care steadied her, and heart strength had improved markedly by day 29. She stayed well at later checks.
pmc-13293658:
André S Alves and co-authors map, in a 2026 bibliometric study, research on fat-derived stem cells for peripheral nerve repair from 2000 to 2025. Nerve grafts from a patient's own body remain standard, yet they cost a second wound and give uneven recovery.

The final set held 555 articles by 2750 researchers in 54 countries, citing 16,466 sources in all. Output rose steadily after 2011 and peaked in 2019. Adjusted for population, Switzerland led in research intensity, ahead of Sweden and Belgium. Topics shifted over time from building tissue scaffolds toward cell signals, tiny vesicles called exosomes, and steps toward clinic use.
pmc-13293758:
Shan Tian and co-authors simplify, in a 2026 food study, the making of smoked jujube, a traditional Chinese treat whose drying and smoking take great labor. Their shortcut pairs brief roasting with sealed aging to build flavor and health compounds faster.

Four batches were compared: plain, sealed only, roasted only, and the combined method, roasted at 190 degrees for 2 minutes then sealed for 14 days. The combined batch tasted best and held more phenolics than the plain batch, at 13.2 versus 9.2 units the authors report. Chemical scans found 854 changed compounds, with richer flavor and antioxidant types. The treat matched the traditional one overall.
pmc-13294058:
Yesnely Anacari Flores and Don Operario write a 2026 perspective on structural harm facing Latinx public health students in the United States. About 68 million people identified as Latinx in 2024, and applications to master of public health programs from Latinx students surged early in the pandemic. Recent anti-immigrant, anti-diversity, and anti-public health policies now press on study, mental health, and careers at once.

An intersectional lens shows how racial, immigrant, and student status combine under those policies. Gains in grants, scholarships, and anti-racism pledges risk reversal. The authors outline campus and professional steps to protect students and keep the future workforce diverse and stable.
pmc-13294158:
Tehseen Riaz leads a 2026 lab study on whether zinc particles kill breast cancer cells more than healthy cells. Standard cancer drugs spread through the body and cause harsh effects, so selective particles draw interest. Spherical zinc peroxide particles in two size ranges, commercial zinc oxide, and four-armed zinc oxide microparticles were tested on MCF-7 cancer cells and RMF-EG fibroblasts.

Zinc peroxide harmed cells in a dose-dependent way, killing far more cancer cells while fibroblasts kept over 75% viability at matched doses. Flow tests showed cancer cells also took up more particles. The authors call for tests in more complex systems before any therapy claims.
pmc-13294358:
Margareta Ramström and colleagues compare sugar patterns on dog blood proteins in infection versus pregnancy for a 2026 study. Pregnancy itself shifts inflammation signals, muddying diagnosis of womb infection and other illness. Serum from ten dogs with pyometra, ten with respiratory infection, ten pregnant dogs, and nine healthy non-pregnant dogs was mapped with a tuned glycan method.

No clear split appeared between pregnant dogs and pyometra cases. Respiratory cases and healthy dogs shared higher levels of some glycan types and lower levels of the dominant glycan than pregnant dogs. Overall sugar patterns thus fail as a test to tell pregnancy changes from infection, a useful negative result.
pmc-13294458:
Yannick Mahlich and coauthors present spammR, an R package for spatial multi-omics, in a 2026 software article. New instruments map transcripts, proteins, metabolites, and chemical marks across tissue slices at fine detail, yet most tools assume sequencing data and fit mass spectrometry awkwardly. Their package aims at end-to-end handling with mass data at the center.

Workflows import, clean, visualize, and integrate several omics layers plus microscope images from the same tissue. Open code on GitHub invites reuse and extension. Bridging data types in place can reveal tumor or organ patterns that single-layer maps miss, such as protein hotspots sitting over quiet gene zones.
pmc-13294958:
Gabriel C. Bueno and co-authors screen 134 candidate coating molecules for perovskite solar cells entirely by computer, in a 2026 study. Coating the crystal surface can stabilize these efficient but fragile cells, yet picking a coating has been trial and error. The team calculated how each organic cation sticks to a small perovskite fragment, then grouped the results with clustering methods to find what separates good stickers from poor ones.

No single trait predicted success. Stiff, flat molecules paid a heavy distortion penalty when they bent to fit the surface, canceling their strong attraction. Bulky, saturated molecules hugged the surface through weak dispersion forces with almost no penalty, and flexible amines anchored cheaply. Electronic analysis added a warning: ring-rich molecules planted energy states inside the crystal's gap that could trap charges, while saturated ones behaved as harmless insulators. Flexibility plus saturation, the authors conclude, marks a good coating.
pmc-13295158:
Jason Liu and colleagues count exercise injuries across the United States in a 2026 national analysis. Weightlifting and bodyweight training both build strength, yet their share of emergency care was not well measured. Records came from a national injury surveillance system covering 2014 to 2023.

National estimates reached 546,655 weightlifting injuries and 108,001 bodyweight injuries over the decade. Weightlifting harm centred on the trunk and fingers, while bodyweight harm hit limbs and dislocated joints more often. After accounting for age and sex, the odds of hospital admission did not differ by exercise type, guiding prevention toward lifting form and safe joint angles.
pmc-13295658:
Amy Leestemaker-Palmer, Stephanie Nuss, and Luiz E Bermudez test antibiotic order against a stubborn lung germ in a 2026 study. Mycobacterium avium infections need long three-drug treatment that still fails often. Bacteria react to first drug contact by changing their workings, so arrival order might shape the final result.

In free-floating growth, order made no difference to drug effect in the tests. Inside biofilms and inside immune cells, order mattered clearly. Starting with the wall-acting drug ethambutol, then the other two, matched giving all three at once, while other orders worked worse. The finding argues that sequencing deserves a place in treatment design.
pmc-13295758:
He Xiao, Mingqin Shao, and Zeng Jiang model winter homes for white-naped cranes under change in a 2026 study. Records from 71 wintering sites between 2015 and 2025 grounded the maps. Height above sea level, distance to big water, driest-month rain, slope, and temperature patterns shaped where the birds settle.

Good habitat today clusters along the middle and lower Yangtze River and North China coastal wetlands. Under low, medium, and high emission futures for 2050 and 2070, the centre of suitable ground shifts southwest overall. Use concentrates in the middle Yangtze while other regions shrink sharply, guiding protection toward that refuge.
pmc-13296158:
Sh. M. Abdo and co-authors make, in 2026, a cellulose-based gel for pulling zirconium out of acidic waste liquid from zircon processing. The gel mixes plant cellulose with polyvinyl alcohol and fumaric acid, giving a porous material dotted with binding sites.

Batch tests found uptake peaked in strong acid within ninety minutes, reaching a high capacity per gram. The pattern of uptake pointed to chemical binding, and the process absorbed heat while running on its own. A dilute acid wash recovered about ninety percent of the metal. The authors pitch the cheap gel for metal separation and purification work.
pmc-13296958:
James G. Lyman and colleagues report seven cases of a single-position spinal operation that removes a damaged vertebra in a 2026 series. The prone-transpsoas route reaches the spine from the side and back at once, so the patient never needs turning mid-operation. Cases covered trauma, severe deformity, and revision surgery.

All seven operations were completed without major complications, and every patient kept stability afterward. Three deformity cases gained large corrections of spinal curvature. Pain and function improved by the latest follow-up in the whole group. One complex revision case drove the longest operating time and highest blood loss. Larger studies are needed, the authors say.
pmc-13297058:
Amira Guirguis and colleagues weigh how methamphetamine acts in the body against related drugs, to inform court sentencing in the United Kingdom, in a 2026 review. The drug sits in the top legal class, yet the main sentencing guide sets no amount thresholds for it. The team weighed human studies, brain scans, poison data, and death records against amphetamine, cocaine, and heroin.

The drug sits closest to amphetamine in how it works, the authors find. It reaches the brain more readily, lasts longer, and shows higher death risk in the reports. Smoked use hits with a force closer to crack cocaine. Treating the two drugs as equal gram for gram is not backed by the data. A raised amphetamine scale is proposed instead, with gaps in human data flagged.
pmc-13297258:
Marco Cascella and colleagues trace a conceptual shift in chronic pain science, from single brain regions to whole networks, in a 2026 narrative review. Older teaching pictured a fixed pain matrix of areas lighting up together. Newer work treats chronic pain as disturbed communication among large-scale brain networks.

Salience, default mode, executive, and sensorimotor networks all show altered interactions in the reviewed literature. Children's chronic pain may involve developmental changes to the same networks, although long-term imaging studies are scarce. Artificial intelligence tools promise objective pain measures and personalised treatment choices in this framework. The authors present network thinking as the route toward precision pain medicine.
pmc-13297558:
Anqi Dai and colleagues review the use of large language models to detect depression, in a 2026 article. Depression ranks among the world's top causes of disability, and early spotting stays hard. The review maps rating scales and public datasets, then traces detection methods from single signals, such as text or voice, to combined streams and language-model systems.

One gap stands out. Real clinics rarely hold every signal type, and methods that cope with missing or noisy inputs remain scarce. The authors call for language-model systems that adapt when a channel drops and draw on medical knowledge to stay readable to clinicians. Ethics and human-centred design close the survey.
pmc-13297658:
George Triantafyllou and colleagues report a rare cluster of extra ankle bones found on a scan, in a 2026 case report. A forty-three-year-old woman was imaged after a fall down stairs, on suspicion of fracture. Fine-slice computed tomography with layered and three-dimensional rebuilds mapped the bones around her ankle.

Alongside a small heel-bone spur, the scan showed an extra bone below the fibula and a navicular bone split into three parts, an exceedingly rare variant. All the extra pieces were rounded and neatly shelled, marks of lifelong variants rather than fresh breaks. Telling such variants from fractures matters, the authors stress, since mistaking one for the other can drive needless treatment.
pmc-13297758:
Tomáš Taubner and colleagues compare the chemistry of hemp and linseed varieties grown side by side in the Czech Republic, in a 2026 study. Both oilseeds feed industry and nutrition markets, but varieties differ. Twelve hemp and eleven linseed lines, from shop catalogues and new breeding, grew under one regime for a season.

Fat content spanned a wide range in both crops, and the fats were rich in two prized unsaturated fatty acids. Broad gaps appeared across most nutrients measured, showing how much variety choice alone can shift a harvest. Both seeds could partly replace soybean meal in animal feed, the authors say, pending digestion and feeding trials. Hemp variety choice also steers levels of the unwanted compound THC.
pmc-13297958:
Melody Moezzi and Bjørn M. Hofmann examine how AI tools for dental diagnosis are sold, in a 2026 ethics-focused study. Promotional material from leading dental AI firms during late 2025 underwent qualitative thematic analysis. The authors read the marketing through principlism, professional ethics, and virtue-based lenses.

Marketing often framed the tools as ways to raise case acceptance, revenue, and practice growth, not only as testing aids. Images and results numbers presented the systems as authoritative and objective, which can press patients toward accepting treatment and hide uncertainty. The authors warn about autonomy, overtreatment, and professional integrity, urging safeguards so the technology stays a clinical support.
pmc-13298258:
Burn care in poor-resource settings needs guidance that bends to what is actually available, argue Hongyu Tang and colleagues in a 2026 evidence synthesis. They mined guidelines, consensus statements, and systematic reviews worldwide to assemble recommendations for the first phase of adult burn treatment.

Fifty-nine high-quality sources yielded 77 recommendations across 13 domains, from scene safety and stopping the burning through airway and circulation support to wound care and transfer preparation. The authors found a gap between written protocols and the staff, supplies, and systems that decide survival on the ground. Their framework tiers actions by resources, prioritizing the ABC steps that save lives while patients await transfer.
pmc-13298758: An earlier paper on heart cell growth from stem cells has been pulled, this 2026 notice states. The paper had claimed that the ISL1 protein drives stem cells to become heart muscle cells. Doubts arose over three figures, 1, 2, and S1. In one, error bars look too much alike from point to point. In the rest, gel lanes show sharp breaks, and bands in unlike rows look too much alike. The item here is the withdrawal note, and it says why the claims can no longer be trusted.
pmc-13299358:
School screening flags suspected scoliosis more often in girls and in leaner teenagers, while some sports link to lower odds, report Josipa Glavaš and colleagues in a 2026 cross-sectional study. They screened 18,216 adolescents with the forward bend test during the 2019/2020 school year and modeled the associations.

Female sex more than doubled the odds (OR = 2.49), and odds climbed with grade level, reaching 2.98 by eighth grade. Higher body mass index lowered odds, as did playing soccer, gymnastics, or martial arts and training more often. The authors stress these are screening associations, not proof of cause, and back school screening with attention to body composition.
pmc-13300158:
Two plant flavonoids, fisetin and pinocembrin, kill leukaemia cells more strongly together than alone, report Narawan Kaewthawee and colleagues in a 2026 laboratory study. The team tested the pair on Jurkat and K562 cell lines, tracking survival, programmed death, and cell-cycle proteins, with computer docking against the Fas receptor.

Fisetin alone cut viability and switched on caspase-8, a marker of death-receptor signaling, while lowering CDK4. A Fas-blocking compound confirmed the receptor's role in the effect. Adding pinocembrin produced synergy scores above 10 in Jurkat cells and sharpened caspase-8 activation. In K562 cells, the pairing also shrank colony growth in soft agar far more than either compound by itself.
pmc-13301058:
J Cravo and co-authors compare starting ventricular tachycardia ablation from the heart's outer surface alone against the conventional combined inside and outside approach, in a 2026 retrospective study. Scans beforehand suggested which patients carried mostly outer surface substrate. Fifty-four patients treated between 2015 and 2025, most with dilated cardiomyopathy and defibrillators and many arriving in electrical storm, split into thirty-one outer only procedures and twenty-eight combined ones.

Complications touched about twenty-nine percent of procedures overall, with major events less frequent in the outer only group, though not significantly. In about five percent of procedures no abnormal substrate turned up at all, meaning the outer access was unnecessary. Over a mean follow-up above two years, recurrence and survival did not differ between strategies. The authors credit imaging triage with picking the right door into the heart and sparing some patients the second route.
pmc-13302158:
H Fukaya and colleagues compare airway methods during cryoballoon ablation for atrial fibrillation in a 2026 retrospective study, focusing on a rare but dangerous complication. Air entering a coronary artery can be fatal, and deep sedation may let air be sucked in through large sheaths when chest pressure dips. A laryngeal mask with positive-pressure ventilation should prevent those dips.

The series covered 491 patients treated between 2017 and 2024 at one university hospital. Symptomatic coronary air embolism struck five patients managed with an adaptive ventilation device, and none managed with the mask. No brain embolism or deaths occurred, and other complication rates were similar. The authors argue that airway control deserves the same attention as the ablation itself.
pmc-13302358:
Corneal transplant surgery in frail, elderly patients got a gentler anesthetic recipe in a 2026 case series from Margita Lucic and colleagues. Fifty consecutive high-risk patients, aged fifty to ninety, received penetrating keratoplasty under a sub-Tenon eye block plus a dexmedetomidine drip given without the usual loading dose. Heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen, and sedation depth were tracked across nine phases of surgery.

Sedation stayed exactly in the cooperative target range for every patient, with breathing unaided throughout. Heart rate eased from 76 to 57 beats per minute and pressures drifted down from hypertensive levels into a comfortable band. Nobody needed opioids. The authors call the results preliminary but promising enough for randomized trials.
pmc-13302758:
Two fungi living quietly inside Thai Itea shrubs include a species new to science, Jutamart Monkai and colleagues report in a 2026 taxonomy study. Strains from healthy stems of Itea japonica and Itea riparia were grown out, examined under the microscope, and placed on family trees built from four gene regions. Close nucleotide comparisons separated look-alike members of the Apiosporaceae family.

The Itea japonica isolate became Nigrospora iteae, formally introduced as a new species. The other matched Apiospora vietnamensis, a first record on that host. The team also reclassifies a Ficus fungus as Apiospora fici, renames a homonym, and appends an updated checklist of Nigrospora species with hosts and activities.
pmc-13302858:
Twelve papers map where ceramic matrix composites stand, Rodrigo Moreno and Oscar Rubem Klegues Montedo introduce in a 2026 special issue overview. The collection spans ten research articles and two reviews on materials built to survive extreme heat and hostile chemistry. Topics run from additively manufactured graded ceramics for armor to carbon composites armored with ultra-high-temperature ceramics against oxidation.

Research contributions cover rocket thruster modeling for green propulsion, silicon nitride boron nitride ceramics tuned by particle size, MAX-phase coatings on silicon carbide fibers, and polymer-infiltrated networks, among others. The editors frame the set as a snapshot of a field balancing performance, reliability, and sustainability.
pmc-13303358:
Hot root-filling settings can push a tooth's outer surface past the safety line, Mihai Paven and colleagues measure in a 2026 laboratory study. Twenty extracted single-rooted teeth were filled with warm injectable gutta-percha at device presets of 180 or 230 degrees while infrared cameras watched three root zones. A bench experiment separately checked what temperatures the devices actually deliver at their tips.

The hotter preset drove middle-third surface readings significantly higher, and three of ten teeth crossed the 47-degree threshold tied to periodontal damage, peaking at 49.6 degrees. Tip output also lagged presets sharply. The 180-degree setting gave the more predictable, safer profile, especially for thin-walled roots.
pmc-13306158:
Shu-Peng Dong named a new plant species from Hainan Island in a 2026 taxonomic account. Argostemma baotingense belongs to the coffee family and grows in southern China, joining nine known members of its genus in the country.

Closest likeness is to A. bachmaense, yet the new plant differs in low or creeping stems, narrow leaves pale beneath, and hairless flower clusters and cups. Photographs and a key separate all nine Chinese species for field and herbarium use. The genus favours damp shade near streams and wet rocks, a habitat note that helps locate further populations.
pmc-13306858:
Giuseppe A. Malfa profiled chemicals and bioactivity in white mignonette extracts in a 2026 study. Leaf, flower, stem and unripe fruit extracts were made with ultrasound help and scanned by high-resolution liquid methods.

Thirty main compounds appeared across flavonoid, glucosinolate, phenolic acid and fat families, with four reported for the first time in this genus. Fruit extract led on calming inflammation and trapping radicals, likely from richer flavonoid content in reported results. Flower extract cut cell growth most strongly, showing plant parts differ sharply in useful chemistry. The part by part split shows why whole plant tests can mask strong plant drugs.
pmc-13306958:
Yu Shuai doped gallium into nickel-iron layered hydroxide to speed alkaline water oxidation in a 2026 study. Green hydrogen needs anodes that stay fast and tough at factory scale, where standard catalysts still fall short.

Computer analysis cast gallium as a strong electron puller that retunes nearby iron sites through indirect orbital links. The doped anode needed only 275 mV extra voltage at 50 mA cm−2 in reported tests and ran over 100 hours at 1 A cm−2 in a membrane device. Live spectroscopy confirmed earlier and wider surface rebuilding under the gallium effect.
pmc-13307158:
Amr Chaabeni mapped plant therapy research in sport across three decades in a 2026 bibliometric study. Records from 1991 to 2024 in a core citation index began at 3404 hits, narrowed to 368 studies after screening.

Growth averaged 11.83% yearly with a peak in 2021, drawing 2103 authors across 199 sources in reported counts. Teamwork across borders hit 22.55% of papers, with the United States, United Kingdom and China as top partners. Hot themes joined exercise, inflammation, oxidative stress and compounds such as curcumin and resveratrol, with gaps flagged by theme mapping. The map shows where plant sport work is thin and where new trials are most needed next.
pmc-13307758:
Solomon Monday Jacob and co-authors check in 2026 odd shaped schistosome eggs in urine from Abuja, Nigeria, to learn which species made them and whether animal forms play a part. Urine came from 1887 people aged five years and up, and eggs were first found by microscope checks.

In all, 507 people carried some schistosome eggs, and 91 carried the odd forms that drew deeper study here. Gene reads from pooled eggs matched both the human species and the cattle species, which hints at mixed spread in the area. Pooled reads cannot prove true hybrids over mixed infections, so single worm gene work and joint human animal studies come next for control teams.
pmc-13309558:
Chun Li and colleagues report a 2026 physics study on light-matter pairs in a layered magnetic crystal called CrSBr. Pairs of light with packet-like energy states, named exciton-polaritons, can carry signals and react to magnetism. Lower-energy pairs in this crystal barely respond to magnetic fields, which limits control.

Higher-energy pairs coupled strongly with light even at room temperature. A modest in-plane magnetic field shifted their energy split by up to 100 meV as the crystal spins flipped between states. In a middle magnetic phase, pair interactions grew stronger in a pattern tied to spin waves. The authors present the crystal as a tunable platform for spin-linked light devices.
pmc-13309658:
Yu Wang and co-authors track deaths from kidney failure across the United States from 1999 to 2024 in a 2026 study. Kidney failure kills many adults each year, yet recent trends by group and place were poorly charted. National death records offer a full-population view of those patterns.

Deaths credited to kidney failure totaled 1,192,598 over the study years in the national database used. Yearly deaths rose from 34,456 to 53,848, while the age-adjusted rate barely moved, easing from 19.57 to 19.05 per 100,000 people in the reported figures. Gaps by sex, age, race, region, and kidney failure type were charted. The authors urge targeted action where rates stay highest.
pmc-13309958:
Rebecca Katharina Kutscherauer and co-authors link chronic gut inflammation to brain cell loss in mice in a 2026 study. Bowel disease raises the risk of Parkinson disease, and a gut-immune-brain route has been proposed. Which brain immune cells drive the harm during colitis was unknown.

Mice with long-term colitis lost dopamine-making neurons in a key midbrain area and showed synuclein clumping, a Parkinson hallmark. Single-cell maps showed midbrain immune cells shifting toward inflammation, with more interferon-ready microglia and immune cells crossing from blood. A drug that removed most midbrain microglia after colitis began fully rescued the neuron loss, cutting microglia by 67 percent in the treated mice. Gut disease itself stayed unchanged.
pmc-13310658:
Xiaoling Huang and co-authors compare two germs behind belly-driven blood infections in a 2026 study. When gut infections spill into the blood, Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae dominate the cultures. Their severity patterns and drug resistance profiles differ, which matters for first antibiotic choices.

Records for 276 patients at one center split into 185 E. coli cases and 91 K. pneumoniae cases for comparison. The Klebsiella group carried higher severity scores and more carbapenem resistance, a last-line drug class. The E. coli group showed more ESBL enzyme carriage and quinolone resistance. Carbapenem-resistant cases faced a 90.0 percent mismatch rate for first therapy and 60.0 percent mortality in the reported subgroup. Thirty-day survival did not split clearly by germ.
pmc-13311158:
Elisandra Bárbara Pontes Carlos writes a 2026 letter on total nail ruin tied to complex regional pain syndrome. A man aged 20 years suffered a motorcycle crash that tore shoulder nerve roots. Three months later all five fingernails on the hurt hand decayed fully, with pain crises and clean skin ulcers on the same arm.

The syndrome brings lasting pain, swelling, vessel instability, skin change, and bone loss after nerve injury. Nails suffer through faulty nerve control and small vessel shifts. The other hand stayed normal, which ties the nail change to the injured limb. Rare nail signs should prompt checks for the wider syndrome.
pmc-13311758:
J Sherally and colleagues report their 2026 participatory survey on sexual and reproductive health among refugee women at the Mavrovouni center on Lesbos, Greece. Nine refugee co-researchers helped design and run the study.

The household survey held 119 questions across eight health areas and reached 247 women of reproductive age in June and July 2023. Birth care looked strong, with most mothers getting antenatal care and assisted births. Care after birth lagged, with nearly half of mothers getting none despite frequent complications. Only 24 percent used modern contraception in this group, and fertility treatment wishes went unmet. Gaps cluster after birth and in family planning.
pmc-13311858:
Shakir Husain Hakim and co-authors describe their 2026 technique for clearing extensive clots from the brain's vein channels when standard tools fail. They name the method pipeline-pigging.

A patient with widespread cerebral venous sinus thrombosis kept worsening despite blood thinners, and standard suction and stent tools could not reopen the channels. The team used a stiff angioplasty balloon to break up the clot while suction ran, plus a clot-dissolving drug placed inside the sinus. Near-complete reopening and a good clinical result followed. The authors present the trick as a cheap, effective backup for stubborn cases, with a literature review alongside.
pmc-13311958:
Nergis Nina Suleiman and co-authors report a 2026 randomized crossover trial testing whether ultrasound guidance improves maxillary nerve blocks in children having cleft palate surgery. These blocks ease pain after repair, and guidance by ultrasound is widely assumed to beat the older landmark technique. Twenty children received both approaches, one on each side, with the side chosen at random, and magnetic resonance imaging then showed where the anesthetic had actually spread.

Anesthetic reached the target fossa and touched the nerve in 13 of 20 landmark blocks and 14 of 20 ultrasound blocks, a difference well within chance. No complications occurred with either technique. Since roughly two-thirds of blocks succeeded regardless of guidance, the authors suggest good pain control does not depend on imaging equipment being available. Future effort, they argue, should go toward raising the success rate of the block itself.
pmc-13312058: Min Zhang and co-authors published this 2026 correction notice for their earlier review of miR-17 and its role in development and cancer. The notice fixes the author affiliations, which had wrongly listed three institutions instead of Yan'an Medical College of Yan'an University alone. It also repairs the author roles: Zhang had been marked as a corresponding author in error, while Feng Hui Wang holds that role. The authors apologize and state that the scientific conclusions of the original article are unchanged.
pmc-13312158:
Shane W. Adams and colleagues present a 2026 cross-sectional study of lasting health problems in active-duty United States special operations personnel seeking treatment. Repeated brain injuries, musculoskeletal damage, and chronic stress are common in this group, yet the full mix of their after-effects has rarely been mapped in one sample.

The study covered 222 personnel and combined 31 measures of behavior, biology, and body function. Symptoms were widespread: sleep problems touched 92.8 percent of the group, and pain, headaches, mental health, and heart-metabolic complaints each affected roughly four in five. Factor analysis found five symptom groupings, and about a third of participants fell into a profile of broad disruption across many domains at once. A dysphoric arousal pattern was the most common mental health picture, ahead of classic anxiety, depression, or post-traumatic stress.
pmc-13312358:
Brian J Biroscak and Peter S Hovmand argue, in a 2026 position paper, that developmental evaluation deserves wider use in clinical and translational science. The standard approach follows a fixed sequence of design, rollout, and measurement, assuming stable conditions. Translational projects rarely offer that stability. They cross scientific paradigms, workplace cultures, and regulatory regimes, and they change as they go. End-of-project verdicts then arrive too late to steer them.

Developmental evaluation instead embeds the evaluator as a critical friend who feeds learning back all along while the work unfolds. The paper contrasts the two approaches across purpose, feedback timing, who gets a say, and decision-making. This style fits complex, uncertain, evolving efforts such as pilot digital health tools. Established trials with fixed protocols remain better served by traditional designs. The authors present complexity not as a nuisance but as the very reason to evaluate differently.
pmc-13312658:
Rebecca Stenberg presents a 2026 document study of how Swedish elderly care prepares for residents with dementia going missing. National dementia guidelines exist, but none set standards for preventing, handling, or following up such episodes. Each municipality writes its own routines, with real risk of harm while a person is gone.

Stenberg collected instructions, checklists, and routines from one county council and eight municipalities covering care homes and home care. Every set of documents showed gaps: texts were rarely updated, prevention leaned almost entirely on technical aids, and staff understanding of risks and police procedures was thin. Instructions could delay calling the police by hours or even days, and neither residents nor their families were involved in prevention or risk assessment. The author argues that care built purely on voluntariness and freedom does not by itself keep people safe.
pmc-13315058:
Lena Easton-Calabria and colleagues measure indoor heat in New Orleans homes in their 2026 study. Extreme heat is a growing health risk, and the worst harm lands indoors, yet most research watches outdoor air and neighborhoods.

The team surveyed residents and logged indoor temperature for 2-week spans in 114 households across two heat-vulnerable wards, across the warm seasons of 2023 and 2024, as the design states. Surveys mixed set questions with open ones on cooling access and energy costs. The aim was to learn which homes overheat and what predicts it, inside the real limits of high bills and patchy air conditioning. Their findings point to cheap, fair fixes for a city where heat and poverty overlap.
pmc-13315458:
Fabio HB da Costa and co-authors tested in 2026 whether blocking the ATR kinase can help immune therapy work better in head and neck cancer. The drug AZD6738 was studied in squamous cell cancer of the head and neck, a common cancer where over half of patients still die of the disease.

Adding ATR blockade strengthened anti-PD-1 treatment by reshaping the tumor immune setting. Killer T cells rose, while regulatory T cells and suppressive myeloid cells fell. The treatment also pushed macrophages toward an attacking state through the cGAS and STING pathway, cut STAT3 activity, raised interferon signals, and lowered a cell-change program tied to spread.
pmc-13315558:
Marcel Bawej and colleagues tested artificial insemination in 2026 for the grey partridge, a European bird whose wild numbers have fallen fast. Captive breeding supports wild stocks, but no set insemination method existed, so the team studied short storage of semen and how dose and extender fluid affect fertility.

Semen from 15 males was pooled, diluted, and stored for 24 hours at 5 degrees in two extenders, EK and Lake. Storage cut motility, survival, and normal shape counts. EK kept survival and shape better, while Lake held motion steadier. Eggs laid after insemination were incubated to measure true fertility under each condition.
pmc-13315758:
Bui Hai Hoang and co-authors report in 2026 a case where standard therapy seemed to fail in severe melioidosis, a dangerous infection from Burkholderia pseudomallei. A 39-year-old man with diabetes and chronic hepatitis B first improved on ceftazidime for spread infection, then relapsed after only one week of oral follow-up drugs.

On return he had septic shock and many deep abscesses. He steadied on meropenem plus ceftazidime, then worsened on meropenem alone even though lab tests said the germ was sensitive. Recovery followed when high-dose ceftazidime was restored and abscesses were drained. The case questions relying on lab sensitivity alone. His care team had to change course more than once.
pmc-13316158:
Yingmei Wu and co-authors modified cassava starch in 2026 to make it better at wrapping olive oil in tiny capsules. Plain cassava starch resists water poorly and firms up again after cooking, which limits capsule use, so the team combined high-speed shearing, esterification, and both steps together.

Shearing alone raised solubility, swelling, and clarity, but broke particles and damaged crystal order, which then helped the chemical step work better. The combined starch beat ester-only starch on modification gains. Structure, thickening, and flow traits were tracked to judge the new material for food and delivery uses.
pmc-13316258:
S. McInerney, P.S. Hall, and K. Cresswell survey in 2026 large language models in oncology, weighing promise against pitfalls on the road to routine use. UK and European cancer services face rising demand, with diagnoses projected to grow by 21 percent by 2040 in the cited forecast, and systems already strained.

Language models could automate record searches, support decisions, and draft summaries, and patients now say they asked ChatGPT where they once turned to search engines. One review counted 4,609 clinical studies in under four years. Yet expected productivity gains have not arrived, and safe adoption needs care.
pmc-13316558:
Meiqi Wang and co-authors report a 2026 feeding study on Huoyan geese, testing whether an amino acid supplement called N-carbamylglutamate improves down yield and quality. The thyroid gland drives feather growth, so the team also read thyroid genes to trace the mechanism.

A flock of 240 young female geese split into control and supplemented groups for 293 days. Supplemented birds gave more total down, longer chest clusters, and finer fibers. Their skin follicle ratios and thyroid shapes shifted in ways that suggest higher activity, even though hormone T4 levels held steady. Gene reads found 122 genes turned up and 1,663 turned down. The results give goose breeders a diet lead worth testing at farm scale.
pmc-13316658:
Yuanjiang Zheng and colleagues report a 2026 case of invasive mucormycosis, a fast fungal attack, growing inside the windpipe of a patient with diabetic ketosis. The infection is rare in the central airway, looks vague on early scans, and kills often.

An emergency tracheostomy opened the blocked airway, and camera views found broad white dead tissue below the voice box. Washing fluid and biopsy both showed the broad, ribbon-like fungal threads that confirm the disease. Strong antifungal drugs, local mist treatment, and repeat camera cleanings controlled the infection, yet the voice box sealed shut for good, leaving lasting dependence on the neck tube. Early suspicion in diabetic patients is the central lesson.
pmc-13316758:
Xiaotong Zhao and colleagues validated, in a 2026 methods study, a quicker way to measure vitamins A and E in infant formula, foods where exact levels are tightly regulated for baby health. Standard testing is slow and fussy for such complex, fatty samples.

Their method merges soap-style breakdown and extraction into one preparation step, skipping the usual salt stage, then reads the vitamins on a fast liquid chromatography system. Recovery ran from 83.2 to 100.5 percent across the tested forms, with tight repeatability. Results matched a gold-standard isotope method and a certified reference powder. The test also worked on milk, yogurt, and dairy drinks, suiting it for routine factory quality checks.
pmc-13318258:
Gaurav Sanghvi and co-authors review erythropoietin in a 2026 survey of tissue engineering and wider medical uses, moving well beyond the hormone's familiar job of driving red blood cell production. Attention falls on repair, new blood vessel growth, nerve protection, and immune effects.

Delivery routes covered include fixing the protein onto scaffolds, packing it into gels, and using altered cells that release it locally. Reported gains span bone, cartilage, nerve, heart, dental tissue, and skin, along with wound healing, organoid work, and cancer studies. Keeping the protein active, releasing it in a controlled way, and avoiding off-target harm remain open problems, as does its double-edged role in tumours.
pmc-13318558:
Ronak J Mahatme and colleagues ask, in 2026, whether birth control pills relate to outcomes after knee ligament reconstruction in young women. Sex hormones affect connective tissue and pain processing, so a link is plausible. The team used a multicentre health database covering females aged 14 to 40 having arthroscopic surgery.

After matching on background factors, 815 pill users were compared with 815 non-users. Pill users had markedly lower rates of chronic knee instability at two years and lower early opioid use after surgery. Reoperation, chronic knee pain, stiffness needing manipulation and infection rates did not differ between groups. The authors present hormone status as a potentially changeable factor in recovery, while noting the study shows association rather than proof of cause.
pmc-13318658:
HyoEun Park, GyeongSook Park, and HwaYoung Kim describe a 2026 nursing education study. They built a home-visit simulation programme about preventing frailty in older adults. Then they tested it on undergraduate nursing students. The design measured students before and after, without a separate control group.

Fifty students took part in the programme. Clinical judgment scores improved clearly after the simulation. Hands-on clinical performance improved as well. Self-efficacy, though, did not change in a meaningful way. Better-rated simulation quality tracked with stronger judgment and performance gains. Self-efficacy linked more closely to satisfaction with the major itself. The authors present home-visit simulation as a useful teaching strategy for community nursing skills.
pmc-13319058:
Kian Emami, Jane Norman, and Titus Augustine report a 2026 retrospective study of post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder at a Manchester transplant centre. The dangerous overgrowth follows long immune suppression and often Epstein-Barr virus activity. Records covered 73 kidney and pancreas transplant patients diagnosed between 2002 and 2025.

Diagnosis came a median of 132 months after transplant. Over half the cases appeared more than ten years out. The commonest type was a diffuse large B-cell lymphoma pattern. Belly symptoms and general B symptoms led presentations. Bleeding or anaemia significantly tracked with slower diagnosis. Remission, full or partial, was achieved in 75 percent of patients. Five-year survival reached 68 percent in the cohort. The authors want faster referral routes and a national registry.
pmc-13320458:
Tingting Yang and co-authors treat chilled tilapia fish with cold plasma in a 2026 study of flavor change in storage. Chilled fish loses flavor fast as fats sour and germs spoil the flesh, a top snag for sellers. Cold plasma is a charged gas that makes reactive forms. It was blown in three gas mixes with low, mid, and high oxygen shares to see how gas choice steers scent over days in the fridge.

Sixty six scent compounds were tracked, with a few sharp aldehydes and a mushroom like alcohol as lead notes. The high oxygen mix lifted total aldehydes by near two thirds in the counts reported, while the low oxygen mix best balanced gains against off notes at day eight. Germ off scents fell under all plasma mixes, and one scent tied closely to fat cutting enzymes.
pmc-13320558:
Yibo Wang, Andi Zhang, and Jianping Ge rank copper trade strength across Belt and Road countries in a 2026 study. Copper is vital for power and industry, and supply shocks worry many states. The team built a broad strength score and tracked 63 countries from 2004 to 2023.

Overall strength rose over time, yet the gap between strong and weak countries widened. Central and Eastern Europe formed a lasting strong core, while West Asia and the Middle East lagged. Most of the leader gap traced to joint institutions and global engagement. Joining the Belt and Road plan itself lifted strength, though gains varied by timing and place. Fairer, targeted policy design is urged.
pmc-13321158:
Xinyu Xu and co-authors sort tinnitus patients into mental health risk groups and build a prediction chart in a 2026 study. Ringing in the ears varies widely in its emotional burden, and tools for early risk sorting were lacking. The team enrolled 534 patients with subjective tinnitus and scored anxiety, depression, life events, and social support.

Profile analysis found four groups, led by a well adapted group at 43.82 percent of patients in the study. A severe anxiety isolated group, at 28.09 percent, was classed as the high distress target. Clinical traits were compared across groups, and a visual nomogram was built from independent predictors and checked with standard accuracy and calibration tests.
pmc-13321458:
Sai Krishna Vallamchetla and co-authors review case reports of Guillain-Barré syndrome after brain bleeding in a 2026 systematic review. The syndrome is an immune attack on nerves with varied triggers, and recent reports place it after intracranial haemorrhage. Searches of two databases to February 2023 found 23 cases from 11 countries.

Patients averaged 60.1 years of age, and weakness began a median of 9 days after the bleed. Bleeding inside the brain was the most common prior event, at 39.1 percent of cases in the review. Illness was severe, with breathing failure needing a ventilator in 78.3 percent of cases. Axonal forms fared worse than demyelinating forms.
pmc-13322858:
Xue Lv and co-authors test spectral CT as a way to track bone change linked to fructose intake in rats, in a 2026 pilot study. Eighteen young male rats were split between normal food with fructose water and normal food with sterile water, for eight weeks.

Scans at weeks 0, 4 and 8 measured calcium, phosphorus and hydroxyapatite values in the left femur, and bone tissue was checked after week 8. The fructose group showed higher bone volume and thicker, more numerous trabeculae at week 8, and its scan values rose above controls only at that point. Scan values also tracked the tissue measures closely, supporting live and repeated imaging of bone change.
pmc-13323158:
Liqi Shu and colleagues build, in 2026, a risk model for stroke occurring within thirty days around a medical procedure, using routine electronic health record data. Such strokes are uncommon overall but cluster in heart, major vessel and brain procedures. Existing calculators often exclude exactly those settings and ignore vessel disease markers sitting in the chart.

The model was derived from over a quarter million procedures at one Rhode Island hospital and tested, unchanged, on nearly one hundred ninety thousand procedures at two sister hospitals. Stroke rates were low in both sets. Prior stroke or mini-stroke, inpatient or emergency setting, vascular brain surgery and open heart procedures were the strongest predictors. Accuracy was high in both cohorts and predicted risks matched observed rates well. A web calculator is offered for counselling and targeted prevention.
pmc-13323558:
Ziyang Xu, Shanshan Huang, and Qian Chu review the growing evidence that nerves and lung tumors talk to each other, shaping how cancers grow and spread. Their 2026 paper draws on cancer neuroscience, a field that studies nerve signals inside tumors, nerve growth into tumor tissue, and synapse-like links between nerves and cancer cells. It notes that blocking beta-adrenergic signals has been linked in several settings to slower lung tumor growth and less spread.

The review organizes the evidence around nerve remodeling in the tumor environment, the routes by which neural signals drive tumor formation and metastasis, and the three-way link among nerves, immunity, and tumors. From that map, the authors point to neuro-modulatory treatments as a possible new avenue, alongside existing therapies. The piece aims to give researchers a shared framework for testing which nerve-based targets could one day be turned into real treatments.
pmc-13323858:
Muhammad Abdul Mabood Khalil and co-authors study the neglected tubulointerstitial compartment in lupus nephritis, in a 2026 study of 100 biopsy-proven patients from Saudi Arabia. Standard grading centres on glomeruli, yet inflammation and damage between the tubules may steer kidney outcomes.

Patients with both tubulointerstitial inflammation and damage, 48 of the cohort, started with lower filtration rates and higher LDL cholesterol than the other 52 patients, plus higher activity scores on biopsy indices. Regression models hunted predictors of the combined pattern, while survival analysis tracked kidney response and poor composite outcomes over follow-up. The authors argue this compartment deserves a formal place in lupus kidney assessment in Middle Eastern care.
pmc-13325158:
Hanne Berggreen and colleagues characterize a chitin-cutting enzyme from a gut-friendly bacterium in a 2026 study. Lactiplantibacillus plantarum holds one LPMO gene yet lacks the usual chitin-breaking toolkit, which makes the enzyme a puzzle.

The enzyme, LpLPMO10A, was produced in its home species and in a host strain for comparison. Modeling grouped it with classic chitin-active LPMOs, and assays showed it cleaves chitin into oxidized products. Its behavior closely matched the Serratia enzyme SmLPMO10A, a known chitin degrader. It even beat the Bacillus enzyme, whose owner carries full chitin machinery. Activity barely shifted across pH 5 to 7. Why the bacterium keeps the enzyme remains open.
pmc-13325858:
Takumi Kagawa and colleagues expose mice to device-like environmental noise to find which part harms the kidney in a 2026 study. Human surveys link noise with kidney trouble, but the guilty frequencies were unknown.

Mice heard whole device noise, low-frequency noise at or below 100 Hz, or higher tones for 12 hours a day over five days. Whole noise at up to 88 dBA raised creatinine and blood urea nitrogen. Low tones alone at up to 70 dBA copied the harm, while higher tones did not. Kidney tissue showed vessel injury markers and swollen filtering units. Blocking endothelin signaling eased both blood markers and tissue damage.
pmc-13325958:
Synnøve Næss Sleire and colleagues track iron stores in Norwegian mothers and infants across pregnancy and after birth in a 2026 longitudinal study. Iron shortfalls threaten mother, fetus, and child, yet local data were thin.

A cohort of 137 women gave blood at weeks 18 and 36 of pregnancy and at 3 and 6 months after delivery, alongside their babies. Iron deficiency among women jumped from 14 percent at week 18 to 65 percent by week 36 on ferritin cutoffs. Depleted stores reached 95 percent late in pregnancy. Infants fared far better, with 90 percent still sufficient at 6 months. Supplement use and breastfeeding showed no link to levels.
pmc-13326458:
Chin-Ying Hsu and colleagues upgrade the 30-second sit-to-stand test with phone video and machine learning in a 2026 study. Counting rises alone misses the wobble and strategy shifts that mark weakening legs.

Thirty-two community-dwelling older adults, 18 normal and 14 weak, were filmed at baseline and months later. Pose software pulled 17 joint points from the phone videos, feeding balance and movement measures. Peak and shape measures of body sway flagged weak participants better than simple averages. Weak adults also shrank their movement range as a guarding tactic. Random forest sorting scored an area under the curve of 0.993 in this small cohort. The setup suits home screening.
pmc-13327658:
Guoyuan He, Aichun Yang, and Hechun Xia search for hub genes after spinal cord injury in a 2026 data study. Cell stress in the protein-folding compartment, and the rescue response it triggers, shape the second wave of damage after injury, yet their links to immune entry were murky. The team mined public RNA datasets and checked findings in mice.

Injury samples showed higher stress scores that rose alongside immune cell entry, and network analysis pointed to two hub genes, Dnajc3 and Hspa5. Only Hspa5 held up across an outside cohort, single-cell data, and mouse tissue checks, while a combined score from both genes separated injury from control samples with an AUC of 0.745 in their model. Hspa5 stands out as a target candidate.
pmc-13327858:
Takuya Yogo proposes a mechanism-based framework for treating dog eye ulcers in a 2026 conceptual article. Corneal ulcers in dogs are common and can melt through the surface or burst if mishandled. Extra treatments have long centered on blocking collagen breakdown, judged by how bad the ulcer looks rather than what drives it.

Drawing on dog, animal, and human studies from 2000 to early 2026, Yogo sets out four treatment domains plus a tailoring layer. Preserving structure, through protease blocking, ranks first when melting is active, followed by calming inflammation, boosting surface repair, and steadying the eye surface. Matching treatment to the dominant driver, not just the ulcer's look, is the core message.
pmc-13327958:
Pavel A Solopov and co-authors test a phosphatase blocker against alcohol-amplified lung injury in mice in a 2026 study. Heavy drinking raises the risk of severe lung failure, and the COVID-19 spike protein alone can injure lungs, worse still in alcohol-fed animals. The drug KVX-053 blocks PTP4A3, a regulator of inflammation and vessel leak.

Mice on alcohol diets showed more white cells and protein leakage in lung wash fluid after spike exposure, plus higher IL-6, TNF-α, and TGF-β signals. Daily KVX-053 for three days blunted each of those changes, restoring barrier tightness and quieting the NF-κB, STAT3, and inflammasome pathways. pmc-13383858:

pmc-13384058:

pmc-13384758:

pmc-13386158:

pmc-13386558:

pmc-13386758:
Ruisi Xie and colleagues compare two overnight lens designs for slowing childhood myopia in a 2026 one-year trial. pmc-13388658:

pmc-13389058:

pmc-13389558:

pmc-13390358:

pmc-13390458:

pmc-13392458:
Xiangyu Li's team boosted crystal-organic tandem solar cells by adding a clumping-induced output compound to the organic sub-cell, tackling its large voltage deficit from non-light merging. Mainstream non-carbon-ball acceptors suffer clumping-caused dimming and low glow yield.

Paired with a wide-band gap crystal, the tandem reached 26.5 percent power conversion efficiency, confirmed at 25.8 percent.
pmc-13392658:
Siti Rakhma Afriana, Widagdo Sri Nugroho, and Widodo Suwito screened Australian beef cattle held in quarantine in Indonesia for a dangerous strain of Escherichia coli that can cause severe food poisoning. pmc-13393258:

pmc-13394458:

A full wafer held a grid of 32 by 32 sensing points.

Every point in the grid worked, with small spread between them. The array answered in just over two milliseconds and stored light levels in five-bit steps. After brief training it named motion direction with near-perfect scores. The authors pitch the chip for cars, traffic watch, and guard systems.
pmc-13394558:

pmc-13394858:

Pooled results point to gains in planning and self-control skills. Proof grade was moderate, though the range of true effects crossed zero. pmc-13394958:
Anpei Li and others test a SETD2 block to boost a menin drug in MLL-fusion blood cancer in a 2026 study. SETD2, a gene-marking enzyme, has played a two-faced role in this blood cancer, curbing tumors when lost yet marking grim odds when raised high.

pmc-13395258:
Tianya Liu, Ji Wu, and Ivan Steenstra test, in 2026, how sharing blame with AI shapes doctors' judgement. Ninety-six doctors worked ten case puzzles in a mock clinic. pmc-13395358:

pmc-13395458:

pmc-13396058:

pmc-13396558:

pmc-13396658:

pmc-13396858:

pmc-13397658:

pmc-13398158:

pmc-13398758:

pmc-13399158:

pmc-13399358:

pmc-13399858:

pmc-13400658:

pmc-13401158:

pmc-13401458:

pmc-13402258:

pmc-13403358:

pmc-13403458:

pmc-13403758:

pmc-13404858:

pmc-13407758:

pmc-13408058:

pmc-13408158:

pmc-13408358:

pmc-13409558:
Cristina Benites and co-authors gather in 2026 every reported case of an inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour inside the jawbone, thirteen in all, and add a fourteenth of their own.
