Their new patient is a fifteen-year-old girl.

Her tumour was removed and the jaw rebuilt in the same operation using the approach nicknamed jaw in a day, restoring normal mouth function with no recurrence at one year. Across the reviewed cases, complete surgical removal likewise produced favourable outcomes. The authors detail the imaging features. They name the look-alike diagnoses pathologists must exclude, and the molecular markers that secure the identification. Oral surgeons gain a compact reference for a tumour most will never see.
pmc-13411158:
Yiming Liu and co-authors survey in 2026 how nanotechnology might calm the misdirected immune attack behind Sjögren's syndrome. The disease dries eyes and mouth as immune cells invade tear and saliva glands. Today's care mostly eases symptoms or damps the whole immune system, without repairing glands.

The battleground is the local immune neighborhood: gland cells, immune cells, signal proteins, and stray lymph tissue. Tiny carriers can aim drugs squarely at that neighborhood. Platforms covered include polymer and fat particles, mineral particles, body-mimicking shells, and gels. Goals stretch beyond quieting inflammation toward restoring immune tolerance and regrowing working glands, with smart, computer-designed carriers flagged as the next wave.
pmc-13411358:
Peng-Yu Chen and co-workers test in 2026 a sponge-derived compound against aggressive mouth cancer cells. Oral squamous cell carcinoma spreads readily and ends poorly for many patients. The compound, stellettin B, comes from the marine sponge Jaspis stellifera.

In two cancer cell lines the compound halted growth while sparing normal mouth lining cells. Death came mainly through a backup route: two DNA-cutting proteins moved from the cell's power stations into the nucleus after damage, bypassing the usual executioner enzymes. Spread slowed as cell identity markers flipped back toward a settled, less mobile state. Gene scans also showed quieter growth signaling. Early dish results mark the compound as a candidate worth animal testing.
pmc-13415558:
Uri Bright and colleagues run the largest genetic study yet of fibromyalgia, in 2026. Their genome wide search combined cohorts holding 85,139 cases and over 1.6 million controls across European, African, and Latin American ancestry groups. Extra power came from borrowing related pain study data in a multi-trait analysis.

Ten loci linked to fibromyalgia in European ancestry participants, one in African ancestry, and twelve across ancestries. Most loci were already tied to pain, thinking, autoimmunity, or general health. Genetic overlap ran strong with chronic pain, post-traumatic stress, and depression, each at correlation levels near or above 0.69. Modeling placed fibromyalgia mainly among pain and autoimmune traits, with nerve mechanisms underneath.
pmc-13415658:
Michelle Juknaviciute Laursen and colleagues dissect how the human lipid flippase ATP8B1 switches itself off, in 2026. Flippases move fats between membrane layers to keep cell surfaces asymmetric. Many carry tail extensions that brake their own activity, and this team tested tail pieces as synthetic peptides against a shortened enzyme.

The far end of the tail proved key, likely touching the enzyme's inner domains in passing. One contact pair stood out: an arginine in the tail binding a glutamate in the moving A domain. A short peptide spanning just thirteen tail residues was enough to inhibit the enzyme. Faults in this flippase cause a liver disease, so activation strategies matter.
pmc-13415758:
Mathou and colleagues compare the brains of four shrimp species at hydrothermal vents, asking how nervous systems adapt to darkness, pressure, and plumes. Vent shrimps occupy niches around the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, from dense swarms to loners farther out. Their 2026 study uses tissue staining, antibody markers, micro CT scans, and 3D rebuilds. It maps the brain and its blood supply in the four vent species, plus a coastal relative.

All vent species shared a brain with mushroom bodies, hubs where senses merge and memories form, outsized for their build. Their visual centers shrank against the coastal shrimp's, fitting the near dark, while the retina stretched along the back, longest in swarm formers. A visual satellite center was missing in vent species, hinting they barely track motion. Smell lobes kept one layout but varied in size and count by species, matching each niche's chemistry and diet.
pmc-13417858:
Sanchit Mehta and co-authors trace a fatal course of methotrexate poisoning in a 64 year old with lymphoma, in a 2026 case report. The chemotherapy drug had been tolerated before, yet prior heart damage from anthracycline treatment changed its handling. After infusion for brain directed therapy, the patient developed kidney shutdown, low blood pressure, and shock.

Drug levels stayed extremely high despite an antidote enzyme and dialysis. Fluid around the lung held a large drug store, a third space trap that kept leaking drug back into the blood. Clearance took 35 days of continuous dialysis, and the patient moved to comfort care. Heart failure is flagged as a key risk.
pmc-13418458:
Chail Shah and colleagues reviewed in 2026 a lethal overlap syndrome that strikes intensive-care patients on cancer immunotherapy. Checkpoint drugs can unleash a triple attack resembling myasthenia gravis plus muscle inflammation plus heart muscle inflammation, mimicking sepsis, pneumonia, clots, and heart failure at first glance.

Early antibody tests and heart imaging often look normal, so the review urges fast multi-system checks with muscle enzymes, serial troponins, heart tracings, and imaging, alongside infection screening and prompt drug withdrawal. Critical-care teams gain a structured rescue path for a syndrome where hours and missed heart inflammation decide survival.
pmc-13418558:
Preeti Sinha and a large team run a pilot trial of probiotics added to standard care for depression in older adults, published in 2026. Fifty eight patients aged 60 or more with moderate unipolar depression were randomised at two centres to daily probiotics or placebo for 12 weeks, with 12 more weeks of follow up. The strains were Lactobacillus helveticus and Bifidobacterium longum.

Depression and anxiety scores improved over time in both groups, with modestly lower overall scores in the probiotic group, though change patterns did not differ significantly. Quality of life rose in both groups equally. A brain growth factor rose higher with probiotics. Over half the participants dropped out, limiting conclusions.
pmc-13418758:
Felix Seelemeyer and colleagues weigh reusable against single-use flexible scopes for bladder checks in outpatient urology. Their 2026 study comes from a German center that performs 337 of these checks each year, many for bladder cancer follow-up. The team counted the full cost of each route, from purchase and repairs to cleaning and staff time.

Cost models covered both a basic setup and full gear replacement, with break-even points worked out for each. A survey added the views of 13 physicians and 25 nursing staff across five practices, scored on set scales. Staff rated both scope types on image quality, handling, and daily workflow fit. The paired cost and user data give clinics a grounded way to choose between the two systems for routine work.
pmc-13419958:
Fang-Hui Zhu and colleagues pool studies comparing catheter valve replacement in patients born with a two-leaflet aortic valve against the usual three-leaflet form. The two-leaflet form is a major cause of valve narrowing, yet trial proof for the catheter route in these patients stayed thin. Their search covered four major databases for studies with one-year outcomes.

The pool held 31 studies and 192,691 patients in total, a very large base for this question. Death from any cause at one year ran lower in the two-leaflet group, with pooled odds of 0.84 in the reported model, while heart-related death showed no firm gap between groups. Safety and benefit profiles otherwise looked alike. The results ease fears that the catheter method suits only standard valve anatomy.
pmc-13420258:
Mu Qin and colleagues build a tiny drug carrier that releases its cargo in acid, aimed at retinoblastoma, the main eye cancer of childhood. Care for this cancer is hampered by the blood-retina barrier, drug resistance, and harsh side effects on the whole body. Their carrier wraps the repurposed drug nitazoxanide inside a metal-framework shell that breaks down where tissue turns acidic.

The particles loaded drug to roughly 58.6 percent of their mass in the reported figure and measured near 231 nanometers across, a size suited to reaching tumor tissue. Acid-triggered release kept the drug held at body-neutral conditions and freed it in tumor-like acidity. Two effects at once, carrier plus drug, slowed tumor growth more than either alone in the study's tests. The system offers a template for gentler eye cancer care in children.
pmc-13420858:
Victor Ogutu and colleagues pooled 25 studies with 1624 children in 2026 to estimate how often clubfoot returns after Ponseti treatment. The casting and bracing method corrects most feet at first, yet relapse during childhood varies widely across reports, leaving families and clinics unsure what to expect.

The paper gives orthopedic teams a global relapse benchmark and a risk-factor synthesis for targeting follow-up and brace adherence, and family counseling in follow-up care.
pmc-13421358:
Parner and colleagues report a 2026 study of worry after major emergency abdominal surgery at a Copenhagen hospital. Patients rated their degree of worry at discharge and at one, three, and six months. The team linked worry levels to days alive and out of hospital.

High worry was common but uneven over time: about a third of patients at discharge, a fifth at one month, then nearly half at three months, and a third at six months. Fear of relapse was the most frequent worry, followed by disease itself, daily function, and daily living. Worries about the body stayed prominent across the period. Tracking worry itself could help teams time support to when anxiety resurfaces.
pmc-13421458:
Y. N. Vashisht Gopal leads a large team testing, in a 2026 preclinical study, personalised drug combinations for melanoma that has stopped responding to BRAF and MEK inhibitors. pmc-13421758:
Christy Bills and five colleagues tell, in a 2026 paper, how citizen scientists found flashing fireflies across Utah, where their presence in the American West was long an open question. A public outreach campaign and an interactive reporting website invited sightings over nearly a decade.

Reports passed 135 distinct localities, verified where possible by site visits and collected specimens. The flood of public data brought headaches — sightings outside the target area and worries about private land — handled by refining the reporting protocol and outreach as the project grew. Media and school engagement widened the haul. The authors plan a western-states expansion with partner organisations, and they present the project as a model for community-engaged species mapping.
pmc-13422358:
Harmke van Kooten and colleagues compared heart risk in 2026 between 78 adults with late-onset Pompe disease and 78 matched controls. The muscle-wasting disease may carry extra heart risk, yet whether risk factors or actual heart events run higher was unclear.

Patients showed faster resting heart rates, larger waists, and more hypertension history, yet past heart events, 19 versus 9 cases, did not differ significantly. The paper advises heart-risk monitoring in Pompe care without overstating event risk, pending larger cohorts. Clinicians can still act on the risk profile with standard heart prevention.
pmc-13422858:
Karar Zunaid Ahsan leads a six-author team asking, in a 2026 study, whether better-equipped health facilities close the wealth gap in Bangladeshi mothers' care. Linking three rounds of national maternal and facility surveys at district level, the team adapted a difference-in-differences design to compare gap changes in high-readiness districts against the rest. Overall use rose substantially, yet the gains were unevenly shared: equity improved only modestly for antenatal care and complication management. The authors conclude readiness alone does not deliver fairness.
pmc-13423158:
Caterina Matucci-Cerinic and five co-authors systematically review anakinra, an inflammation-blocking drug, for Kawasaki disease that resists standard immunoglobulin treatment. Between 10% and 20% of children with this vessel-inflaming illness fail the first therapy, and those children face a higher risk of coronary artery aneurysms, making rescue options important.

Fever and inflammation settled in 94.9% of treated patients. Existing artery aneurysms fully resolved in 32% of cases and shrank or stabilised in a further 56.3%. No serious safety signal appeared, though the authors stress how thin the data remain.
pmc-13423958:
Liao and co-authors introduce a training-data-free method for restoring damaged images, in this 2026 computer science paper. Such images are degraded by some mixture of blur, downscaling, noise, and missing pixels. Most modern restoration tools learn from huge paired datasets; their framework, MG-SpaIR, instead fits each corrupted image individually using an implicit neural representation, a network that encodes the picture itself.

The method refines the reconstruction in grades. It recovers broad structure first and fine detail later. That counters the known tendency of such networks to blur high frequencies. A sparsity penalty applied directly in the full-resolution image domain suppresses invented textures while keeping genuine edges sharp. The authors prove convergence of their alternating optimization under standard conditions. They report that the method consistently beat strong training-free baselines on mixed-degradation benchmarks. Deep Image Prior was among the baselines beaten.
pmc-13425458:
Mechati and colleagues published a 2026 study on making dye-cleaning particles from olive waste. Olive pomace, the pulp left after oil pressing, served as the natural helper. With it, the team grew magnesium oxide particles just nanometers wide. The particles were then tested on Congo red, a stubborn textile dye.

Lab checks confirmed clean, round crystals with a porous, active surface. The particles cleared more than nine-tenths of the dye within 30 minutes. Under tuned settings, removal passed 95 percent in their test runs. Computer models showed strong electric pulls between dye and particle surface sites. The work turns farm waste into a tool for cleaner wastewater. The method needs no harsh chemicals, which keeps the whole process green.
pmc-13425958:
Clio Berry and colleagues design a mentoring program to lift hope among young women in deprived coastal England who are out of school, work, and training. That group fares worse for mental health and social outcomes than peers who work or study, and coastal disadvantage deepens the gap.

The co-developed program, called HOPEFUL, is flexible and modular, helping each woman set and chase goals that matter to her, with a mentor she may pick from her own circle. This paper is the feasibility-stage protocol, testing whether a full trial can recruit and run. Services get a hopeful, person-led alternative to one-size-fits-all job schemes.
pmc-13426058:
Anton A. Gladkov and colleagues describe a light-driven route to aryl indium reagents in a 2026 chemistry article. Shining visible light from LEDs at 400, 455, and even 520 nanometers on indium(I) bromide mixtures generates a highly active low-valent indium species. That species performs halogen atom transfer, a trick rare for main-group metals and usually linked with transition metals, to form aryl radicals and then arylindium(III) products.

The method tolerates air, moisture, and many functional groups, works with or without a photocatalyst, and gives high yields simply. Resulting reagents can themselves release aryl radicals under photoredox conditions, creating a two-way bridge between single- and two-electron chemistry.
pmc-13426358:
Ammad Ahmad Farooqi and coauthors review natural products that target the NRF2 and KEAP1 pathway in a 2026 article framed around gentle, precise pharmacology. NRF2, discovered in 1994, sits at the center of a wide molecular web controlling cell defense responses, with many regulators upstream and targets downstream. Interest has surged in compounds that can tune this node for disease prevention and treatment.

Natural products with distinctive structural features and multipronged actions receive special attention as candidate modulators. The review maps the pathway landscape so drug hunters can spot where plant-derived chemistry might intervene safely.
pmc-13427458:
Yoshihito Mima, Masako Yamamoto, and Ken Iozumi report sleep gains with nemolizumab in prurigo nodularis in a 2026 retrospective study of 22 patients with refractory disease. This intensely itchy nodular skin condition wrecks sleep, mood, and social functioning, and easing itch is most patients' chief goal. Three patients stopped by week sixteen for asthma flare, swollen redness, or acute eczema, leaving the rest for analysis of sleep duration and night awakenings beyond standard itch scales. Real-world sleep data extend trial findings for a symptom patients rank first.
pmc-13427658:
Nana Li leads a huge multicenter team that built, in 2026, a tool to predict low blood oxygen during gut endoscopy under sedation. Such dips in oxygen are common and can turn serious, yet clinics lacked a purpose-built risk score. Data came from outpatients at seven hospitals across China between May 2020 and November 2023. The eight cover body mass index, throat and jaw features, tongue size, snoring history, neck shape, and starting blood pressure. Standard checks for sleep apnea and difficult airways fed the comparison work behind the model. Performance was judged on accuracy, calibration, and whether using the score would help real decisions. A separate patient group tested the model independently, a step many risk tools skip.
pmc-13427858:
Calegari and colleagues published a 2026 study on repeating DNA in two true bug species. Satellite DNA is stretch after stretch of the same short DNA code. These two Edessa bugs carry oddly large blocks of dense chromosome material. The team mapped their full sets of satellite DNA families in detail.

They found 31 satellite families shared between the two bug species. One species packed more satellite DNA with fresher, more uniform copies. The other held less, with older copies drifted further apart over time. The biggest families filled the ends of chromosomes in both species. Shared families back the idea of an ancestral library of repeats. Some families clustered on the Y chromosome, hinting at sex-linked roles.
pmc-13428158:
Chenxu Jia and colleagues reviewed natural products, meaning compounds from plants and other living sources, as possible treatments for osteosarcoma, a bone cancer. The cancer spreads often, most often to the lungs, and standard drugs lose effect as tumours grow resistant.

The review covers three big families of compounds, polyphenols, alkaloids, and terpenoids, and the cell pathways each one acts on. In lab studies, these compounds slowed tumour spread, reset the cell cycle, and pushed cancer cells toward orderly death. They also helped tumours respond again to standard chemotherapy drugs that had stopped working. Jia flags real limits, including liver harm from some compounds and poor uptake in the body, and urges better delivery designs.
pmc-13428258:
Iterbeke and colleagues test whether texture in muscle MRI scans can separate two genetic diseases that both waste muscle. One is myotonic dystrophy type 1, a muscle disease. The other is Charcot-Marie-Tooth type 1A, a nerve disease. A fat fraction map shows how much muscle has turned to fat but misses the pattern of the change. Both patient groups carried more fat in every leg muscle than controls. The geography differed: dystrophy hit the back compartment hardest, while the nerve disease hit the front outer compartment and faded from ankle to hip. Texture measures told the same story: the nerve disease's fat wove a net, with higher disorder readings, while dystrophy's fat pooled in smooth sheets. Adding texture to standard maps, the authors argue, sharpens non invasive diagnosis.
pmc-13430858:
Oluyinka Ajibola Iyiola and colleagues test how well malaria mozzies in Nigeria's Sudan Savannah zone still die from pyrethroid sprays and nets. These mozzies spread malaria across Africa south of the Sahara, and rising drug-proof traits now threaten vector control.

pmc-13431858:
Julie Considine and colleagues observe what emergency triage nurses actually do, beyond the triage desk, in Australian emergency departments. Triage nurses also manage waiting-area patients, yet the full scope of that role was little mapped.

Fifteen triage nurses from three Melbourne emergency departments were watched for two to two and a half hours each between January and May 2025, with lapel microphones recording the work. Transcripts were coded deductively against the HIRAID nursing framework, covering history, danger signs, assessment, actions, tests, re-checks, and talk. Managers get a grounded picture of triage work for staffing and training.
pmc-13432858:
Geoffrey Shouse reviewed in 2026 a twin-grip antibody drug for a slow-growing lymph cancer, gathering trial proof and real-world reads from 2020 on. The drug grabs one mark on cancer B cells and one on killer T cells, which drags the killers onto their prey. It holds approval for patients who have burned through at least two prior care rounds.

Trials show low rates of the grave immune storm that haunts this drug class, and fit patients can take doses as outpatients. Shouse walks through the drug's build, its mode of work, gains, and harms. The review frames the drug as a model of immune care gains in lymph cancers.
pmc-13432958:
Selma Kronsteiner-Gicevic and co-authors mined a vast British cohort in 2026 for ties between salt intake and fresh asthma in adults. Near twelve thousand new cases arose. The top fifth for urine salt marks met asthma at half again the rate of the low fifth. The tie ran stronger in women than men, in never-smokers than in past or live smokers, and in people with low counts of one white cell type. Always adding salt at the table also tracked with more new cases. The authors urge diet trials to test the salt link.
pmc-13434558:
Gaige Wang and colleagues scramble the atomic order of a fuel cell part in 2026 to make it work better on hydrocarbon fuels. Solid oxide cells turn fuels such as methane straight into power. Carbon buildup and slow fuel use have held back the anode, the fuel side part.

Five rare earth metals share one site in the new anode in equal parts. The mixed, disordered layout opens more oxygen gaps and holds water better. Those traits speed fuel cleaning and carbon removal at once. The cell gave strong power and ran past 1,000 hours on wet methane at 700 degrees. Disorder becomes a design tool.
pmc-13434658:
Cai and many collaborators identify the RNA helicase DP103 as a driver of Wnt signaling and stem-like behavior in triple-negative breast cancer, an aggressive subtype with no targeted therapies. pmc-13434758:
Kaleb Wagner and coauthors date the first huge Eurasian ice sheet to 2.4 million years ago in 2026. Gravel in the Netherlands carried there by ice tells the tale. Burial dating of two isotopes plus zircon fingerprints pin the gravel to Scandinavian ice.

The first ice push overlaps in time with the peak of the North American ice sheet. A second push 1.72 million years ago shut down the Baltic river system. Layer patterns hint at fresh water pulses into the North Atlantic. Paired timing ends a long mismatch between land and sea records. Both ice sheets grew large far earlier than once thought.
pmc-13435258:
Gomeni and Bressolle-Gomeni test deep learning as a partner for traditional drug development modeling in this 2026 paper. A neural network, by contrast, learns such patterns directly without a preset structure. It reached that performance while needing far fewer assumptions about the underlying system in advance. The authors argue the two styles are complementary: mechanistic models offer biological interpretability, deep learning offers flexible prediction, and combining them should strengthen drug development decisions.
pmc-13435758:
Ahmet Yılmaz, İbrahim Doyuran, and Mehmet Yiğit Gökmen compare hip replacement routes for a bone break risk in 2026. Charts cover 118 patients with cement free hip joints placed from 2019 to 2023. Twenty eight hips used a front side route, while ninety used a back side route.

Breaks at the greater trochanter struck 25.0 percent of front route hips versus 3.3 percent of back route hips. Within the front route, patients with breaks carried higher body weight scores. Hip function scores ended alike for both routes. Cup shift past two millimeters tracked worse function. Surgeons may weigh route and weight together when planning.
pmc-13436558:

The team searched three large databases for studies on case-based learning in obstetrics training, weighing gains, weak points, and open questions. Studies linked the method to stronger engagement, clinical reasoning, practical skills, and teamwork among residents. Results still hinged on teacher skill, case quality, and school resources, and most studies tracked only short-term gains. Chen sees promise in blended learning, simulation, and artificial intelligence tools, but notes that solid proof of long-term benefit is still missing.
pmc-13437658:
Emily Durant and colleagues asked what veterinary medicines in farm manure do to the fungi feeding crops from below ground. Spreading manure closes a nutrient loop, yet animal drugs ride along. Checks of farm reuse, they argue, should weigh living function underground, not only chemical leftovers.
pmc-13437958:
Hao Zhang and colleagues asked a question every exerciser faces: how fast do gains melt away when training stops? pmc-13439058:

pmc-13439358:

At two sites, lone drought years cut yearly plant growth by more than a tenth and net carbon uptake by a fifth to two fifths. Widespread yearly damage was rare, though. Dry air episodes have risen across the region in the last decade, which the authors name a likely factor in slower Nordic forest growth.
pmc-13439558:

Diagnosis also lagged at every step for that group, from first symptoms to confirmed imaging. The authors urge earlier vascular checks in this group.
pmc-13439758:

Brain teams get a more trustworthy papers and gene assistant. Its answers still need expert checking, especially for clinical decisions.
pmc-13440458:

Two side effects, rash and joint pain, did rise a bit with higher exposure, but the added chance was small and judged not clinically relevant. pmc-13440758:

Warming the base up to 150 degrees during deposit erased the islands. pmc-13441158:
Mpho R. Tlali's team surveyed suicidal thoughts and behaviors in 2026 in two Cape Town communities, recruiting 613 adults with and without HIV at public clinics. Diagnostic interviews measured ideation, attempts, violence exposure, stress, mental disorders, and HIV status, with effects expressed as percentage-point differences.

Past-month ideation hit fourteen percent and lifetime attempts twenty-two percent, with higher ideation among women, violence-exposed people, highly stressed people, and those with depression, PTSD, or alcohol use disorder. Stress and community violence links persisted after adjusting for mental disorders, while HIV showed no link. Public health teams get a social-determinants case for suicide prevention beyond clinic walls.
pmc-13444258:
Xuran Zhou and colleagues fix sound-speed warps in 3D photoacoustic scans without extra gear in a 2026 paper. The method images tissue by light-born sound, yet water and tissue carry sound at unlike speeds, which blurs edges and spawns ghosts. Past fixes fit crude shapes or bolt on costly ultrasound kits.

Their signal-only frame finds the true tissue edge in raw data from a 1,024-element bowl array. Self-set thresholds sort real signals from scatter spikes and flash arcs. A twin-speed model then re-times the waves with light compute load. Fake scenes, odd phantoms, and live mouse scans all sharpened under the fix. Liver microvessels regained crisp form in the mouse runs, the authors report.
pmc-13445958:
Yao Li and Xuejiao Du run two class experiments on which kind of cue in teaching videos helps students with weak attention, in a 2026 study. Cues come in two forms: visual marks that point at content, and social cues that mimic a teacher's gaze or gesture. Which form suits which attention weakness was unclear.

Those with low sustained attention transferred learning better after social cues than after visual ones. In the second study, one hundred four students with high or low selective attention took part. Those with low selective attention kept more after visual cues. The split gives video designers a rule: match the cue to the weakness.
pmc-13446358:

pmc-13447058:
Ning Dong and colleagues pool twenty-two studies to compare three artificial intelligence styles for judging whether hazy lung spots are invasive cancer, in a 2026 review. pmc-13447158:
Francisco Fernández and colleagues revisit in 2026 how much of the drug eculizumab is needed in blood to fully block a part of the immune system called complement. The drug treats several rare diseases, yet some patients respond poorly and need higher doses. A widely cited target range rests on weak data, which the team set out to test.

Adding carefully made synthetic data barely changed accuracy, yet it narrowed the uncertainty around the effective level a great deal. The steadier estimate sat well above the usual target range. Because the work generates hypotheses rather than proof, the authors require testing in fresh patient groups before any change to care.
pmc-13447358:
Ziyi Yan and a large team review how pneumococcal vaccines reshape antibiotic resistance in a 2026 mini review. Removing vaccine-targeted types that often carried resistance helps head-on, while fewer illnesses mean fewer antibiotic courses overall.

Bacteria can switch their outer coat type, shuffle resistance genes and pass mobile elements between lineages, so resistant clones can rebuild under vaccine pressure. pmc-13447558:
Connor Smith and colleagues report an extremely rare adrenal gland cancer in a 2026 case study. The tumour grows from blood vessel lining cells, appears in fewer than sixty reported adrenal cases, and usually carries a poor outlook. A seventy-year-old woman arrived with severe upper belly pain and a fast-growing right adrenal mass that lab tests showed made no hormones.

Scans showed a large, unevenly enhancing mass pressing on the main vein returning blood to the heart. Surgeons removed the gland by keyhole surgery, and tissue staining confirmed the rare diagnosis rather than spread from elsewhere. Chemotherapy with a standard agent followed, and she remained disease-free two years after surgery. Prompt removal plus chemotherapy can beat expectations, the authors argue, despite the tumour's aggressive nature.
pmc-13447858:
Xilai Hu and coauthors develop a 2026 bioactive scaffold for sick wounds, joining PLGA-tweaked gut lining with stem cells primed by astragaloside IV. The team tested strength, cell conduct, and healing in vitro and in a sick wound model.

The scaffold boosted strength and backed stem cell sticking and growth, while priming boosted living and healing signals VEGF and TGF-beta. In animals, treated wounds closed faster with less swelling, about 50 percent more fiber, thicker new skin, more vessels, and calmer signals. The multi-use design holds out better chronic wound care, pending medical trials.
pmc-13448658:
Ying Chen and co-authors use a time-and-heat trade-off principle to design metal-organic framework glass composite membranes in a 2026 study. Framework glasses can split gases well, yet hot processing degrades the crystalline fillers meant to boost results. Borrowing that overlap idea, where longer time at lower heat equals a brief hot spell, offered a gentler making dial.

A glassy framework formed the continuous phase, with three different crystal frameworks dispersed inside as fillers. Precise control of processing time and temperature remelted the glass at low temperature with minimal filler breakdown. The membranes separated carbon dioxide and methane mixtures from nitrogen, plus heavier hydrocarbon blends, scoring high in the authors' tests. A platform that can be tailored for a wider family of crystal and glass composites is claimed.
pmc-13448858:
Yan Jiang and a large team examine in 2026 whether swings in blood sugar leave marks on the eye even in people who do not have diabetes. They recruited 338 adults at high risk of type 2 diabetes whose tolerance tests confirmed they were nondiabetic. Wrist-worn style glucose sensors measured each person's fluctuation size, and detailed scans imaged blood flow in the retina and the choroid layer beneath it.

The 73 participants with abnormal fluctuation showed lower retinal blood flow density in several central and surrounding zones, in both shallow and deep vessel layers. Their choroids were thinner, with a smaller share of large vessels yet a higher overall vascular index. Sensor measures of swing size and variability tracked downward with flow density in both tissues. The authors suggest erratic glucose may strain small eye vessels years before diabetes is diagnosed.
pmc-13449058:
Umur Anil Pehlivan, Gurcan Erbay, and Elif Karadeli write in 2026 to the editor about the stubborn misuse of two old names for vascular anomalies in children. The authors argue that loose naming distorts diagnosis, treatment choices, and what families expect, and that precise terms matter more now that the classification also encodes flow behavior and genetic cause.
pmc-13449458:
Chengjian Wu and colleagues tested a small surgical trick for tight knees in 2026, aimed at making meniscus repair safer. When the outer knee compartment is very tight, surgeons struggle to see and reach the lateral meniscus, and forcing instruments risks cartilage damage. Standard moves such as repositioning the leg and adjusting portals sometimes fail to open enough space.

In a single-center series from 2020 to 2022, the team made an incomplete cut at the femoral attachment of the lateral collateral ligament only after those standard moves had failed. The primary test was whether the repair could then be completed with adequate visibility. Scores for pain and function, healing on scans, and complications were also tracked. The paper gives surgeons an option of last resort for a tight compartment.
pmc-13449658:
Bincheng Tang and co-authors run in 2026 a multi-omics hunt for the genes behind erectile function in male geese, a trait that decides mating success in breeding flocks. One gene, PCDH7, surfaced in both the genome scan and the expression data, and the analysis ties it to cartilage development through the MAPK signaling pathway. The authors offer the findings as breeding targets for improving male goose reproductive performance.
pmc-13450558:
Alexa Kwang and colleagues gather a 2026 case series on a slow skin lymphoma that posed as a common flaky scalp-and-face rash. The lymphoma, mycosis fungoides, is the most frequent skin T-cell cancer and is known for copying mild skin diseases. Late labels raise the risk of wrong care and spread.

The series tracks three patients already treated for the lymphoma at Yale who grew new spots that looked like seborrheic dermatitis. One woman aged 84 grew a scaly patch beside her nose that was treated as the mild rash for months. When creams failed and the spot thickened, deeper checks told the true story, a lesson in retesting stubborn patches.
pmc-13451258:
Robert Olek and Zsolt Radak review in 2026 a gut-made compound long cast as a heart risk, asking what exercise does to it. The compound, TMAO, forms when gut microbes process certain foods and the liver finishes the job. Levels also depend on how fast the kidneys clear it.

Across human work, TMAO levels did not track fitness or training load in a steady way. Exercise alone rarely moved levels, while diet shifts and precursor doses moved them a lot. Hard sessions and muscle damage nudged levels for a short while in some studies. The pair argue the compound mirrors diet, gut activity, and body stress at once, so it should not be read as pure harm.
pmc-13451358:
Ruilong Kou and co-authors report in 2026 that a calming protein eases colon swelling in ulcerative colitis by jamming a danger switch. The protein binds a key switch part, ASC, and blocks its grip on the switch, which lowered the main swelling signal and cell death. Mouse tests backed the cell work.
pmc-13451858:
Shuo Pang and co-authors set out in 2026 a gut-prostate link for a lasting pelvic pain illness in men whose cause stays unclear. The illness mixes pelvic pain with urinary and sexual trouble, and care often stalls. New work hints that a skewed gut germ mix may prime the body toward it in some men.

Their model needs two hits: a body-wide immune and fuel-use priming from the gut, plus a local cue in the prostate or pelvic floor. The pair sort hard human proof from animal work and from guesses that still need tests. They urge trials that sort men by body marks first, so gut-based care is tested where it can plausibly work.
pmc-13452158:
Jingwen Yang and co-authors find in 2026 that ketamine shields net-like wraps around brain cells in mice worn down by long restraint stress. Those wraps, perineuronal nets, hug fast-firing brake cells and steer brain flex, and stress thins them. The team stressed mice, dosed some with ketamine, and counted wrap marks, brake cells, and immune cell marks in two brain zones.

Ketamine eased the mice's low-mood acts and saved wrap counts in both zones. It barely moved brake cell counts or the genes that build and cut the wraps. What fell hard was the count of active brain immune cells. The authors read the save as ketamine quieting those cells, which spares the wraps.
pmc-13453458:
Kevin Corti and Meghan Leaver set out a formal method for building prompt grids that test how chat AI systems answer. Their 2026 methods paper names the tool a factorial prompt matrix: a set of base questions crossed with set factors so each change can be read on its own. The four factor classes cover the model, the product shell, the user context, and the question design.

As a worked case, the authors use the ICD-11 disease list as the spine for medical questions. They then watch when the AI calls on web search, among other retrieval behaviors. The design supports both watch based and controlled studies, with one factor or many varied at once. The authors aim the framework at social and behavioral scientists who study AI answers with care.
pmc-13454258:
Raneem Darraj and others built a design-led HPLC test in 2026 for two syrup preservatives, methylparaben and propylparaben. Preservative doses in syrups matter for grade checks, but old one-factor tests miss how factors act as a pair and give shaky methods. The team used a design-led plan with risk maps.

Organic solvent kind and share swayed peak split most. Best settings of forty degrees, one point five millilitres per minute, pH six point one, and just under sixty-eight percent methanol gave clean split in six minutes. Grade labs gain a firm, checked test for syrup preservatives.
pmc-13454458:
Junyan Pan and four colleagues report, in 2026, a light-driven catalyst that breaks down diclofenac, a pain drug that pollutes wastewater and resists cleanup. Light and electrical tests showed the cobalt helped separate the charges that drive the chemistry, so fewer were wasted. The catalyst kept working in messy water conditions and across repeat runs. The authors offer the recipe as a cheap route to clearing drug residues from wastewater.
pmc-13455358:
Alexandra G. Hames, Geronimo Bejarano, and Insiya B. Poonawalla study, in a 2026 claims analysis, whether an insurer-run specialty pharmacy gets costly drugs to patients faster and cheaper. Health care mergers worry critics, who fear market power will raise prices. After adjustment, the integrated model filled prescriptions about 5.7 days sooner. Members also paid about 106 dollars less per year in pharmacy costs, with about 77 dollars saved on the specialty drug itself. Members who also used the insurer's own primary care services gained extra benefit. The authors read the results as a point in favor of coordinated payer and pharmacy models, at least inside Medicare Advantage. They note that one insurer's data cannot settle the wider merger debate.
pmc-13457058:
Nasar Alwahaibi surveys, in a 2026 mini-review, how artificial intelligence is entering the reading room for prostate biopsies. pmc-13457458:

pmc-13457858:

Mean temperature rose by 0.02 degrees Celsius per year, with daytime heat rising most in dry months and night temperatures rising most in the main rainy season, squeezing the daily temperature range. Annual rainfall edged up by 2.69 mm per year, yet seasonal rain stayed highly concentrated and swung sharply between dry and wet years, with warmer south and cooler north and east zones. pmc-13457958:

Turns about the X and Y axes caused the largest size drifts, while Z-axis angle barely mattered, and pull strength stayed stable across angles. Makers gain a handy rule: choose angle for fit first, since strength will likely hold, and use the model to pick the best build pose before printing.
pmc-13458758:

pmc-13459058:

pmc-13459158:

pmc-13459358:

pmc-13459458:

pmc-13459958:

pmc-13460058:

pmc-13460558:
Hannah R. pmc-13461158:

pmc-13461458:

pmc-13461658:

pmc-13462058:

Tagged that way, the partner protein worked more strongly under cold stress. pmc-13462258:

The authors argue the sign should prompt a check of growth factor levels and a search for the histiocyte disease.
pmc-13462358:

pmc-13462458:

pmc-13462558:
Tingting Sun and colleagues report, in a 2026 study, that a small RNA called miR-506-5p acts as a brake on glioma, the brain tumor with few treatment options. Small RNAs fine-tune gene activity, and this one was tied to other tumors. The team measured it and its target gene, MAPK7, in glioma tissue and cells. Reporter tests confirmed the small RNA binds the target's tail region, a control point.

The small RNA ran low in gliomas while MAPK7 ran high. Boosting the small RNA in glioma cells slowed growth, movement, and invasion, and reversed the shape-shifting program. Two tissue-cutting enzymes fell, a sticking protein rose, and markers shifted in a tumor-suppressing direction. Rescue tests sealed the logic: restoring MAPK7 erased the brake, while silencing it erased the harm. In mice, boosting the small RNA shrank grafted tumors and lowered a growth marker.
pmc-13462758:
Pooria Pezeshknejad and colleagues tested a combined soil treatment in 2026 to help maize cope with salty soil, a growing threat to yields in dry regions. The mix pairs tiny silicon particles with a salt-tolerant soil bacterium, Streptomyces albogriseolus. Pots were run at three salt levels with four silicon doses, with and without the bacterium.

Each aid alone helped, but together they gave the strongest rescue under severe salt, lifting shoot dry weight by 55% and root length by 82%. Cell damage fell by 35%, sodium build-up fell by 19%, and nutrient balance improved, while usable soil silicon pools also grew. The pair offers a low-chemical route to steadier maize on saline ground, pending field trials beyond pots.
pmc-13462958:
V. Jeyajeev and colleagues built a 2026 forecasting system that pairs a transformer model with rule-based reasoning and agent-style decision aids for stock prices. Market prices swing hard and hide tangled time patterns, so plain models often give shaky forecasts. The system first predicts closing prices for India's NIFTY Consumer Durables index, then checks those calls for sense and risk.

A neuro-symbolic layer tests predictions against stated rules and market behaviour, while an agent layer pulls in outside financial feeds and past data to shape trading choices. Together the layers aim for forecasts that adapt to shifts and can be explained, not just scored. The authors pitch the mix as a clearer aid for investors, though the work stops short of live trading proof.
pmc-13463058:
Haitao Zhang and colleagues unveil, in a 2026 study, the atomic order inside nanowires of rare-earth chlorides sealed within carbon nanotubes. Thread-like materials can show odd electronic and magnetic behavior, yet reading their atomic layout is hard when long-range order is weak. The team grew the wires by trapping rare-earth chloride inside single-walled carbon tubes, forming stable hybrids with four rare-earth metals. A symmetry-guided screening matched microscope images against simulated candidate structures.

The search combined electron imaging with force-field motion simulations and quantum calculations to pick structures fitting both the pictures and energy stability. Analysis of the dysprosium version, using quantum methods, showed how local symmetry and tight confinement shape its electronic and magnetic traits. The authors offer the combined experiment-and-theory route as a general tool for decoding short-range-ordered nanomaterials and designing low-dimensional materials.
pmc-13464258:
Majeed and colleagues presented in 2026 three patients whose hearts failed in three very different ways from the same rare disease. The disease is eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis. In it, allergy-linked white blood cells inflame small blood vessels. Cardiac scans and pressure measurements sorted each case along a spectrum, from reversible inflammation to permanent scarring.

One patient's severe weakness of both heart chambers reversed. Intensified immune-suppressing treatment and standard heart medicines achieved the reversal. A second patient arrived in cardiogenic shock, the heart unable to pump enough blood, and needed temporary then durable mechanical pumps. The third patient kept relapsing with inflammation around the heart despite several immune regimens. Pumping strength swung back and forth. The authors stress that heart involvement can worsen while the rest of the disease quiets. A common antibody test does not predict it, so hearts need their own watching schedule.
pmc-13464658:
Oana Lia Botezatu (Mocondoi) and five co-authors audit a mother and child health program in Bacău County, Romania, from 2021 to 2024. Budget execution, the share of funds spent, is the usual yardstick for such programs. The team argues the yardstick hides how much work actually gets done.

Counties spent about eighty-four percent of funds on average, yet like spending rates hid wide gaps in activity and coverage. Newborn hearing screening ran the highest volume at the lowest cost per child, though its coverage swung sharply year to year. Prevention and nutrition work ate most of the budget at higher unit costs. Watching money and operations together, the authors say, spots bottlenecks early.
pmc-13464958:
Wang and co-authors review plant hormones called strigolactones in this 2026 agriculture paper. These compounds help plants endure drought and attract helpful soil fungi that supply nutrients. The same signals also wake parasitic weed seeds, which then steal water and food from crops and cause billions of dollars in losses worldwide. The review asks how science can keep the benefits while removing the harm, a separation the authors call decoupling.

One proven trick uses designer chemicals that fool weed seeds into sprouting when no crop is present, so the seedlings die. Breeders have also created crops that release less of the weed-attracting signal. Uses for drought tolerance and nutrient efficiency remain at an early stage, the authors note, held back by high production costs and formulas that break down quickly.
pmc-13465058:
Almut Bauder and Harald Werneck interview nine women with endometriosis about self-esteem under a chronic, often doubted illness. The disease affects about one in ten women of childbearing age, bringing pelvic pain, fatigue, and fertility worries. Self-esteem had rarely been asked about head-on, so the pair used deep semi-structured interviews.

Women tied shaken self-esteem to daily limits, lost control, and their own harsh performance standards. Being dismissed by doctors or others fed self-doubt and withdrawal, whatever the symptom load. On the steadier side stood acceptance, self-kindness, firm boundaries, and rethinking what femininity means. The authors urge clinics to treat self-esteem as a real part of care planning, not a side note.
pmc-13465358:
Jing and co-authors studied in 2026 why the golden leaves of the elm cultivar Jinye turn green again as they develop. The regreening spoils the tree's ornamental value. The team tracked three stages, Golden, Yellowish-Green, and Green. Pigments, leaf anatomy, gene activity, and chemical profiles were all measured. The work tested whether the golden stage is a hormone-held pause in development.

The color shift came from a rising chlorophyll-to-carotenoid ratio. Chlorophyll accumulated while carotenoids stayed flat. Golden-stage chloroplasts, the leaf's green factories, showed loosely stacked membranes, a sign of delayed development. Genes for building chlorophyll switched on while breakdown genes switched off. Several active gibberellins and abscisic acid, two plant hormones, ran high in the golden stage. Spraying both hormones together suppressed regreening and held the golden color. The signature matched the natural golden state, supporting the arrest idea.
pmc-13466658:
Shaikha Almheiri and Asma Musa report a newborn girl found at delivery with both knees bent backward and locked, in a 2026 case report. The rare condition, congenital knee dislocation, left the baby's knees hyperextended with almost no ability to flex, though the rest of her movement was normal. She was delivered by caesarean section to a twenty-eight-year-old mother in the Emirates.

Doctors gently manipulated the knees back into place and applied a series of casts, checking progress with repeated X-rays. Most such cases settle during infancy without surgery when treatment starts early. The authors use the case to press for quick recognition in the delivery room, since delay risks lasting limits on walking.
pmc-13466758:
Tomáš Toporcer and colleagues report a heart defect carried for nine years under the wrong name before surgery revealed its true form, in a 2026 case report. A woman first learned of an abnormal channel near her heart valves at forty-four, during pregnancy, and it was labeled a Gerbode defect. She stayed largely symptom-free on watchful care until breathlessness on effort returned at fifty-three.

Catheter tests measured a significant left-to-right shunt at the upper heart chamber level. During surgery the channel proved to start above a different valve cusp and drain into the right atrium, a congenital fistula from the aorta's sinus. An infected growth at its opening, caused by a skin bacterium, complicated the picture further.
pmc-13467058:
Rui Yang and colleagues speed up the math for predicting how patterned electromagnetic surfaces scatter waves far away, in a 2026 study. Coding metasurfaces tile many small elements, each shifting a wave's phase or strength, so rearranging the tiles steers reflections for antennas and radar control. Full simulation of a big surface is slow.

Their improved method treats each element as a stand-in source, then rebuilds the whole far-field pattern from the parts, using a new way of extracting those sources. Checks against older synthesis routes, earlier source methods, heavy full-wave simulations, and real measurements all backed the approach. The gain is design speed without giving up accuracy.
pmc-13467158:
Wang Wei and a large team search for one shared inflammatory program running through both frailty and osteoarthritis in older adults, in a 2026 multi-source analysis. Muscle from frail donors and joint lining from arthritis patients shared a sixteen-gene program rich in inflammation and cell movement genes. Network pruning refined it to a fifteen-gene hub.

Blood cell data showed the hub switched on together across several immune cell types, strongest in monocyte and macrophage families. Knee meniscus data painted a shifting cell mix in arthritis, with fewer stressed inflammatory cells and more cartilage-like cells. A lab model pairing immune cells with cartilage cells tested how the two tissues talk.
pmc-13467258:
Sergey Chudievich and colleagues reviewed laser heat therapy for high-grade gliomas, the most aggressive brain tumours, and the growing role of AI in planning it. The therapy threads a laser fibre into the tumour and burns it from inside, reaching deep tumours surgery cannot.

From 196 papers found, 69 studies met the review's rules for human evidence on the therapy. Ablation succeeded in 85 to 98 percent of treated tumours, with median survival of 11 to 16 months in new glioblastoma. In returning tumours, survival ran 8.5 to 14.1 months, with fewer complications and far shorter hospital stays than open surgery. AI tools may sharpen patient selection and outcome prediction, Chudievich notes, but they remain at the proof-of-concept stage.
pmc-13467958:
Willem Vandenhoudt, Tony Van Havenbergh, and Frederic Van Havenbergh present a case report and literature review, published in 2026. It covers a rare nerve-tissue tumour in an adult. Ganglioneuroblastoma usually affects children. This patient was a 57-year-old man. His tumour was found in his left adrenal gland. This is the small hormone gland above the kidney.

The gland was removed and the diagnosis confirmed. Scans then showed the cancer had spread through his skeleton. Most striking was a large destructive growth in his skull. It sat in the right front of the skull. It pressed into a major vein channel. The authors stress the malignant potential of this tumour in adults. Full-body imaging is needed when it is found.
pmc-13468458:
Amr Sayed Ghanem and co-authors link eating habits to how Hungarians rate their own oral health in 2026, using a national survey of 5,146 adults from 2019. Untreated decay, gum disease, and tooth loss are common in Hungary, and diet is a modifiable driver. The team built a six-part nutritional risk score from fruit, vegetable, sugary drink, sweets, processed meat, and water habits, then related it to poor self-perceived oral health.

Survey-weighted models adjusted for social, lifestyle, and health factors. The authors went further, estimating population-attributable fractions with Monte Carlo uncertainty ranges from a thousand resamples, under three scenarios of improved national diet. Such fractions translate individual risk into public health terms: the share of poor oral health that better eating could, in principle, prevent. That number is what ministries need when deciding whether diet programs belong in dental budgets.
pmc-13469358:
Huiying Hou and colleagues propose DFB-PPGSQ in 2026, a way to search encrypted graph databases of sensor networks without exposing their contents. Graphs stored in the cloud may hold sensitive layouts from factories or power systems. Earlier private search tools mostly assumed the data never changed, so additions, deletions, and relabeling broke them.

The new scheme gives each time period its own search tokens and marks deleted records with placeholders instead of rebuilding everything. Tests used a Python prototype driven by random sensor network workloads. Filtering speed stayed close to a fixed database version, while single updates took less than a tenth of a millisecond. After a data refresh, attempts to link tokens across periods succeeded in fewer than six cases out of a hundred.
pmc-13469458:
Xinhong Yu and colleagues report a sensor study, published in 2026. They built a highly sensitive detector for carbon monoxide gas. The device uses light-induced thermoelastic spectroscopy. Absorbed laser light makes a quartz tuning fork vibrate. A fibre-coupled multipass cell is combined with it. The cell folds the light path to forty metres.

The team compared five ways of shaping the light. Focusing the light leaving the cell was also varied. Squeezing the spot smaller steadily strengthened the signal. A tapered fibre performed best. It gave the smallest spot. It detected carbon monoxide down to a few parts per million. Longer averaging improved detection further. This suits industrial safety and air monitoring.
pmc-13470458:
Sherzod Ramankulov and colleagues tested STEM project-based learning in 2026 for research autonomy and engineering thinking in solar energy education. Solar workforce training is urgent for energy security, yet methods to build research and engineering skill remain debated. A literature meta-analysis of 15 studies from 2015 to 2025 preceded a pedagogical experiment with 88 students at Khoja Akhmet Yassawi International Kazakh-Turkish University.

Meta-analysis found a large overall effect size of 1.75, and the experiment showed no pre-test difference but a significant post-test gap with effect size 1.27 favouring project-based learners. Structured solar projects thus build research and engineering capacity beyond lecture teaching. Wider adoption should test the approach across institutions and cohorts.
pmc-13470558:
Guangyang Zhou and colleagues studied how sugar-driven browning changes chicken skin collagen and its grip on smoky aroma compounds. Keeping aroma in smoked meat matters for flavour, and collagen is the main protein holding those compounds in skin.

Glucose browning, the Maillard reaction, shrank collagen particles and raised their surface charge, the team measured. The treatment also freed more reactive sulphur groups and raised surface water-repelling character, unfolding the protein's ordered coils. Above all, one aroma compound, 2-acetylfuran, changed its airborne level most as the collagen grew more altered. Computer docking pointed to two amino acid sites where hydrogen bonds and greasy contacts anchor the aroma molecules, Zhou reports.
pmc-13471358:
Bhatt reviewed in 2026 whether Astragalus, a plant genus long used in traditional medicine, can protect the brain in Alzheimer's disease. The review gathered lab and early human studies by standard PRISMA rules. Astragalus yields saponins, flavonoids, and polysaccharides, plant chemicals with reported brain effects.

Across studies, these compounds acted on several cell pathways at once, including PI3K/Akt, Nrf2/ARE, MAPK, and NF-κB. Together they cut oxidative stress, calmed brain inflammation, reduced cell death, and improved synapse function. Some studies also found less amyloid harm and less damaging tau change. The author frames the pattern as systems-level: one plant family pressing many connected targets at once. Human proof is still thin, though. The review presents Astragalus as a multi-target candidate that needs rigorous trials, not a proven remedy.
pmc-13471558:
Wang and colleagues dressed a probiotic in a self-made polymer coat so it can survive stomach acid and set up shop in an inflamed colon. Their 2026 study wrapped Lactobacillus in polymerized ferulic acid, a plant compound, and loaded zinc ions into the coat to mop up hydrogen sulfide, a gas that worsens ulcerative colitis.

The coat barely leaked in simulated stomach fluid, releasing only 4.79% of its ferulic acid after 12 hours at pH 2.0, then broke down at colonic pH above 7 as designed. Zinc made up 20.3% of the finished product by mass and scavenged hydrogen sulfide efficiently, clearing 73.4% of it within 30 minutes in the standard assay. In colitis models the coated bacteria calmed inflammation and restored the gut barrier.
pmc-13471658:
Gordillo-Rosas and colleagues publish the protocol for a meta-analysis of automated insulin delivery, the artificial-pancreas systems that dose insulin from sensor readings, in type 2 diabetes. Their 2026 plan will search five databases through November 30, 2025 for randomized trials comparing these closed-loop systems with conventional insulin strategies in adults.

The review follows Cochrane methods, pools results with random-effects models, and grades certainty with GRADE. The question matters at scale: about 589 million adults live with diabetes worldwide, and over 90% of them have type 2 disease, yet automated systems are proven mainly in type 1 care. Insulin users with type 2 diabetes battle treatment inertia, low blood sugar episodes, and glucose swings the technology promises to smooth.
pmc-13472158:
Kyosuke Yanagawa and Norbert Perrimon review in 2026 what fruit flies and mammals share in their use of extracellular vesicles, the tiny membrane wrapped parcels cells release to message each other. Mammalian vesicles are studied heavily for roles in development, immunity, healing, metabolism, cancer, and brain health. The fly offers genetic tools that let researchers manipulate vesicle pathways inside a living animal and watch organs talk.

Fly work has shown vesicles moving cargo at synapses, guiding development and reproduction, steadying neurons, and rallying body wide immune responses. Most machinery for sorting, budding, and secreting vesicles matches between flies and mammals. The review weighs where the fly model misleads as well as where it shines. Comparative work, the authors argue, sharpens both mechanism and medical translation.
pmc-13472258:
Hwiho Hwang, Sangwook Youn, Jinwoo Park, Dayeon Yu, and Hyungjin Kim propose in 2026 a hardware fingerprint built inside a 3D NAND flash array. Physical unclonable functions turn random manufacturing variation into device identities that cannot be copied, but circuit based versions eat area and power. Their design reads the natural current differences among flash memory strings instead of writing to them, avoiding wear.

Each wordline acts as an independent fingerprint chip, and answers come from comparing summed string currents, so one array stacks many chips with a huge challenge space. Test arrays confirmed the current scatter, traced partly to grain boundaries in the silicon. A stacked implementation built from measured data scored near ideal on fingerprint quality metrics. It also passed all sixteen standard statistical randomness tests and machine learning attack simulations.
pmc-13473358:
Jia and colleagues studied in 2026 which lung cancer patients develop venous thromboembolism, a dangerous clot in the veins. They also asked whether machine learning predicts it better than standard statistics. Clots are a common, severe side problem in lung cancer, so early warning signs matter. The team reviewed records from one Chinese hospital.

Of 180 patients, those with higher D-dimer, a blood marker of clot breakdown, faced greater clot risk. Early chemotherapy rounds also tracked with more clots, though the authors suspect that link reflects who gets chosen for treatment, not a true cause. Among four learning models, random forest ranked risk best but was poorly calibrated. A penalized regression gave the most trustworthy probabilities. The authors conclude that learning tools added little over standard methods in this small dataset.
pmc-13473458:
Yongfei Liu and four colleagues proposed in 2026 a smarter way to compress signals from wearable sensors that track muscles and movement. Surface electromyography, which records muscle electrical activity through the skin, and accelerometers, which record limb motion, are naturally linked, since muscle activation drives movement, yet current compressors handle each signal alone. Their framework aligns the internal representations of the two signals during training. Matching frames and temporal patterns teaches the compressor their shared structure.

Tests on two Ninapro datasets showed gains across compression ratios from 20 to 90 percent. Correlation ran up to 28 percent higher than traditional methods, and signal quality ran 1 to 3 decibels above deep learning baselines. Gesture recognition stayed above 80 percent accurate at 40 percent compression, a level rivals needed 50 percent or more to match. Because the alignment module is dropped after training, the deployed system costs no extra computing, a point that matters for small, battery-powered wearables.
pmc-13473658:
Erdinc Ikinciogullari and two colleagues used in 2026 three-dimensional fluid simulations to improve the flow capacity of contracted weirs, the barriers that control water levels in channels. Stepped and diagonal platforms on sharp-crested weirs promise more discharge, but their hydraulics had not been compared with standard slit designs. Numerical models, validated against laboratory experiments, tested varied stepped and diagonal layouts across a range of water heads.

The advanced shapes clearly beat standard designs, raising discharge efficiency by up to 30 percent across all tested heads, largely because their longer crests pass more water. Adding more steps, however, created interference where flows met at corners, trimming the discharge coefficient. Asymmetric vortices with streamline contraction reduced efficiency per unit of crest length. The authors confirm a flow-area-based dimensionless parameter that captures these hydraulic limits, and present stepped and diagonal weirs as a viable way to boost capacity.
pmc-13474558:
Takashi Hongo and fellow authors review rescue choices in 2026 when the heart stops during pregnancy. Two bold steps can be tried: delivering the baby during resuscitation, and using a heart-lung machine to take over circulation. Past reports were gathered from thirty-four countries across twenty-five years. The pool held 268 patients and 274 newborns, sorted by which steps came first.

Most cases used delivery without the machine, and outcomes varied widely by group. Favorable brain outcomes ranged from about a quarter to four fifths across groups, though machine-only cases were very few. Newborn survival sat near half to three fifths in each group. The review shows how thin the proof base remains for rare, high-stakes care.
pmc-13474658:
Sevenur Sarıkaya, Filiz Altay, Guohua Zhao and Fayin Ye published this 2026 food science study on keeping purple sweet potato pigment in starch noodles. Anthocyanins, the purple antioxidants, degrade easily during processing and cooking, draining colour and health value. The team tested whether citrus peel pectin, a gelling fibre, could protect the pigment by binding it. They measured the effect on noodle texture, stretch and cooking behaviour at two pectin doses.

Measurements confirmed the pectin and pigment form nanoscale complexes in a pattern fitting the Freundlich adsorption model. Pigment retention after cooking rose from 37.82 percent without pectin to 48.75 percent at the low dose and 52.24 percent at the higher dose. The pigment softened the noodles and reduced chewiness. The low pectin dose with pigment gave the best balance, maximising tensile force and stretch without changing cooking yield or loss. The authors propose pectin complexing for pigmented starch foods.
pmc-13474758:
Najat Y. AlSejari and colleagues pool trials in 2026 on oxygen levels during heart-lung bypass in heart surgery. High oxygen has long been standard to guard against low blood oxygen, yet excess oxygen may stress tissues. Twelve randomized trials with 2,732 patients were pooled with random-effects math. Death, kidney injury, and other harms formed the main checks.

No clear gap appeared between high and standard oxygen for short- or long-term death. Kidney injury and other harms such as heart attack and stroke also looked alike. Ventilator time, intensive care stay, and hospital stay did not differ in clear ways. Either strategy seems acceptable on current proof, which invites bigger trials.
pmc-13474858:
Onyeje and colleagues studied newborns with brain injury from oxygen shortage around birth at a Nigerian teaching hospital in Nnewi. The condition, called hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, can kill babies or leave lasting nerve damage. Their 2026 study enrolled 70 full-term babies admitted within 72 hours of delivery between September 2023 and May 2024, then tracked which mother and baby factors predicted poor early outcomes.

Nearly half the babies, 45.7 percent of the 70 enrolled, had a poor early outcome, and 12 babies died in the group followed here. Among those with complications, seizures were most common, affecting 80 percent of that subgroup, followed by failure to suckle. Babies born outside the hospital fared worse than babies born inside it, and low five-minute Apgar scores, a quick rating of newborn condition, also flagged higher risk. Blood sugar levels tracked with outcomes too, leading the team to urge skilled birth care and prompt glucose checks.
pmc-13474958:
Zhao and colleagues report a rare cancer case in 2026. A 64-year-old woman had 13 separate leiomyosarcoma tumors growing in the great saphenous vein of her leg, the long surface vein running up the inner thigh. Leiomyosarcoma is a cancer of smooth muscle that in veins is easily mistaken for ordinary vein disease. She came to hospital in February 2023 for painful varicose veins, and early scans read her lumps as clots.

Surgery removed 11 firm masses clinging to the vein wall, and lab tests confirmed the cancer, which had also spread to her lungs. A lung nodule later grew and was removed, proving it was spread from the vein tumor rather than a new cancer in the chest. The authors stress that this cancer travels through blood to the lungs, so any new lung nodule in such patients should be treated as likely spread, with several specialties planning care together.
pmc-13476058:
Maureen Watt and co-authors break down disease burden in 2026 for adults with hereditary angioedema, a swelling disorder caused by a missing control protein. A web survey across thirteen countries drew 260 adults. Burden was split by sex, felt control, and quality-of-life harm using four standard surveys. Three quarters felt their disease was poorly controlled.

Women reported worse life quality, weaker felt control, and far higher anxiety and depression rates than men. Poor felt control tracked with more attacks and worse scores on every measure. Large life harm hit just over half of respondents. Care plans should weigh sex gaps and felt control, not attack counts alone.
pmc-13476558:
Pebrier and colleagues studied a cell receptor called P2X4R in fatty liver disease in 2026, testing whether blocking it shrinks the fat droplets stored inside liver cells. The receptor sits on lysosomes, the cell's recycling compartments, and helps drive macroautophagy, the process that digests worn cell parts. The team used mice lacking the receptor, a blocking drug called BAY1797, and three different diet or fasting models that fatten the liver.

Blocking the receptor slowed autophagy in liver cells and shifted fat handling toward direct breakdown in the cell fluid instead. Across all three mouse models, treated animals developed many small fat droplets rather than the large droplets seen in untreated animals with fatty livers. In 24 human patients with fatty liver disease, receptor levels tracked with droplet size and autophagy measures, so the authors propose the receptor as a drug target worth pursuing.
pmc-13478358:
AlRoujayee presents in 2026 a systematic review of treatment for temporal triangular alopecia. This non-scarring hair loss leaves a triangular patch of fine hair at the temple, often in children. No previous review had gathered the scattered evidence on its two main treatments.

Searching three databases through the end of 2025 yielded just nine studies covering 23 patients in all: three reports on topical minoxidil and six on hair transplantation. Transplantation produced cosmetic improvement in twenty patients, with one result documented as lasting six years. Minoxidil also improved appearance in its three cases, though one patient relapsed after stopping. No serious adverse events appeared for either approach. The author is candid that this is low-level evidence from case reports, suited to description rather than firm recommendation, and calls for prospective studies.
pmc-13478458:
Leonardo Cardoso Saraiva and a large global team published a 2026 brain imaging study of obsessive-compulsive disorder that goes far beyond the usual checks. Most studies check only thickness, surface area, or volume. This project measured nine traits of the outer brain and four of deep brain regions, including a new network score for how alike deep regions look, in 2,255 patients and 2,264 controls.

Each trait changed in its own places. Curvature shifted in default mode and frontoparietal networks, network linkage rose in movement-sensing regions, and drug use tracked with broad volume loss. Curvature scores foresaw patient traits best in brain-behavior models. Gene activity mapping tied outer-brain changes to pathways of signal-sending neurons. Tissue gene reads from surgery showed that genes turned down in patients' prefrontal cortex fed into those same patterns.
pmc-13479458:
Laura M. Orsel and colleagues report a 2026 survey of surface cleaning and disinfection for respiratory viruses in Dutch hospitals and long-term care facilities. Five years after COVID-19 began, international guidance still advised disinfecting rooms after such patients, while Dutch guidance shifted in March 2023 to cleaning only. The team surveyed infection prevention professionals in June 2023.

Respondents described current practice for SARS-CoV-2 and for other respiratory viruses, plus how practice compared with the first pandemic wave. The survey probes whether facilities follow the relaxed national advice or keep disinfecting from habit and caution. Differences between hospitals and care homes also matter for policy. The authors use the snapshot to judge whether guidance changes actually reach the ward floor.
pmc-13479658:
Ugnė Rukšėnaitė and colleagues present a 2026 cross-sectional study of chronic kidney disease in Lithuanian children at the Vilnius University Hospital pediatric center. Childhood kidney disease is uncommon but carries heavy lifelong burden, and, unlike adult disease, it usually stems from congenital malformations of the kidney and urinary tract. Lithuanian data were sparse.

Children under eighteen with disease stages two through five were staged under the 2024 international guideline definitions and grouped into seven cause categories. Body measurements, treatments, and guideline alignment were reviewed. The study describes who these patients are, what caused their disease, and where everyday practice diverges from guideline recommendations. Such a single-center census gives national planners their first concrete basis for pediatric kidney services.
pmc-13480058:
Shiguftah Khalid and co-authors present a 2026 genetic study of natural colour in upland cotton fibre. Dyed cloth relies on synthetic colours that raise environmental worries, so cotton that grows coloured holds fresh appeal. The team combined genome-wide scans, trait mapping, and gene activity profiles to find the controls behind brown tones and whiteness.

Two main regions stood out, one on chromosome D11 tied to whiteness and one on A07 tied to pigment making. Three candidate genes on D11 showed distinct activity patterns, while A07 held known pigment regulators plus three further active genes. Crosses in three groups supported a model where three genes act together, with pigment loss and graded fading across types. Traits for fibre quality overlapped with colour traits, which warns breeders that gains in one may drag the other.
pmc-13480258:
Naoki Furukawa and co-authors report a 2026 study of spread markers in early lung cancer after full tumour removal. The team reviewed 692 patients whose cancer had not reached the lymph nodes and split them by tumour width into three bands. Three signs of local spread were weighed: growth into the lung lining, into lymph channels, and into blood vessels.

Which sign mattered shifted with tumour size. Lining growth drove return risk in the smallest band. Lymph channel growth took over in the middle band and grew stronger still in the largest band, where lining growth also counted. Blood vessel growth added little once tumours grew large. The authors argue that post-surgery drug choices should weigh these signs by size band rather than by a single staging rule.
pmc-13480858:
Xu and co-workers in China told in 2026 of a man whose throat muscles failed five days into drug care for a chest tumor. The man, 55, had a type B3 thymoma, a tumor of the thymus gland. He had just had his first round of a three drug mix. He could not swallow or speak clear, yet the rest of his nerve exam was clean. Such lone throat failure is a rare face of a myasthenic crisis, where the immune system jams nerve to muscle talk.

Blood tests found the mark: attack proteins aimed at the muscle's signal dock. An ice pack test and a drug probe backed the call. Fed by tube and treated with steroids, pooled immune protein, and a signal drug, he spoke and ate well in four days. He then had the tumor cut out whole, and stayed free of both ills since.
pmc-13480958:
Mikalauskaite and colleagues studied in 2026 how a gene regulator called Atrophin shapes Hippo signalling in the growing fruit fly wing. Hippo signalling controls organ size by setting how strongly a factor named Yorkie turns genes on. Atrophin works as a co-repressor, a helper that dampens gene activity. The team removed Atrophin in different wing regions and tracked what happened to Yorkie's targets.

Mikalauskaite found opposite effects by region. Near the wing's middle boundary, losing Atrophin raised Yorkie target activity, because it weakened Notch signalling and lowered a factor that normally competes with Yorkie for a shared partner. In outer regions, losing Atrophin lowered Yorkie activity by cutting levels of Dachs, a protein that restrains Warts, the main brake on Yorkie. The team also showed Atrophin binds that competing factor directly. Their map adds new links between gene regulators in organ growth.
pmc-13481558:
Leucht and colleagues argue in a 2026 editorial that evidence based medicine has dropped one of its three legs. The founding recipe mixed best research evidence, patient preferences, and clinical expertise. Evidence synthesis now runs to living guidelines. Patient preference enters through shared decision making. Yet hard won clinical experience stays largely unrecorded and unused, the authors say, especially in psychiatry, where trials enroll narrow patient groups.

pmc-13483858:

pmc-13487258:

pmc-13487958:

pmc-13488058:

pmc-13488158:

pmc-13490358:

pmc-13490458:

pmc-13490858:

pmc-13491758:

pmc-13491958:

pmc-13492858:

pmc-13508258:

pmc-13508358:

pmc-13508458:

pmc-13510258:
