Old beliefs, such as heavy bones making people sink, may discourage learning that skill.

One hundred and one volunteers joined the study, and ninety-six attempted a two minute back float after instruction and practice. Massey reports eighty-nine of them floated successfully for the full two minutes. Body fat percentage correlated strongly with buoyancy in the group's measurements. The authors back community based, jointly designed practice sessions alongside existing safety campaigns to close the equity gap.
pmc-13515958:
Joseph B Bernstein argues, in a 2026 essay, that a number engineers treat as a mere fitting knob in transistor ageing actually carries physical meaning. Bias temperature instability slowly degrades modern chips, and lifetime forecasts lean on a power-law curve whose exponent varies oddly between identical devices. Bernstein re-examines a published multi-heat dataset from ring oscillator circuits stressed under the same conditions.

Each circuit showed its own exponent, yet the values held steady. Spread across a wider heat range, the supposed scatter formed a clear pattern. Feeding the measured exponent into the standard heat analysis produced a strikingly steady lifetime relation and a much smaller true activation energy. Part of the accepted energy value, he suggests, was an artefact of ignoring how the exponent drifts with heat. A Gibbs free energy reading casts the exponent as a measure of how degradation events correlate.
pmc-13516758:
Dula and colleagues assessed how well maternal health nurses in southern Mozambique handle two obstetric emergencies, severe pre-eclampsia and bleeding before birth, in 2026 health workforce research. Pre-eclampsia is dangerous high blood pressure in pregnancy. The team surveyed nurses at 80 primary-level health facilities between November and December 2022, using a structured questionnaire plus written clinical scenarios that tested real decisions rather than self-rated confidence alone.

Of 191 participants, most were mid-level nurses, averaging 33 years of age across the sample. On the survey day, 82.7 percent had provided prenatal consultations, yet only about half knew the national standards for those visits. Just 44.5 percent scored above 50 percentage points on the competency measure used in the study. Dula argues the gap between daily practice and tested emergency skill is wide. Training and supervision, the authors suggest, need to target the emergencies most likely to kill mothers.
pmc-13517258:
Jodi Schilz, Erica Dashner-Titus, Karen Torczynski, and Laurie Hudson compare how four toxic metals reprogramme human kidney cells in a 2026 study. The kidney filters arsenic, cadmium, uranium, and vanadium out of the body and suffers for it. Primary tubule cells were dosed with each metal, and their gene activity was read at six and twenty-four hours.

Arsenic and cadmium answered fast and shared a core stress-and-detox programme by one day. Their flavours differed: arsenic leaned toward membrane transport and immune signalling, cadmium toward protein quality control. Vanadium and uranium kept quiet early, then developed their own signatures by twenty-four hours, vanadium touching transport and cell division, uranium touching RNA splicing and cell-death signals. Schilz's team concludes that shared pathways explain common kidney harm, while each metal's private signature shapes its particular risk profile.
pmc-13518458:
Xin Huang leads a ten-author study tracing how pigment cells die in vitiligo in a 2026 paper. Oxidative stress ignites the disease, and melanocytes, whose pigment work already generates reactive oxygen, sit exposed. In a human pigment-cell line, stress pushed down Lonp1, a mitochondrial housekeeping protease that guards the powerhouse's DNA and clears faulty proteins.

The loss cascaded. A key clean-up protein, PINK1, fell too, so damaged mitochondria escaped the recycling system called mitophagy and piled up. Their distress tripped the NLRP3 alarm complex, which released the inflammatory signal IL-1β and drove the cells into pyroptosis, a fiery, bursting form of death. Huang's team presents the chain, from protease loss through failed clean-up to inflammatory death, as a mechanistic thread worth pulling for vitiligo therapy, since each link is in principle druggable.
pmc-13518858:
Mario Meloni leads a ten-author team hunting blood markers in 2026 for the non-motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease, problems such as hallucinations, poor memory, and low mood. These symptoms weigh heavily on patients yet lack reliable blood tests. Tiny vesicles shed by nerve cells into blood may mirror brain processes.

In 68 patients, the team captured nerve-derived vesicles from serum and measured their protein cargo. Higher levels of clumped alpha-synuclein, the protein that aggregates in Parkinson's, tracked with worse total non-motor scores, hallucinations, and attention or memory problems. Other vesicle proteins linked to mood-related severity. Meloni and colleagues present clumped alpha-synuclein as a candidate marker needing follow-up over time.
pmc-13519458:
Mandeep Kaur and colleagues compared three root canal file systems by how much tooth tissue each removed. Published in 2026, the in vivo study shaped 45 lower premolars, fifteen per file system, and measured canal volume before and after with 3D scans and reconstruction software. Over-shaping can strip dentin and weaken a tooth, so the kindest file matters as much as the fastest.

Every system enlarged canal volume markedly, with Blueflex Acer removing the most, OneShape next, and Standard Mani-Silk least. Mani-Silk also best preserved the canal's natural shape, marking it as the most conservative choice. The authors frame the trade-off plainly: aggressive cutting cleans fast but costs tooth structure. Readers gain a ranked guide for choosing files that shape well while sparing dentin.
pmc-13519858:
S Sindhuja Devi and five colleagues chart impacted lower wisdom teeth in 2026 among patients at a dental institution in Tirunelveli, India. Impacted third molars bring pain, infection, and gum disease, and knowing the impaction pattern helps plan surgery. From 690 panoramic X-rays, 330 patients with impacted lower third molars entered the analysis.

Mesioangular impaction, where the tooth tilts toward its neighbor, was most common at 39.4 percent, followed by vertical impaction. Bone removal with tooth sectioning served as the main operation in 48.5 percent of cases, and 15.2 percent of patients had complications afterward. Sex, depth, jaw relationship, and age each linked significantly to pattern, approach, or complications.
pmc-13520258:
Nana Liu, Qiang Chen, and Ying Zhao run a randomized trial in 2026 comparing two flap designs for covering multiple receded gums on lower front teeth in patients with thin gum tissue. Both designs were paired with a connective tissue graft. Fifty-nine patients contributed 103 recession sites, split between a tunnel approach and an envelope flap.

By six months, the tunnel group achieved mean root coverage near 79 percent against about 58 percent for the envelope group, a clear adjusted gap. Complete coverage occurred at 62.7 percent of tunnel sites versus 31.8 percent of envelope sites. Both methods thickened tissue and widened the firm gum band, while aesthetics and patient satisfaction scored consistently higher with the tunnel.
pmc-13520458:
Chenhao Xu and colleagues review in 2026 cartilage organoids, lab-grown mini tissues that copy the structure and cell mix of real joint cartilage. Natural cartilage heals poorly and lacks blood vessels, while animal and flat cell models copy human joints imperfectly.

Coverage spans how cartilage forms, how organoids are built and checked, and how disease models mimic joint degeneration. Uses include drug screening, toxicity testing and gene therapy trials. Weaknesses such as missing blood supply and limited strength are discussed openly. The review aims to guide translation toward repair treatments, with ethical and clinical hurdles noted for later stages.
pmc-13520658:
Eryk J. Yarkosky and colleagues launch in 2026 MicrobioME, a class module where microbiology students study germs from their own skin. Classic research slots reach few students. Placing real research inside a class widens access for all.

Students grow skin germs and name them. They then test if germ-made molecules slow biofilm growth by a common pathogen. Trials ran in two university courses. The courses differed in size, skill level and meeting times. That spread let the team compare results across settings. Outcome data and full setup tools are shared. Cost and planning hurdles get direct treatment in the write-up.
pmc-13522458:
Young Ju Oh, Gyu-Seong Choi, Jongman Kim, and Jinsoo Rhu follow inflammatory signals after liver transplantation for liver cancer in a 2026 prospective study. Forty-two patients who received a living-donor transplant were tracked for blood cytokines, graft congestion on scans, and tumor features. Blood was tested repeatedly in the early period after surgery.

Two signals, interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha, rose alongside early graft regrowth, explained in the text as proteins that drive inflammation. Patients with larger congested areas in the graft tended to show higher levels of both signals. Cancer recurrence was also linked to higher interleukin-6. The authors suggest that tracking these blood signals could help clinicians manage recovery and watch for problems after transplantation.
pmc-13523258:
Weihao Deng, Yantao Shi, and Hui Tang present a computational method for mapping tumor stage across tissue in a 2026 study. Spatial transcriptomics records gene activity while preserving location, yet most tools ignore clinical features such as malignancy stage. Their method first finds stage-specific gene sets from large bulk datasets, then projects them onto spatial data at fine pixel level before summarizing back to standard spots.

The method outperformed leading alternatives at identifying malignant regions across diverse tumor tissues. Applications included finding early microenvironment markers that separate primary liver cancer from liver metastasis, and scoring how seven drugs affect the tumor surroundings. The authors offer the framework as a bridge between cellular context and clinical phenotype for more precise tumor analysis and treatment decisions.
pmc-13523358:
Jianing Cui and collaborators test a revised cancer staging edition for mouth cancer in a 2026 retrospective cohort study with an external database check. The eighth edition staging system added tumor invasion depth and spread beyond lymph node capsules to the classification. Patient data came from a university hospital cohort treated between 2014 and 2021 and from a large United States registry.

About three in ten patients were upstaged under the new edition. In the hospital cohort the new system separated survival between middle and advanced tumor categories more clearly than the old one, although the two earliest categories still overlapped. In the registry cohort, separation at the same boundary stayed weak. The authors propose a refined tumor classification based on their cohort and evaluate it against established criteria for staging quality.
pmc-13523458:
Minoo Bakhtiari and colleagues review, in 2026, next-generation CAR-NK cell therapy for cancer. Natural killer cells are part of innate immunity and watch for malignant change. Fitting them with chimeric antigen receptors, lab-built targeting molecules, creates a treatment. Early work suggests it may cause less cytokine release syndrome and graft-versus-host disease than CAR-T therapy, with scope for ready-made donor products.

The review covers NK cell biology, engineering strategies, and early clinical results in blood cancers and solid tumors. Barriers include short persistence in the body, poor travel into tumors, suppressive tumor surroundings, uneven manufacturing, and limited long-term data. Proposed answers include gene editing, cytokine-armored designs, combined engineering, checkpoint blockade partners, and oncolytic virus approaches, each weighed for safety and practical delivery.
pmc-13523758:
Miller and colleagues showed a synthetic tree that pulls water from moist soil without any pump, in a 2026 engineering study inspired by how real trees move water. The device buries its base in water-saturated soil. It seals its nanoporous artificial leaf inside a condensing still, where evaporation draws water upward and a cold plate turns the vapor back into liquid for collection.

Miller built a hydraulic model balancing the suction created inside the leaf against gravity and flow resistance in the tubes and soil. The model showed the harvest rate can be tuned directly by controlled heat applied to the leaf. Their analysis distinguishes depth limits set by water weight from those set by soil resistance. It concludes a synthetic tree could lift water from depths beyond conventional pumps, albeit at lower flow rates, opening a passive route to water in dry regions.
pmc-13525858:
Lee and co-authors audit a social media community in this 2026 content analysis of TikTok videos. The videos concern hidradenitis suppurativa. That is a painful chronic skin disease of recurrent boils and scarring. It falls hardest on women and people with skin of color. They coded the most visible videos under four disease hashtags, ending with 133 after removing duplicates and off-topic posts.

Patients, not clinicians, dominate the conversation: 90 percent of creators were patients and 90 percent were women, with testimonials making up 80 percent of content. Representation of deeper skin tones was strong, with Fitzpatrick types IV to VI in 57 percent of videos. Treatment talk leaned away from guidelines, though: guideline-supported therapies appeared in 24 percent of videos against 29 percent for over-the-counter adjuncts and 19 percent for alternative remedies. Empowerment themes filled 88 percent of videos. The authors urge dermatologists to join the platform with accurate, inclusive education.
pmc-13526058:
Hu and colleagues published a 2026 case report on a genetic immune disorder striking only the brain. Familial HLH drives runaway inflammation and usually storms the whole body. Their patient, a 13-year-old girl, showed the disease only in her nervous system. Such brain-only starts are easily missed or mistaken for other diseases.

Doctors confirmed familial HLH type 3 through genetic testing of the girl. A donor stem cell transplant remains the only lasting cure available. Her transplanted cells took hold, with blood counts recovering within three weeks. She developed no graft-versus-host disease, a feared transplant complication. At day 679 after transplant, she stayed free of any relapse. Her calm course shows brain-only disease can end well with transplant.
pmc-13526858:
Ghatpande and colleagues present Ribo-ITP in 2026, a method for finding translons, meaning genome regions that cells actually translate into protein pieces, using very small tissue samples. Standard ribosome profiling needs large samples, so rare tissues stayed out of reach. Ribo-ITP works on samples such as tiny dissected brain regions and single early embryos.

The team identified thousands of translons from these limited samples. A green fluorescent reporter system confirmed that many translons start translation at standard and near-standard start signals in mouse stem cells. Comparing over a thousand ribosome profiling datasets showed distinct patterns across cell types. A machine learning model further predicted that certain upstream translons control how strongly the main protein-coding region is translated.
pmc-13527958:
Dávid Géza Horváth and three colleagues report a 2026 veterinary case of an unusual gut disease in young pigs. Three post-weaned pigs from an outdoor farm were examined after death. The herd had shown rising deaths and wasting over two batches. One pig had a rare mix of proliferative and granulomatous inflammation in the ileum, the last part of the small intestine.

Stains and antibody tests found the bacterium Lawsonia intracellularis inside the inflamed tissue. That germ usually causes a simpler thickening of the gut wall. Tests ruled out porcine circovirus 2 and mycobacteria, the usual suspects for this pattern. A second bacterium, Brachyspira pilosicoli, turned up in two pigs and may have added to the colitis. The authors urge including Lawsonia in the differential diagnosis.
pmc-13528158:
Mehmet Kavaklı validates a Turkish scale for the wish to belong in public on social media in a 2026 study. Belonging is a basic human need, and feeds now display it openly. Three studies with 1,046 Instagram users tested the eight-item scale. Factor checks ran in the first study. Later studies confirmed the shape and probed stability over four weeks.

The scale held together as one clean factor. Internal consistency was high, and repeat scores stayed steady. It tracked with social comparison habits and heavy Instagram use. It also tracked with feeling shut out. Links with personality were modest, and the scale stayed distinct from general belonging. Kavaklı says the tool can serve research on digital self-display. It may also help clinics spot belonging needs that play out online.
pmc-13529658:
Matthew Mollerus and colleagues built resLens, a family of DNA language models for spotting antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs). Published in 2026, the method fine-tunes a pretrained DNA language model on curated ARG datasets, learning hidden DNA patterns rather than matching sequences to lists. Older alignment tools falter when ARGs diverge from known references or when lists lag behind fast-evolving drug resistance.

ResLens matched or beat rivals across test settings, including cases where ARG sequences and defense tricks differed from list data. Because it learns from DNA context rather than exact matches, it can flag candidate novel ARGs in mixed-sample data. The authors pitch it for watch programs and discovery where list-based tools go blind. Readers get a transfer-learning advance for tracking a moving target.
pmc-13530558:
Ellis and colleagues present in 2026, as conference paper 33, short-term results for fixing osteochondral fractures with an absorbable suture bridge instead of screws or pins. The fractures are fragments of bone and cartilage knocked loose when a kneecap dislocates. The bridge spreads pressure evenly and leaves no hardware to remove.

The single-center review covered 65 patients, mean age fourteen, with 67 fractures treated from 2019 to 2024, alongside reconstruction of the kneecap's stabilizing ligament. Return to sport averaged just under six months. At a mean sixteen months of follow-up, only three lesions needed repeat surgery. MRI in just over half the lesions showed full union in about four fifths and stable union in the rest, with no nonunions in the imaged group here. All four patient-reported knee scores rose sharply and significantly.
pmc-13531758:
Cui Deng and co-authors trace in 2026 how a gut bacterium product eases Alzheimer-like damage in tiny worms. The E. coli strain HB101 improved learning, slowed nerve loss, and delayed paralysis in worm models of the disease. Chemical screening singled out glutarate, a small molecule the bacteria release, as a key active product.

Glutarate switched on the cell cleanup system centered on lysosomes and self-digestion, clearing clumps of the harmful amyloid protein. Stress-response pathways inside cell power stations and protein factories also woke up. The work points from gut microbes toward a candidate molecule for future therapy research.
pmc-13531858:
Clara Gómez-Velasco and colleagues validate in 2026 a faster DNA test for a parasite disease of dogs spread by sandflies. Samples from 66 dogs at several disease stages, plus healthy infected and clean dogs, were tested in six tissues by the new two-target method and an older nested method. Sick dogs were rechecked after a month of treatment.

Lymph node samples carried the most parasite DNA and matched disease severity best. Mouth swabs led the painless options, while blood proved weak and urine and hair weakest. The new test edged out the older one in most tissues and tracked treatment response.
pmc-13531958:
Jie Liu and co-authors describe in 2026 a pituitary tumor that secretes two hormones at once in a 61-year-old Chinese man. Weight loss, palpitations, and breathlessness came with raised thyroid hormone and raised thyroid-stimulating hormone, a pairing that points to the pituitary rather than the thyroid gland itself. Scans and function tests confirmed the double-secreting growth.

Low platelets and heart disease made immediate surgery unsafe, so the hormone-blocking drug octreotide came first. Thyroid tests normalized on the drug, confirming the diagnosis in practice. The case warns against mistaking this rare tumor for ordinary Graves disease.
pmc-13533258:
Alec Wang and a large team present a nanomedicine study, published in 2026. They built drug-carrying polymer micelles. The micelles can be watched on PET scans as they travel to tumours. Nanoparticles accumulate unevenly in different tumours. The team made their micelle platform carry a radioactive label. Doctors can measure uptake in each patient. This happens before judging treatment.

Micelles with one or three chelator anchors held the zirconium label stably. The platform is designed to load cancer drugs into the same particles. The authors position the system for theranostics. This pairs therapy with diagnostics. Patients whose tumours take up few particles can be spared ineffective nanotherapy.
pmc-13534658:
Yang Xu and colleagues compare in 2026 immune profiles of two stroke types, blocked-vessel stroke and bleeding stroke, against healthy controls. Care for both types stays mostly supportive, with few immune-targeted options. Groups held 73 blocked-vessel patients, 28 bleeding patients, and 31 controls for blood and immune checks.

Bleeding patients showed lower levels of several blood fats than both other groups, while blocked-vessel patients showed lower protective cholesterol than controls. Both stroke groups had higher shares of regulatory T cells, yet their links to signalling proteins ran in opposite directions, suggesting distinct immune diseases.
pmc-13534858:
Darshali A Vyas and Sean D Levy examined why race-neutral lung function equations struggle to reach clinics. Published in 2026, the commentary tracks the shift away from race correction in clinical algorithms, with at least eight revised since 2020. New Global Lung Initiative Global equations for lung tests pose special hurdles, since they redefine how organ function itself is judged.

Unlike kidney equations, lung testing lacks a gold standard to settle which formula is right, fueling uncertainty. The Veterans Affairs system paused its transition after studies warned of benefit redistribution and possible surgical bias, despite adopting race-neutral kidney reporting in 2021. A survey of 66 providers found about half of labs had adopted the new equations, though response was low. Readers get an implementation case study in equity versus uncertainty.
pmc-13536558:
Fatmakhanim Osmanova and colleagues study in 2026 how red blood cell transfusion affects inflammatory signals and illness in very preterm infants. Most tiny infants receive transfusions, yet immune effects beyond blood counts need checking. The single-centre study followed 33 infants born at 32 weeks or earlier who were transfused after day seven.

Blood counts rose as expected after transfusion. Major inflammatory signals did not change clearly, while one vessel growth factor rose and one binding protein fell. Breathing support needs eased over follow-up weeks, though the lack of a control group makes these patterns descriptive only.
pmc-13536758:
Wei Chen leads a 2026 randomized trial comparing two ways to prevent blood pressure drops after spinal anesthesia for cesarean birth. Fluid loading with colloid was compared with a steady norepinephrine infusion, a drug that supports blood pressure. Sixty healthy mothers and sixty mothers with preeclampsia took part. Pressure inside the skull was tracked indirectly with ultrasound measures of the optic nerve covering at several time points.

Mothers with preeclampsia started with higher nerve covering measures than healthy mothers. Fluid loading raised those measures more than the drug infusion did in both groups. Blood pressure control was similar for mothers with preeclampsia under either approach. Headache, kidney measures, newborn scores, and cord blood tests did not differ clearly. The authors favor the drug infusion as safer for brain pressure.
pmc-13540158:
Misao Fujita leads a 2026 policy paper on the ethical, legal, and social questions raised by research using human fetal tissue in Japan. International stem cell guidance sets consent standards, yet Japan has no clear legal framework for tissue obtained through induced abortion.

Three live issues structure the discussion. Hospitals chosen for donation should be able to minimise burden on women who donate. Consent from the male partner raises a question the authors weigh carefully. An old ordinance governing placentas and dead fetuses needs clarifying for modern research. The paper argues that global standards only work when fitted to local law and practice.
pmc-13540858:
Tamara Rodríguez Pérez and three colleagues scope, in a 2026 review, research on grief among LGBTQ+ adults in health and end-of-life care. Bereavement for this group is often complicated by stigma, hidden relationships, and services built around straight norms.

Six databases were searched for work published between 2021 and 2026, and only seven primary studies survived screening, most of them qualitative and from English-speaking countries. Four themes recurred: minority stress, the difficulty of disclosure, grief that society refuses to recognise, and thin professional training. Transgender people were scarce in those studies, and quantitative or intersectional work was largely missing.
pmc-13540958:
Thanawin Jantheang leads a 2026 rat study on a plastics chemical. The chemical is bisphenol A, known as BPA. Dams were exposed before birth. The team asked how BPA rewires the young cerebellum. They also asked whether males and females differ. The cerebellum is tied to autism, a condition with a male skew.

Gene reading found wide changes in splicing in newborn rats. Splicing is the editing step that lets one gene make several proteins. The changed genes sat in autism-linked pathways. Computer docking said BPA could grip splicing proteins directly. Lab checks confirmed some splicing shifts. Synaptic markers changed in cultured neurons too. One gene shifted only in males.
pmc-13543358:
Yu Dong and colleagues published a 2026 cross-sectional study of how depressive symptoms relate to everyday functioning in older Chinese adults. Data came from the 2017-2018 Chinese Longitudinal Healthy Longevity Survey, covering 12,261 people, most aged eighty or over. Depression was screened with a standard ten-item scale, while functioning was scored on instrumental activities of daily living, tasks such as shopping, cooking, laundry, and using public transport.

About 26.7 percent of participants had depressive symptoms, and those who did showed clearly greater difficulty with daily tasks. The link strengthened steadily across symptom levels, suggesting a dose pattern rather than a threshold effect. The team also examined whether age, sex, and outdoor activity changed the strength of the association. Understanding how mood and independence intertwine can help services spot older adults whose low mood is quietly eroding their ability to live unaided.
pmc-13543558:
Jingjing Gao, Bin Jiang, and He Cheng published a 2026 case report of a ten-year-old Chinese boy with atlantoaxial subluxation. In that condition the top two neck vertebrae slip partly out of place, and this boy's case came with persistent dizziness. The condition is usually managed either conservatively, with frequent relapses, or by surgical fusion, which sacrifices neck movement. Their patient was treated with a combination: traction through a band linking the back of the head and the jaw, followed by a full exercise programme.

Traction first restored the joint's alignment; exercises then rebuilt the muscular stability that keeps the joint in place. After the combined course, the boy's symptoms resolved completely. One case cannot set policy, but it illustrates a middle path for mild-to-moderate subluxation. Correct the position mechanically, then train the muscles to hold it, reserving fusion for cases where this staged approach fails.
pmc-13545058:
Saeed Najafian and colleagues published a 2026 simulation study of pressing mini-tablets, the tiny pills used for children and precise dosing, where narrow dies make powder behaviour hard to predict. Using the discrete element method, which tracks every particle, they varied particle size, the spread of sizes, and fill weight. They then watched compaction force, particle-level forces, and where inside the die those forces concentrated.

Particle size swayed force unevenness more than fill weight did. Larger particles carried higher, patchier loads, organised into chains that localised stress, and forces peaked near the die wall where confinement bites. Uniformly sized powders paradoxically needed higher pressing force, because their load-bearing structures locked together, while mixed sizes shared force more evenly and compacted more willingly. The lesson for formulators: the architecture of the force network, not the average particle force, decides how a powder presses.
pmc-13545258:
Delia Franchini and co-authors reported a 2026 pilot study of 39 cats treated with electrochemotherapy for squamous cell carcinoma, a skin cancer found here on the nose or eyelids. The treatment uses electric pulses to open tumor cells briefly so chemotherapy drugs can enter more easily. The team recorded the tumor's electrical resistance in real time during every pulse and session.

Resistance fell as treatment progressed, and cats whose tumors showed lower resistance were more likely to reach a complete response. Values also differed by tumor site, grade, and stage. The authors propose that watching resistance during treatment could give veterinarians a quick, noninvasive sign that the pulses are working as intended.
pmc-13548658:
Franco Mascayano and colleagues argue for a social determination framework in mental health, in a 2026 debate article rooted in Latin American social medicine. Mainstream global mental health, they contend, fixates on individual risk factors and biomedical treatment while treating colonialism, globalization, and market reforms as background noise. Drawing on the work of epidemiologist Jaime Breilh, the authors recast those forces as active drivers that get under the skin.

Short accounts from Latin America on work, discrimination, and environment show how global economic arrangements filter through institutions into daily life and surface as distress. The framework stresses power relations across levels, collective agency, and research done with communities rather than on them. The authors urge global mental health policy to aim at structural justice, not only symptom relief.
pmc-13549458:
Antonio Tursi and a large consortium of Italian clinicians report how the drug risankizumab performs for Crohn's disease in everyday practice, in a 2026 real-world study. All patients had already failed a first advanced therapy. The drug blocks interleukin-23, an immune signal, and trial data were strong, yet clinic populations are messier. Records covered 487 patients across many centers, tracking remission on a standard symptom index at three, six, and twelve months.

By maximal follow-up, just over three quarters of patients reached clinical remission. Success ran highest when the drug was used second in line, at about eighty-six percent, and lower in later lines. Most patients also achieved remission without steroids, half of those checked endoscopically showed healed bowel lining, and only six needed surgery. Side effects appeared in about one patient in eight and were mostly mild, supporting the drug's tolerability.
pmc-13550458:
Wang Kai and colleagues improve a flowable soil used for backfilling trenches and cavities, in a 2026 experimental study. They swap part of its cement for industrial byproducts and mix it under vibration. Plain cement binder is costly and carbon-heavy. The team replaced cement in stages with fly ash or mineral powder, then with a three-part blend, measuring strength at twenty-eight days, water stability, and resistance to wet and dry cycling.

Fly ash alone weakened the soil step by step, while mineral powder strengthened it. The blend of seventy percent cement with fifteen percent each of the two powders beat plain cement by a third in strength. Vibration mixing added nearly eight percent more strength and better water stability at the same recipe. The authors present the recipe as a cheaper, greener backfill that uses up industrial residues.
pmc-13551758:
Somphob Leetachewa, with five colleagues, published a 2026 study of two amoebas that look alike. One invades human tissue and causes amoebiasis. The other is thought to be harmless. The team split and named the proteins of both species with a lab method. They sorted the proteins by job. They then checked some proteins with antibodies to see where they sit in the cell.

Each species held over a thousand proteins. The two shared 801 of them. Proteins found only in the invader clustered around nitrogen use and transport. Proteins found only in the harmless species leaned to fat handling and stress defense. Two protein families sat in different places by species. The team offers them as leads for tests and drugs.
pmc-13551858:
Mitsuru Otsubo, Shun Konno, Ami Konno, Harumasa Yokota, and Taiji Nagaoka published a 2026 case series of eye surgery for endophthalmitis, a severe infection inside the eye after operations. Seven consecutive patients at Asahikawa Medical University Hospital between November 2024 and September 2025 received vitrectomy, removal of the eye's gel, assisted by an endoscope with a fine 25-gauge system. Anesthesia choice depended on pain severity.

Before surgery, vision was at hand motion or light perception in every case in the reported series. The endoscope let surgeons shave the peripheral gel without pressing on the eyeball, useful when the cornea is cloudy. Vision improved in all seven patients, with final acuity significantly better on average, leading the authors to present the technique as a useful option for this emergency.
pmc-13553658:
C. E. Secu and four colleagues published this 2026 study of how europium ions, prized for their red glow, attach to particles of the polymer polyaniline. They probed it with electron microscopy and spectroscopies.

Microscopy showed porous micro-sized particles. Photoelectron spectroscopy found the europium bound to the polymer's imine and amine nitrogen groups. Raman and infrared spectra confirmed europium-nitrogen bond formation, a sign of a complex rather than mixing. Under ultraviolet excitation the hybrid emitted the polymer's blue band at 420 nanometres alongside europium's red lines. This works through an antenna effect: the polymer harvests light and hands the energy to the ions. Yield was low, about four percent, limited by poor energy transfer, a target for fixing them.
pmc-13554058:
Elżbieta Speina leads a seven-author team asking whether human cells kept in dishes keep evolving over a full year. Some mixes faced fresh plain rivals that could not evolve back.

Early shifts looked like chance drift, then plain cells slowly gained ground. In one line, a likely helpful mutation flipped the contest after four to six months. In the other line, plain cells kept their edge to the end. Gains were small throughout, matching weak selection. The authors conclude that lab-grown human cells evolve slowly, without fast takeover by new clones.
pmc-13554158:

Bacteria in vaginal samples were sorted into community types, from those ruled by helpful lactobacilli to mixed types.

Helpful communities stayed fairly stable over time. Mixed communities shifted more, often drifting toward the helpful types. Antibody levels in vaginal fluid followed much the same pattern in every community type. No clear link tied bacteria makeup to how much antibody arrived or when. The authors call the analysis exploratory and small.
pmc-13554858:
Alyssa Naimi leads a nine-author team reporting a young mother whose heart failed catastrophically after childbirth in a 2026 case report. The thirty-two-year-old had antiphospholipid syndrome and lupus, conditions that push blood toward clotting. After a cesarean delivery for a pregnancy complication, she fell into cardiogenic shock. Heart scans showed both sides of the heart failing, while artery imaging found no blockage.

Her condition worsened despite drugs, and a heart-lung machine took over her circulation. Clots formed heavily around the catheters and machine tubing, fitting a catastrophic flare of her syndrome. Blood washing, steroids, and stronger blood thinners followed. Ten days after arrival she received a heart transplant, and her removed heart showed wide dead tissue and healing zones.
pmc-13555058:
Molina and colleagues advanced in 2026 a theory of cultural signatures, the idea that shared culture leaves readable traces in the shape of people's personal networks. Drawing on the concept of the propriospect, each person's inner model of their culture, the authors argue that institutions like markets, mosques, courts, and schools sculpt whom people connect to and how. They revisit a classic ethnography of Sohar, Oman, to show the idea at work.

To test it, the team surveyed people in six countries, collecting about eighteen hundred personal networks of thirty contacts each. Computer models could guess a respondent's country from network shape alone, with togetherness measures carrying much of the signal. Politeness codes, the Sohar case suggests, can hold a diverse town together while institutions pattern men's and women's networks differently.
pmc-13555158:
Arisa Kato leads a five-author team probing why sensitive skin stings, looking at nerve endings and a sealing protein in a 2026 study. Sensitive skin reacts with itching, burning, or stinging to mild triggers. In healthy skin, tight junctions in the upper skin layer shield nerve endings from outside irritants. One junction protein, claudin-3, drew the team's focus.

Skin samples came from people classed as sensitive or not by survey and a lactic acid sting test. Sensitive skin lost more water through its surface, hinting at a subtly weaker barrier. Nerve fibres in sensitive samples reached higher, pushing up through zones marked by a sister junction protein. The authors link missing claudin-3 to this nerve exposure, offering a physical basis for the condition.
pmc-13556058:
Mariana A S Artur and twelve colleagues released in 2026 a detailed atlas of how Arabidopsis seeds mature, gene by gene. During maturation, seeds gain the traits that let them survive drying and long storage, guided largely by the hormone abscisic acid. The team tracked developing seeds from twelve days after pollination to the dry stage in normal plants and in ten mutant lines with faults in hormone making, sensing, or breakdown.

Alongside gene activity, they measured when seeds gained the ability to germinate, tolerate drying, stay dormant, and survive storage. Network analysis grouped genes into modules that rose and fell with particular traits. Modules tied to drying tolerance and longevity were rich in stress response and hormone regulated genes. The atlas, presented as an explorer tool, helps seed scientists find which genes build which quality trait.
pmc-13557858:
Ying-Bo Xie and eleven colleagues built in 2026 a scoring model that predicts whether a blood test will find EGFR mutations in advanced lung cancer. Roughly eighty-five percent of lung cancers are the non-small cell type, and EGFR changes guide targeted drugs that extend life. Tissue sampling can fail or carry risk, while blood testing for tumour DNA is gentler yet misses cases where little DNA is shed.

Their case-control study used 384 patients treated at a Guangzhou hospital between 2018 and 2024, split almost evenly between blood-positive and blood-negative results. Regression analysis distilled clinical features into a predictive model and a simple score. The tool aims to pick out patients whose blood test is likely to succeed, sparing others a wasted wait when tissue is scarce. Faster answers matter because blood testing can shorten the detection cycle by weeks.
pmc-13558258:
Nobuhiro Watanabe and twelve colleagues looked in 2026 for ultrasound signs that a heart artery might be injured during a procedure that grinds away hardened calcium. Calcified nodules inside coronary arteries are treated with orbital atherectomy, a spinning device that can tear the vessel wall. The team reviewed 67 patients treated with ultrasound guidance between 2020 and 2023 and classified how the guidewire sat relative to each nodule.

Nine patients suffered an injury, mostly bleeding into the vessel wall and once a perforation. One wire pattern carried by far the highest injury rate. In that pattern the wire hugged the healthy wall on both sides of the nodule. It stood alone as an independent predictor in the final model. Older warning signs, a tenting appearance and an undesirable wire position, showed no clear link. Spotting the risky pattern beforehand could change how operators proceed.
pmc-13559558:
Yafang Kang and colleagues investigate how hypoxia-inducible factor-1α, a protein that switches on under low oxygen, drives cervical cancer growth through sugar metabolism. Their 2026 study starts from cancer atlas data, then tests the mechanism in HeLa and Caski cervical cancer cell lines. The team raised or lowered the protein's levels and watched cell behavior.

Atlas analysis showed the protein abundant in cervical tumors, tied to poorer survival and to altered immune cell presence. In the dish, extra protein made cells multiply and invade more strongly, while removing it reversed both effects. The protein also raised levels of LDHA, an enzyme central to glycolysis, together with lactate output and reactive oxygen species. Blocking that chain weakened the aggressive behavior. The authors propose this oxygen-sensing protein as a possible marker and treatment target, while their evidence so far rests on databases and cell experiments.
pmc-13559958:
Harold Pollack, Richard Frank, and Sherry Glied argue that states can widen community support for people with serious mental illness by borrowing lessons from services for intellectual and developmental disabilities. Their 2026 policy analysis reviews six decades of deinstitutionalization in the United States. Both groups moved out of institutions, yet community systems matured far more successfully for the disability community than for people with mental illness.

The authors urge the federal government to give states Medicaid authorities with real budget flexibility, favoring Section 1915 waivers over Section 1115 routes that demand budget neutrality. New federal programs, they add, need rules and oversight that let states actually carry out the stated intent. Broad programs such as 988 crisis lines risk drifting from their mission without clear accountability. The piece closes with contrasting histories framed as practical guidance for state policymakers.
pmc-13560258:
Yamada and colleagues set out in 2026 the protocol for a nationwide Japanese web cohort following children's mental health from birth to late adolescence. The design cuts across diagnoses rather than studying one condition at a time. Prevention needs long data from before the teen years, and such data are scarce. Recruitment opens in early 2026 through community channels and clinics, with extra effort to include children with autism or attention conditions alongside their peers.

About seven thousand children and their caregivers, up to fourteen thousand people, will answer yearly online questionnaires, with teens also reporting for themselves. A standard difficulties questionnaire anchors the repeated outcome, and an optional saliva group adds genetic material. Analyses will chart how symptoms develop and which risks and protections act at which ages, aiming to time preventive help well.
pmc-13560358:
Omer Ogutcen, Nursema Demir, and Dilek Ozkan Sen examine how cigarette smoking tracks with periodontitis severity among patients at a periodontology clinic. Their 2026 cross-sectional study includes 781 adults whose records captured smoking habits, systemic parameters, and full periodontal findings. Smoking was split into none, ten or fewer cigarettes daily, and more than ten.

Daily consumption linked significantly to worse disease stage, with stage IV periodontitis concentrated among the heavier smokers. Probing depths, a direct measure of tissue destruction, also deepened with consumption. Adjusted ordinal modeling kept heavy smoking tied to higher stage after other factors entered. Brushing at least twice daily, by contrast, lowered the odds of severe disease, while visit frequency and education showed no link. The authors conclude severity climbs with cigarette dose, and they frame daily brushing as a measurable protective habit.
pmc-13562558:
Tomasz Waldziński and seven colleagues compare how professional tennis players and active men respond, in muscle and blood, to a bout of all-out anaerobic effort. Tennis demands repeated sprints and hard strokes with short rests, which may train adaptations. The 2026 study tested 14 professionals and 15 active non-players. Both groups performed two 30-second Wingate cycling efforts, with knee contractions and muscle electrical recordings before and after. Blood was sampled at rest, right after, and at three and 24 hours.

Players produced higher peak power, by 7.8 percent absolutely and 10.1 percent relative to body weight. They also kept their fast knee-flexion force after the effort, while the other group lost 26 percent of it. Players' front thigh muscle fired harder after the effort. Their blood showed stronger antioxidant capacity and more IL-10, with a blunted rise in IL-6. Years of elite play, the authors argue, reshape fatigue handling and recovery chemistry.
pmc-13563358:
Manuel Marques-Cruz and colleagues built a checklist extension for bringing artificial intelligence into health guideline development, publishing the work in 2026. AI can already help select studies and extract data, yet guideline groups lacked conduct standards for using it openly and safely. The Guidelines International Network AI working group started by prompting a language model for candidate items across every step of the existing McMaster checklist.

Iterative expert discussion cut 149 draft items to a refined set, added 17 new ones, and a trial run on the 2024-2025 allergic rhinitis guidelines polished four wordings. The final extension holds 49 items that modify or add to the original checklist. Guideline teams can use it to make AI use in their work more complete, transparent, and auditable.
pmc-13563858:
WenHui Qi and seven colleagues test a two-colour fluorescence stain that promises faster, clearer diagnosis of the four kinds of vaginitis. Routine microscopy is slow and skill-hungry. Under blue light, the 2026 assay paints microbes red and the patient's own cells green, so shape and colour together name the culprit. The team mapped how cultured cells and reference strains look under the stain, then judged it on vaginal samples from 758 women against the microscope workup.

Agreement ran strong. For bacterial vaginosis the test caught 88.6 percent with 95.8 percent specificity. For yeast infection it caught 95.3 percent with 97.8 percent specificity, the best pairing of the four. Aerobic vaginitis and trichomoniasis scored well, though case counts for the last were small. Mixed infections could be read in the same view. The authors position the stain as a test that merges the strengths of wet-mount and Gram methods for clinics.
pmc-13569458:
Floris Huider's team mapped the genes behind major depression in a Dutch group rated by one set of rules, in a 2026 genome-wide mega-analysis. Gene studies of depression have suffered from loose, mixed labels that swap rigour for size, limiting new finds. The team pooled 64,941 people from the BIONIC group, all rated with standard clinical rules for lifetime major depressive disorder.

Common gene variants explained a large share of risk, gene overlap with the largest global depression study was high, and polygenic scores worked across groups and labels. Twin work suggested family mix-ups did not drive prediction, and one new locus in PALMD awaits outside replication. The work shows one set of rating rules can sharpen gene finds even without the biggest cohort.
pmc-13569558:
Lim and colleagues published a 2026 study on how medicine counts miss many real drugs. Older adults often take many medicines at once, a pattern called polypharmacy. Standard counts in health data tally only pills taken by mouth. Creams, patches, and drops slip past those counts entirely in records.

The team compared both counting styles in Western Australian data for older adults. Adding non-pill forms raised measured medicine burden in both groups studied. The jump ran larger for people living in residential aged care homes. High medicine counts grew most, revealing hidden load in complex cases. Fairer counts matter for safety checks, the authors argue to readers. Care homes showed the sharpest undercount under the old method.
pmc-13569858:
Samuel Minucci Camargo and colleagues test, in a 2026 study, automatic nervous system balance in long COVID patients using a tilt table that shifts the body upright and stresses circulation control. Thirty-nine patients and twenty-two healthy controls had heart rate variability and blood pressure tracked through the test phases.

Patients showed a blunted stress response when upright, with rhythm measures pointing to weak sympathetic activation and poor adjustment to standing. Blood pressure recovery after the tilt was also muted. The results give clinicians measurable signs of the dizziness and intolerance many long COVID patients report, and a test protocol that can quantify progress during recovery programs.
pmc-13570858:
David Fitz-Patrick and a large trial team report, in a 2026 phase three study, a COVID-19 vaccine adapted to the Omicron BA.1 variant in adults aged eighteen to fifty-five. Three groups covered people already vaccinated with the original vaccine and people never vaccinated, totaling nearly fifteen hundred participants, with antibody levels, response rates, and side effects tracked.

The adapted shot aimed to beat the original on neutralizing the matched variant, judged by antibody ratios and the share of participants mounting a response. Two-dose results in vaccine-naive participants were compared against the original vaccine's earlier trial. Safety and soreness data complete a picture regulators used for variant update decisions.
pmc-13572458:
Manogna R. L, with two colleagues, benchmarks 2026 computer models for winter wheat yield forecasts across India. District-level forecasts guide food plans and policy in the world's second largest wheat producer. The team tested nine model types on 23 years of data from 275 districts in seven states.

The data joined soil depth profiles with weather and satellite series from 2001 to 2023. A hybrid model that routes each data kind through its own path won, with a mean error of 273.2 kilograms per hectare. That cut error by 43.8 percent against a random forest base model. A plain forecast that just repeats last year's yield nearly tied it, though. The hybrid pulled ahead in the dry 2023 season, and its edge centred on the February to March grain-filling window.
pmc-13572558:
Jun Lei Gao, with seven colleagues, reports a 2026 mouse study of breathing hydrogen sulfide, a toxic gas found in industry and farm waste. The gas can harm the lungs, immune system, and nerves, but the gene-level picture in lung tissue was unclear. The team varied the dose and read both body markers and lung gene activity.

At set doses, the gas raised an inflammatory signal and two defence enzymes, while high doses shifted more immune signals and stress measures. Some markers of cell damage fell, a mixed pattern the authors note. Lung gene reads found 963 genes whose levels changed across groups. Those genes cluster in immune response, DNA change, enzyme work, and cell cycle control. Four genes, among them FGFBP1 and GATA3, look central to the response. The data set seeds later work on how the gas harms lungs.
pmc-13574858:
Luping Qiu and colleagues built a model to flag severe drug-induced liver injury without biopsy. Severe injury carries a poor outlook, yet blood markers are vague and biopsy means cutting into the liver. Their study at many centres signed up 305 patients who had both liver biopsy and dual elastography, a scan method that yields activity and scarring scores. Eight machine-learning models were tried, with the best tuned by cross-checks.

The best model, a tuned regression, scored 0.862 on the standard accuracy scale in testing, with 81 percent sensitivity and 75 percent specificity, and the scan scores were its top predictors. The team also put out an online risk tool. The authors present the model as a clear aid for sorting risk and guiding early care choices.
pmc-13578758:
Arianna D'Ulizia, Alessia D'Andrea, and Riccardo Denni refine a way to rank the best spreaders in a network when some kinds of nodes matter more than others, in a 2026 study. Classic peeling methods strip a network layer by layer to find its core, yet they score every category alike. Their version peels with a priority order over categories, honoring a user's ranking of which groups count most.

The method raced seventy nine rival measures on seven real networks. It placed the true top spreader highest on five of the seven sets. Ties were its weak spot, since many nodes shared top ranks. Pairing the peel order with a simple degree count broke ties best, reliably lifting true spreaders into the top group. The code is shared freely for other teams to test.
pmc-13579858:
Maryam Adelipour and colleagues tune a cheap polymer method for harvesting healing vesicles from stem cell broth, in a 2026 study. Stem cells release tiny packets called exosomes that calm immune attack and aid repair, yet pulling them out cleanly at scale has lagged. The team tried three weights of a common polymer, polyethylene glycol, which crowds the packets out of solution so they can be collected.

The middle weight won on yield and purity. Its packets measured under two hundred nanometers and carried the right surface badges. A deep scan counted hundreds of proteins and over a thousand small molecules inside, proof the cargo stayed intact. Extra rinse cycles through a sizing column stripped away stray junk. Cancer cells bathed in the packets stayed alive and, at high doses, thrived a bit more.
pmc-13580258:
Jisha Kuttiani Ali and Emad Alhseinat build a membrane from porous organic cages whose holes widen or shrink with the solvent, in a 2026 study. The cages were cast onto a plastic support film from two building blocks at room temperature. Solvent choice flips the pore size, a switch confirmed by crystal pattern checks, and the change runs both ways.

In water the tightened pores let only a trickle of heavy metal ions through while blocking most test dye. Looser pores in alcohol passed more of both. Metals trapped upstream could then be washed back out, with about half the nickel and slightly less of the zinc recovered. The authors pitch the switchable film for pulling valuable metals from waste water while sorting molecules on the side.
pmc-13582858:
Bing Liu and colleagues solved the crystal structure of USP15, an enzyme that strips ubiquitin tags from proteins, caught in the act of gripping ubiquitin. USP15 shapes immune responses and cancer, but how it recognises ubiquitin and switches shape was poorly understood. Their 2026 study reports the catalytic domain at 2.3 angstrom resolution, covalently bound to a ubiquitin probe.

Binding flips the enzyme from a closed, inactive shape to an open, active one, realigning its catalytic trio and swinging a finger-like subdomain outward. Two conserved parts, an alpha-8 helix and a loop, proved essential: deleting the helix killed activity, and a cancer-linked mutation in the loop weakened binding. The authors point to these parts as targets for selective drugs against this enzyme family.
pmc-13583358:
Raj Whitlock, Robert NL Fitt and the Darwin Tree of Life Consortium, with several Wellcome Sanger Institute teams, published this 2026 genome sequence note for Hypericum pulchrum, slender St John's-wort. The plant is a hairless perennial herb of heaths and open woodlands, widespread across the British Isles and western Europe but declining in central England. The assembly forms part of the Darwin Tree of Life project, which is sequencing the eukaryotic species of Britain and Ireland.

The assembly resolves two haplotypes, the two chromosome sets, totalling about 373 and 368 megabases. Most of the first haplotype, about 95 percent of its length, is organised into nine chromosomal pseudomolecules. The team assembled the mitochondrial genomes, at about 218 and 277 kilobases, and the plastid genome at about 149 kilobases. Annotation through Ensembl identified 29,497 protein-coding genes. The authors present it for studying the species' ecology, including its antifungal seed coat and poorly known insect relationships.
pmc-13585158:
Gregory A. Hosler, Matthew S. Goldberg, and Etan Marks present eight hard-to-call skin cases in this 2026 series. The growths at issue are melanocytic, meaning they arise from pigment cells, and some are melanoma, a dangerous skin cancer, while others are harmless moles. A stain test called PRAME often helps, yet its readings can clash or stay unclear, leaving experts split.

Each case drew four or five separate expert opinions. The team then ran a 23-gene test, which reads the activity of a set of genes in the tissue, to see if it could tip the balance. In cases where the stain was muddy or conflicting, the gene results pushed the final call up or down in risk. The authors offer the test as a tiebreaker, not a replacement for expert review.
pmc-13586358:
Francisco M. Nadal-Nicolás and colleagues established the thirteen-lined ground squirrel as a translational model for head-injury vision loss. Rapid head acceleration damages the optic nerve and visual system, but mice and rats, being nocturnal with rod-dominated retinas, translate poorly. The ground squirrel is diurnal, with a cone-rich retina, dense retinal ganglion cells, and an astrocyte pattern shared with primates and humans. Their 2026 study tested repeated closed-head impacts in this species.

Impacts caused lasting harm, including abnormal seasonal weight control and persistent visual dysfunction, with retinal thinning, reduced ganglion-cell function, dorsal cell loss, and late optic-nerve glial change. The authors present the squirrel as a strong animal stand-in for human head-injury vision loss, capturing systemic, behavioural, and visual effects of human closed-head injury.
pmc-13592458:
Clarissa Dine leads a protocol for a feasibility study on spotting depression relapse early with a smart ring. Magnetic brain stimulation can lift treatment resistant depression, yet many who improve slip back within a year, and no firm warning marker exists. Their pilot will enroll 25 outpatients at two Ontario hospitals. Each will wear an Oura ring through treatment and six months of follow up, with mood, anxiety, sleep, and well being scales taken at set points.

Success will be judged on recruitment, ring adherence, retention, missing data, and ease of use. Exploratory checks will probe whether ring derived signals track treatment response or herald relapse. Dine and the team stress the work is a groundwork step toward larger relapse prevention trials.
pmc-13593558:
Robert H. Anderson, Richard Sutton, and Damian Sanchez Quintana dispute a claim about where a pacing lead was placed in the atrium, arguing from the anatomy itself. In their 2026 commentary they contend the images in the report show the lead sitting in the front wall of the right atrium. It is not in the septum between the atria, as the report's authors suggested.

They follow the path a signal would take from that site. It runs through a recess of the right atrial appendage and then along a bundle between the atria before reaching the left atrial walls. Neither structure belongs to the atrial septum, they point out. Their message is practical: work on new ways to pace the left atrium will only succeed if the underlying anatomy is described correctly.
pmc-13594458:
Yohei Kikuchi and colleagues asked whether electrical signals measured before implanting an atrial leadless pacemaker predict pacing thresholds three months later. Thirty-nine consecutive patients received the Aveir AR device at one Japanese hospital between February and September 2025, mostly as part of dual-chamber systems. The primary outcome was atrial capture threshold at three months.

Premapping pacing threshold tracked with the three-month threshold, but the link was confounded by operator-driven site selection and was not an independent predictor. Waveform measures such as amplitude, current of injury, and voltage change added no further discrimination. Atrial tissue and anchoring differ enough from ventricular pacing that dedicated prospective markers are needed.
pmc-13597158:
Meridiana Dodaj and co-authors report a 67-year-old man whose atypical carcinoid tumor, a slow neuroendocrine cancer of the lung, returned beneath his vocal cords almost twenty years after the original surgery. The growth blocked about eighty percent of his windpipe, causing bleeding and breathlessness, and open surgery was not the chosen route.

Through a bronchoscope, the team first used laser treatment to burn away the bulk of the tumor, reopening the airway and stopping the bleeding in the same session. Five months later they froze the remaining tissue with cryotherapy, completing the clearance without major complications. His symptoms resolved, and a check three months on showed the airway still open. The authors present the staged pairing of fast thermal debulking with gentle freezing of residue as a lung-sparing option for late central airway recurrence.
pmc-13599158:
Anne-S. Helvik and three colleagues present a 2026 systematic review asking how often people with dementia who live at home are in pain. Pain in this group is easy to miss, since memory and speech problems can hide it, yet it harms both patients and the family members who care for them. Earlier reviews had focused on nursing homes, leaving the home setting poorly mapped.

Following standard review methods, the team searched seven databases and kept 25 articles drawn from 22 studies, with group sizes from 36 to 1,379 people. Reports of any pain in the past month ranged from 36 to 76 percent. Studies used very different definitions and rating tools, which made direct comparison hard. Helvik's group calls for one shared, routine way to check pain in people with dementia at home.
pmc-13610258:
Hans Demmelmair leads an eight-author team in Bangkok examining how a mother's body and the hormone leptin relate to her baby's size. Birth weight predicts later obesity risk, and leptin, a satiety hormone made by fat tissue, was a candidate link. In a subgroup of 38 mother-infant pairs, the team measured leptin in maternal blood at delivery and at four months. Cord blood and infant blood at four months were also measured.

Maternal leptin fell sharply after birth, from 32.4 to 11.1 nanograms per milliliter. Cord blood leptin ran more than twice as high in girls as in boys, and mothers' and babies' levels did not correlate. Birth weight tied strongly to the mother's pre-pregnancy BMI. Higher maternal leptin at delivery went with lower birth weight, a twist the authors flag. Cord leptin only tended toward a positive link with birth weight.
pmc-13612258:
Oliver Vasilj and three colleagues follow children exposed to gestational diabetes before birth into their tenth year. Diabetes in pregnancy has been linked to early childhood effects, but long-term motor evidence was thin. This follow-up revisited a recorded cohort: 100 children, fifty exposed to diet-treated gestational diabetes and fifty from uncomplicated pregnancies. Each child was tested in six motor domains, from coordination to balance and explosive strength.

Overall motor function looked largely the same in both groups. Three exceptions survived statistical correction. Exposed children did worse at squats and at rolling a ball with the non-dominant hand, a large effect, yet did better on the straddle forward bend. The authors read this as subtle, task-specific fingerprints of the prenatal environment rather than general impairment. They call for longer work to learn whether these differences persist and matter in daily life.
pmc-13616358:
Xinru Xiao and colleagues link excess copper in the body to flare-ups of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, the lung disease that narrows airways, and trace a mechanism in the airway lining. Three sources pointed the same way. National survey data came first. A hospital comparison of 30 flare-up patients with 30 healthy controls came next, plus a year of follow-up. Higher blood copper meant more flare-ups and sooner returns.

Working across mice, zebrafish, lab-grown lung tissue, and airway cells, the team showed extra copper breaking the lining's seal, letting leaks through. A signalling chain running through an inflammation messenger and a copper-handling protein called ATP7A carried the harm, with oxidative stress and failing cell power plants in the mix. Copper control, rarely discussed in lung clinics, may deserve a place in flare-up prevention.
pmc-13617658:
Sara A. Fortin-Miller and four colleagues report a 2026 analysis of how toddlers' diet quality changes between their first and second birthdays. Habits formed in the first two years often persist and shape later risk of obesity and heart disease. The team scored recalls from one hundred sixty-six Kansas City children at twelve and twenty-four months with the Healthy Eating Index for toddlers.

Scores sat below recommended levels at both ages, under sixty points at twelve months and slightly lower at twenty-four months. That dip lost statistical significance after correction for multiple testing. Component shifts were clearer: vegetable intake fell while refined grains and added sugars rose, with the sugar increase the largest change. Four eating styles appeared at twelve months, and adherence to the healthiest fat pattern faded by age two. The authors flag year two as a window where diets worsen.
pmc-13618858:
Miao-Qing Zhang and colleagues report a 2026 study of a newly described form of the autophagy protein ATG10, called ATG10S, as a possible brake on cytokine storms. Cytokine storms, the runaway release of inflammatory signals, worsen many illnesses, yet drugs aimed at single cytokines often fall short because the cascade is broad. The team tested ATG10S in zebrafish and human cell models inflamed with viral spike protein or bacterial lipopolysaccharide.

ATG10S lowered a set of inflammatory cytokines all controlled by the transcription factor MEF2A, and it did so by two routes at once. It bound MEF2A directly and sent it for selective destruction through the cell's recycling system, while also blocking a rival signaling partner from binding MEF2A. That dual action cut both MEF2A levels and activity, restored recycling flow that inflammation had impaired, and spared unrelated transcription factors.
pmc-13618958:
Qi Ouyang and eight colleagues test whether dioscin, a plant-derived compound, can slow the aging of retinal pigment epithelial cells, whose senescence and identity loss drive early dry age-related macular degeneration. Using a sugar-induced aging model in cultured human retinal cells and in mice, they combined gene-expression assays, protein blotting, microscopy, and senescence staining. Computational docking hunted for the compound's target.

Dioscin eased cell senescence and the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition that degrades the retinal layer. Docking and simulation pointed to the signaling protein TGF-beta2 as its likely target. Experiments showed dioscin dampened that protein's downstream pathway in the aged cells. Single-cell data placed TGF-beta2 highest in the choroidal lining cells of macular degeneration patients, suggesting diseased vessels signal harm to the neighboring retinal layer. The authors present dioscin as a candidate worth testing in models closer to human disease.
pmc-13619758:
Daniel Brockes and five colleagues ran a pilot study on whether an e-learning platform can sharpen dentists' skill at reading cone-beam CT scans, in a 2026 paper. German dentists need special training and a license to use this 3D imaging in practice. Thirty-two dentists took part, half licensed and half not, working through a pre-test, then eight to ten weeks with a platform holding 104 annotated cases, then a similar post-test.

Scores rose significantly after the learning phase for the whole group. Licensed dentists started ahead, yet the gap vanished by the end, with both groups finishing in the low eighties percent range. An experience questionnaire showed dentists on both sides found the platform practical, user-friendly, and well built around real cases. The authors present online case practice as a workable route to stronger diagnostic skills.
pmc-13620258:
Diana Stratulat and seven colleagues interviewed the people who lived through a virtual day treatment program for teenagers with eating disorders, in a 2026 study. The program ran six to eight weeks alongside usual in-person care, a format born during the pandemic. Twenty-five people shared their experience: eight adolescents, nine parents, and eight healthcare professionals.

Three themes ran through every group: teenagers' well-being improved, the virtual format made care easier to reach, and the same format brought real challenges, from intensity to screen fatigue. Parents and clinicians added a fourth theme, a lift in parents' own well-being. Participants also offered concrete fixes for future programs. The authors say virtual day treatment earned its place after the pandemic, provided designers listen to the friction points all three groups named.
pmc-13621458:
Stephanie M Brunner and nine colleagues dissected how barley genes and growing conditions interact, segment by segment, instead of treating each plant variety as one lump. Whether a gene helps or hurts depends on the weather and soil it meets, a puzzle called genotype-by-environment interaction. Their commercial dataset held 961 spring barley varieties grown at twelve sites.

The team grouped the sites into four environment types using a statistical model, then chopped the genome into about seventeen hundred blocks of linked markers. For each block they estimated breeding value inside each environment group. Some blocks held one clearly best version everywhere, while for others the winner flipped completely between environments. Those flipping blocks, found across several chromosomes, mark where breeders must match seed to place. The authors offer the haplotype-level method for other traits and crops facing a changing climate.
pmc-13621558:
Alexandre S Pires and four colleagues examined how large language models judge right and wrong in social dilemmas, and what happens if people take those judgments to heart. Humans cooperate partly through reputation: we help those judged good and shun those judged bad. The team asked twenty-one leading models to grade more than forty thousand fictional decisions, then fed the resulting norms into an evolutionary model of cooperation.

The models agreed remarkably when judging actions toward people seen as good. Toward the ill-reputed, verdicts scattered widely, both between models and within a single model across runs. Those differences mattered: simulation outcomes for long-run cooperation swung substantially depending on whose norms ruled. Prompt tweaks could steer a model's norms, especially when given concrete goals. The authors warn that deploying language models as moral advisors quietly picks a future for human cooperation, so their norms deserve deliberate design.
pmc-13621658:
Xueyan Zhu led a large team hunting body-chemistry links to anhedonia, the flattened ability to feel pleasure, in bipolar depression, in 2026. Anhedonia predicts worse outcomes and resists standard drugs, but its chemistry is unsettled. The study compared eighty-five bipolar patients, sixty-one of them depressed, with eighty-eight healthy volunteers. The team checked pleasure capacity, childhood adversity, oxidative stress markers, and BDNF, a growth factor that feeds neurons.

Depressed patients reported far less pleasure, both in anticipation and in the moment, alongside more anxiety and more childhood adversity. One antioxidant enzyme, catalase, differed clearly between groups. Within the depressed group, higher BDNF and catalase levels tracked with lower enjoyed pleasure, an unexpected negative link. BDNF stood out as a predictor of that pleasure loss in the final model. The authors argue anhedonia in bipolar disorder is partly written in this chemistry, opening a route toward biomarker-guided treatment.
pmc-13623958:
Katrin Rietscher and Benjamin Klein comment on a study in Science by Winge and colleagues that found two rival chemical tagging systems battling over the fate of skin cells. The epidermis renews itself constantly as stem cells in its base produce keratinocytes that harden and rise. Tags added to proteins after they are built help steer that journey.

Winge's team combined gene-perturbation screens, protein measurement, and spatial gene mapping in human keratinocytes and animal models. Two tag types pulled in opposite directions: adding NEDD8, a small protein tag, pushed cells to stay undifferentiated in effect, while blocking that pathway triggered differentiation. The second tag system, built on SUMO2, worked the other way, since breaking it stalled maturation. Rietscher and Klein frame the pair as a balance dial for skin renewal, with consequences for wound repair and skin disease when the dial slips.
pmc-13624958:
Ingrid D Van Iperen, Marleen Flim, and Peter E Spronk check whether a handheld grip meter can track recovery in patients weakened by long intensive care stays. Thirty-six patients with intensive care unit-acquired weakness squeezed the K-force dynamometer at the start and again one week later. A standard bedside muscle score served as the comparison measure.

Grip strength in the stronger hand rose from about two and two-thirds kilograms to about three and a half, and the weaker hand gained as well, with large effect sizes for both. The bedside score also improved over the week. Since the meter caught clear change in just seven days, the authors back it for following rehab progress in critically ill patients.
pmc-13625958:
Amita Rani Sahoo, Nisha Bhattarai, and Matthias Buck simulate how two sibling receptors sit in the cell membrane. EphA1 and EphA2 guide cell growth and movement, and EphA2 is notorious in cancer for switching on without its usual trigger. Using coarse-grained computer models of a realistic membrane, the team watched the receptors pair up through their membrane-spanning parts and noted how nearby domains leaned on the membrane.

Both receptors formed steady pairs, yet EphA1 favored a symmetric grip while EphA2 chose a zipper-like interface. A neighboring domain in EphA2 clung to a special membrane lipid, and cutting the construct down to one outer domain blocked pairing until the second domain returned. The differences trace to linker flexibility and gene history, offering testable models for cancer and brain disease.
pmc-13627258:
Mohammad Reza Heidari and co-authors hunt a dangerous food germ along the milk chain of Yazd Province, Iran. Listeria monocytogenes can turn dairy into a vehicle for severe infection, above all in the vulnerable. Between 2022 and 2023 the team collected 370 samples. They came from raw and pasteurized milk, and also from equipment, transport containers, and workers' hands and gowns. Lab and gene tests confirmed the germ, and antibiotic disks challenged it.

Ten isolates turned up, all under three percent of samples, with raw milk the most contaminated source and pasteurized milk and workers clean. Every isolate resisted three older antibiotics outright, while the first-line drugs used in clinics still worked fully. All carried the core virulence genes. Raw milk, the authors warn, is a reservoir of resistant listeria that hygiene and steady monitoring must contain.
pmc-13627658:
Patricia García-Fernández and co-authors show how to grow human Schwann cells from the sliver of nerve a diagnostic biopsy provides. Schwann cells wrap peripheral nerves in insulation, and their failure drives many nerve diseases, yet patient samples are tiny, about four millimeters of sural nerve. Their protocol coaxes those fragments into living cultures of multiplying Schwann cells that can be frozen, thawed, and expanded, and a full gene expression profile checks what the cultured cells have become.

Reproducible cultures from real patients open a door that animal work cannot: testing disease mechanisms and drugs in the very cells that fail. The transcriptome map anchors the cells' identity against drift in the dish. For clinics that already biopsy nerves for diagnosis, the method turns a one-time sample into a lasting research resource.
pmc-13628558:
Matilde Micillo and nine colleagues tested a new antibody-drug conjugate against Richter transformation, an aggressive lymphoma that erupts out of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia and answers poorly to standard chemotherapy. Their candidate, SLV-404, aims at RYK, a cell-surface protein found across many lymphomas yet absent from healthy blood cells.

The conjugate pairs an anti-RYK antibody with deruxtecan, a powerful drug that blocks an enzyme tumours need to copy DNA. In laboratory cultures and in patient-derived tumour grafts it triggered strong cancer cell death while sparing normal blood cells. Mice carrying such grafts lived significantly longer with much smaller tumour burdens, leading the authors to propose RYK as a fresh target for aggressive lymphoma therapy.
pmc-13629258:
Oliver Ozioko and colleagues review soft skins that can reversibly change their own thickness, bulging outward or pulling back on command. Their 2026 review treats this thickness morphing as a design strategy for haptic interfaces, devices that create a sense of touch, and for soft robots working in tight spaces.

The authors survey the triggers used to drive the change, the material platforms, structural designs borrowed from origami and kirigami, and fabrication methods.
