They give special attention to layered rubber composites, electrohydraulic systems that move fluid with electric fields, hybrid designs, and data-driven control. Remaining problems include wear under repeated cycling, energy use, manufacturing at scale, and combining sensing with movement. Solving these, they argue, could yield self-powered skins that perceive contact and act safely on their own.
pmc-13629458:
Pedro Henrique Magalhães Cardoso and six colleagues identified which bacteria caused columnaris disease in ornamental fish at a large São Paulo distributor running a shared recirculating water system. Published in 2026, their two-step DNA workflow screened lesion scrapings from 123 fish across twenty-eight species.

About half the samples tested positive for the columnaris species complex. Of those, species-level typing succeeded in just under half, finding Flavobacterium covae dominant by a wide margin and a second species, F. davisii, in a couple of cases, while over half the positives resisted typing altogether. The authors present the results as baseline surveillance data for multispecies ornamental systems, where shared water spreads pathogens quickly and species-level knowledge guides biosecurity.
pmc-13632758:
Ning Zhao and seven colleagues report a battery that breathes carbon dioxide and delivers unusually high voltage. Lithium-carbon dioxide batteries could store large amounts of energy while using a greenhouse gas. Their usual discharge product is hard to break down during charging, which caps performance. The team added a crystalline iron-based material as a helper that steers the chemistry toward a different product, lithium oxalate.

With that change, the battery reached a discharge level well above the usual range for this chemistry. It also delivered very large capacity for its weight and kept cycling for many hundreds of hours. Performance held across a wide span of temperatures, from deep cold to strong heat. Pouch cells built the same way packed high energy for their total weight and cycled reversibly for days. The work points toward practical versions of this battery type.
pmc-13635858:
Soawapak Hinjoy and eight colleagues adapted a United States disease-ranking tool for province-level use in Thailand. The tool helps governments rank animal-to-human health threats under the One Health idea, which treats human, animal, and environmental health as one system. National rankings can miss local realities. The team ran four-day participatory workshops in two provinces during 2025, each drawing about seventy people from health, farming, environment, government, and community groups.

The provinces ranked threats quite differently because they weighted the criteria differently. One province prized biomedical severity and cross-sector impact, putting emerging infections and rabies on top. The other prized workable governance, so air pollution, open waste burning, stray dogs, farm chemicals, and climate disasters led its list. The authors conclude that community-led adaptation makes rankings legitimate and useful. Local lists, they argue, strengthen early warning and prevention better than a single national table.
pmc-13637058:
Saadat and a large team combine two molecular layers in this 2026 study of Wilms tumour, the most common childhood kidney cancer, which arises from derailed kidney development. They profiled DNA methylation, chemical tags that switch genes off, alongside gene activity in 27 primary tumours and matched healthy kidney tissue from the same children.

Roughly 9,000 methylation sites split tumour from normal tissue and from other childhood cancers, forming a tumour-specific signature. Cases clustered into three methylation groups matching gene-expression subtypes with different immune landscapes and predicted drug responses, one favoring paclitaxel and another doxorubicin in the models. More than 900 genes sat under such control in the combined analysis. Tumours with a methylation gain at the classic 11p15.5 imprinted locus showed the deepest epigenetic damage, while shrinking tumours with a normal locus were least affected.
pmc-13639558:
Shota Miyakuni maps the published evidence on therapeutic software in Japan in a 2026 scoping review. Such software, including digital therapeutics and software classed as a medical device, delivers treatment through apps, yet the Japanese study record sits scattered across diseases and designs.

Searching PubMed records from 2015 to early 2026, the author sorted each publication by how rigorous its evaluation was and how clinical its main outcome was. The resulting maturity map shows where solid trial evidence exists and where only early feasibility work has appeared. The snapshot gives developers and regulators a shared picture of remaining gaps.
pmc-13641458:
Natalia-Guillemina Target and five colleagues present a 2026 study comparing physical activity in short daily home dialysis against standard in-center hemodialysis. Dialysis for kidney failure burdens daily life heavily, and treatment setting and schedule may change how active patients can stay.

The international prospective study enrolled patients in French and Belgian centers between late 2018 and mid 2021, with each person's dialysis route chosen outside the study. Alongside activity, the researchers tracked treatment effectiveness, tolerance, acceptability, and side effects. The design reflects a patient-centered view that the best dialysis plan should fit individual lives, not only lab targets.
pmc-13642458:
Two artery-blocking treatments for liver cancer are compared head to head by Mosconi and colleagues. Hepatocellular carcinoma that cannot be removed by surgery is often treated through the arteries feeding the tumour. Treatment either blocks blood flow alone or blocks flow while releasing chemotherapy from drug-loaded microspheres. The team ran a multicentre randomised trial in 111 patients with early or intermediate unresectable disease, testing whether plain embolisation was non-inferior to the drug-loaded approach.

Time until the disease progressed was similar in both arms, at roughly eight months, and formal equivalence testing confirmed the treatments matched within the preset margin. Overall survival, tumour response, severe side effects, and hospital stay also showed no meaningful difference between the groups. Mosconi and colleagues conclude that plain embolisation performs comparably for these patients, which matters because simpler treatment may ease cost and complexity without sacrificing outcomes.
pmc-13643458:
MHD Osama Srour and five colleagues report a 2026 project to cut overuse of heart rhythm monitors in hospital wards. Extra days on a monitor raise costs and alarm fatigue. They bring no clear gain for the patient.

At their hospital, staff ran talks and put up posters based on the 2017 heart group rules. They then compared early 2025 with late 2025. Mean monitor time per patient fell by about a fifth. Doctors also knew the rules far better and scored much higher on case questions. The team says steady teaching plus checks in the record system could lock in the gains.
pmc-13645558:
Hua Chen and seven colleagues report a 2026 cross-sectional survey of older patients with osteoporosis in Henan Province, China, about how well patients grasp their own fall risk. Staff at two campuses of a bone specialty hospital collected 294 valid questionnaires. Patients answered scales on fall awareness, daily function, frailty, mood, and felt social support. The team then looked for factors tied to awareness scores.

Awareness of fall risk differed across the scale's dimensions and linked with many factors at once. Age, sex, marital status, household income, and living alone all played a part. Fall prevention teaching, daily function, depression, and social support also mattered, and together the factors explained a large share of the score spread. The authors suggest nurses shape fall prevention work around these patient traits. Better awareness, they argue, could cut fall injuries in this group.
pmc-13649458:
Carolina Valle and seven colleagues tested whether the main scent compounds in rosemary oil act on the brain's serotonin transporter, a key target of antidepressant drugs. Rosemary oil has shown calming and mood-lifting effects in past work, but the molecular route was unknown.

Computer models placed all three compounds, pinene, camphor, and cineole, into both binding pockets of the transporter. Lab tests then showed each compound pushed a labelled drug off the transporter, with pinene the strongest. In living cells, all three partly slowed serotonin uptake, even at high doses, but never blocked it fully. The authors propose these scents as mild, partial blockers that may help explain rosemary's effects.
pmc-13650558:
Zemin Qing and thirteen colleagues build a framework that connects autism genetics to behavior across three layers of biology. Autism varies widely. Its syndromic forms are tied to a known genetic condition, while non-syndromic forms may share some mechanisms while differing in others, a puzzle the review tackles by comparing both groups.

The first layer lists gene functions, the second groups them into core pathways, and the third maps onto clinical traits. Genes range from local parts of the synapse, the junction between nerve cells, to global controllers that repackage DNA and switch whole gene programs. Chromatin control and synapse building recur as shared ground, while each subgroup also carries enriched factors of its own that ripple into circuit-level integration problems. The authors offer the hierarchy to guide biomarker hunting and to sort patients by biology rather than behavior alone.
pmc-13651458:
Jaume Noguera-Gómez and three co-authors build a field-diagnostic method that watches outdoor perovskite solar cells with cameras and electronics at once, to separate passing weather effects from genuine, irreversible failure. Perovskites are efficient but fragile, and ordinary output records blur reversible daily and seasonal swings into permanent decline.

Encapsulated cells were monitored in Alpine and Mediterranean climates with matched electrical, spectral, temperature, humidity, and color image streams. Using two healthy reference cells to cancel the shared environmental response exposed four persistent failures at the Alpine site, while the winter slump of the reference cells themselves reversed with the season. Color changes sometimes came days before electrical ones, yet the audit showed the lead depended on the marker chosen and was not unique to failing cells. At the Mediterranean site the timing did not reproduce. A hidden test confirmed the cameras read surface wetness and thaw reliably.
pmc-13651558:
Ignacio Silva-Llanes and seven co-authors test whether high blood pressure worsens Parkinson-type brain damage in mice, a plausible fear since vascular disease and inflammation travel as a pair in aging brains. Their model forces mouse brains to make too much alpha-synuclein, the protein that clumps in Parkinson's disease, inside the substantia nigra on one side.

Chronic infusion of angiotensin II produced hypertension, yet neuron loss in the dopamine system matched normotensive animals exactly. Support-cell activation in astrocytes and microglia also refused to budge. The inflammatory gene program switched on by the protein, including the inflammasome machinery that matures inflammatory signals, ran no hotter under hypertension. The pyroptosis executioner protein rose where the protein was made in excess, mainly inside microglia, whatever the blood pressure. The authors conclude that synuclein pathology drives this inflammation, and that hypertension may need aging or other vascular partners to matter.
pmc-13652358:
Alexander Muacevic and four colleagues describe a difficult diagnosis of DRESS syndrome, a severe drug reaction, in a man being treated for a bone infection in his foot. The patient, a man in his thirties with major burn history and bipolar disorder, had failed home antibiotic infusions and was admitted for stronger treatment. On the fourth hospital day he developed a spreading rash, rising liver enzymes, and high eosinophil counts.

His medication list made the culprit hard to pin down, since it included two psychiatric drugs and two antibiotics at once. The team stopped the suspected drugs, started high-dose steroids with a long taper, and gave N-acetylcysteine to protect the liver. DRESS can turn fatal when recognition comes late. The case shows how a new rash plus blood changes in a patient on many drugs should trigger fast action even before every test returns.
pmc-13652658:
Alexander Muacevic and eight colleagues report a case where a large abdominal mass in a teenage girl turned out to be something other than what scans suggested. Imaging pointed to a tumor of the mesentery, the tissue that supports the intestines. She had arrived at the emergency department with acute abdominal pain, and the uncertain diagnosis led the team to operate and look directly.

During surgery the mass proved to be a mature ovarian teratoma, the most common benign germ cell tumor of the ovary, and the surgeons removed it completely. Lab examination of the tissue confirmed the finding. Teratomas usually affect women of reproductive age and can present in misleading ways. The report reminds clinicians that a confident scan reading can still be wrong, with surgical exploration sometimes the only route to the right answer.
pmc-1781458:
Provenzano, Eliceiri, Campbell, and co-authors study how collagen is rearranged where a breast tumour meets nearby tissue. Links between the tumour lining and its supporting tissue matter greatly in the breast. When those links go wrong, cancer can form and begin to invade.

Dense collagen in breast tissue is known to raise the risk of breast cancer. The team examined how fibres line up at the tumour edge and how that layout affects local spread. Their findings link fibre patterns to invasion, suggesting the tissue around a tumour helps decide how far it travels.
pmc-2933358:
Kumarasamy, Toleman, Walsh, and co-authors report the emergence of a new antibiotic resistance mechanism called NDM-1. Certain gut bacteria carrying this trait resist carbapenems, a class of last-resort antibiotics. The authors warn that such bacteria could become a major world health problem.

They investigated how common NDM-1 was among drug-resistant bacteria in India, Pakistan, and the United Kingdom, using molecular, biological, and epidemiological methods. Finding the trait across countries showed resistance genes can travel with patients and shape treatment far from their origin.  Travel-linked cases in Britain showed the trait had already crossed borders quietly.
pmc-3738458:
Lawrence, Huber, Pages, and co-authors describe Bioconductor infrastructure for computing with annotated genomic ranges. Genomic data are naturally expressed as ranges: stretches of DNA along a chromosome, each carrying labels and values. Their software represents and computes on such ranges inside the R statistics environment.

Three packages sit at the core: IRanges, GenomicRanges, and a third integrating them with experiments. That foundation lets many other tools share one data language. Standard range infrastructure quietly powers thousands of genomic analyses, from sequencing pipelines to genome browsers.  Range operations such as overlap and counting form the grammar of genomic analysis.
pmc-4556158:
Kang, Froula, Egan, and their team presented MetaBAT in 2015 for metagenome work. A metagenome holds DNA from a whole community of microbes mixed together. Grouping assembled fragments into bins, one per organism, lets researchers study single species from that mixture.

MetaBAT was built to reconstruct single genomes from complex communities in an efficient and accurate way. Earlier binning tools struggled with the tangled nature of real communities. Better bins reveal organisms that cannot be grown in the lab, along with their roles. That advances studies of oceans, soils, and the human gut, where most microbes remain uncultured.
pmc-7919858:
Jennifer Dan and co-authors measured in 2021 how long immune memory to SARS-CoV-2 lasts after infection. Knowing the durability of that memory matters for vaccine design, for testing, and for predicting the pandemic's future course. The team examined several parts of immune memory at once, including antibodies and memory cells that can reactivate on a new encounter.

Their samples came from nearly two hundred confirmed cases, with follow up reaching about eight months after infection. They report that most parts of immune memory were still detectable at that point, though levels varied between people. The findings calmed early fears that protection might fade within weeks, while leaving open how memory performs over years.
poems-pg11558:
S. G. Goodrich published this illustrated volume of Poems in New York in 1851, from the house of G. P. Putnam. Goodrich, known to generations of children as Peter Parley, wrote improving books by the shelf, and this collection dresses his verse for the parlor. A frontispiece, vignettes, and thirteen listed illustrations drawn by artists such as Billings and Harvey and cut by named engravers.

Fairy subjects dominate the picture list, the Departure of the Fairies, the Voyage of the Fairies, the Fairies' Search. The Fairy Dance, alongside American scenes such as Lake Superior and the Indians' discovery of hummingbirds. The frontispiece verse broods on forest oaks flourishing over buried races, a reminder that Goodrich's fancy always carried a moral. The book is a handsome specimen of the American gift-book trade at mid-century.
poems-pg2558:
George P. Morris, the American journalist and songwriter, gathered his Poems in a volume that circulated widely in the nineteenth century. Morris co-founded the New-York Mirror and wrote lyrics that America sang for decades, above all Woodman. Spare That Tree, a plea for an old oak that became one of the century's most beloved songs. His verse aimed at the parlor and the heart rather than the study.

Morris wrote in the popular modes of his day: sentimental ballads, patriotic pieces, and songs of home. Nature, and lost love, many of them set to music and carried far beyond the printed page. Critics placed him among the genteel poets, yet his best songs outlived sterner reputations because ordinary people memorized them. The collection preserves the work of a songwriter-poet who helped define American popular taste before the Civil War.
starkey-pyrotechny-asserted-1658:
George Starkey was an American-born chymist, raised in Bermuda and trained at Harvard, who worked in London's alchemical circles. His Pyrotechny Asserted and Illustrated, published in 1658, defends alchemical practice against its scorners. Starkey taught the writer known as Philalethes, whose books spread his methods worldwide.

Pyrotechny, the art of fire, is Starkey's name for the furnace work by which metals and medicines are made and tested. He answers critics with experiments, weights, and furnaces rather than with riddles alone. The book shows the most skilled American-born chymist of the seventeenth century arguing for his craft in public.
swedenborg-earths-universe-1758:
Emanuel Swedenborg said spirits from other worlds spoke with him at length. His Earths in the Universe came out in 1758. He tells of trips in spirit to the Moon and to the planets. Each world holds folk with its own traits and faith.

Swedenborg tells how the folk of Mars, Venus, and the rest live and pray. He links their traits to parts of the mind and body. Later occult readers drew hard on these strange tales. The book is the oddest claim of many worlds from its age. His tales still draw readers who chase the roots of the other-worlds idea.
swedenborg-heaven-and-hell-1758:
Emanuel Swedenborg, a Swedish sage and man of science, wrote this account of heaven and hell in Latin in 1758. The text here is the English form in which most readers have met it. Swedenborg had once been a lead mind of his land in mines, maths, and the work of the body.

He tells of the worlds of spirits he said he saw and roamed for years in trance. Heaven, hell, and the mid realm each have their lands, towns, and laws in his calm scheme. The book founds the faith that bears his name and marks the lore of the West.
swedenborg-heaven-hell-1758:
Emanuel Swedenborg wrote Heaven and Hell in Latin in 1758. He said he had spent years in talk with angels and spirits. The book gives his full map of the worlds past death. It is his most read work and the base text of his church.

Heaven, hell, and a mid world of spirits each get a full tale. Swedenborg says the dead keep a form, a home, and work much like life here. None are sent to bliss or pain by a judge; each drifts to his own kind. The book shaped views of the next life for two hundred years.
the-great-round-world-and-what-is-going-:
Dated December 16, 1897, No. 58 of The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It is a weekly newspaper for boys and girls. Its lead item asks how it feels to live through history instead of learning it from books. Cuba, Turkey, Haiti, and Hawaii have each been supplying the news; now Austria takes her turn. What is happening there, the paper says, proves that kings can no longer reign as unchecked masters. The people's voice has to be heeded.

The trouble began with Austrian fury at Count Badeni and the ministry he led. The Emperor backed Badeni and meant to keep him in place. Austria's constitution does let the Emperor rule by his own word in an emergency. Still, Francis Joseph could not shield the minister he favored. He shrank from using the power the constitution grants him.
the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-seing:
Convent Affairs, part of To Paris and Prison in Jacques Casanova's memoirs, comes from Arthur Machen's translation of the 1894 London edition, with chapters discovered by Arthur Symons. Chapter Sixteen turns on a beautiful nun who has not yet spoken to Casanova. He marvels at her boldness: a casino at Murano, freedom to sup in Venice with a young man. He suspects an acknowledged lover arranges her liberty to satisfy her caprices.

The chapter introduces Countess Coronini, presented to him by a nun related to M. Dandolo. Once famous for beauty, wit, and political intrigue, the countess has retired to the Convent of St. Justine. Ambassadors and leading Venetian nobles still visit her there, and she knows everything happening in the city. Casanova admits the adventure already makes him unfaithful in thought to his beloved C---- C----. Readers enter the strange half-world where convent walls shelter Venice's best-informed salon.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i: Only the title sheet of Volume 14 and the opening of its first memoir are present for this record, so no full article appears here. The sheet, printed by J. Limbird at 143 Strand in 1829 under a December 24 heading, repeats the magazine's contents promise of essays, narratives, memoirs, and discoveries. It then opens a memoir of Thomas Campbell under his portrait. Campbell, the memoir begins, has not written one line which, dying, he could wish to blot, and he is styled the Tyrtaeus of modern English poetry.

The Mirror's number for Saturday, December 5, 1829, No. 403, illustrates the fall of the Staubbach in Switzerland. The editors open with the sublime: poets, philosophers, and lovers of nature must feel ecstasy and awe before such a scene. Even the mere man of the world is overwhelmed as by the torrent itself, though he soon recovers. The lover of nature reads lessons of infinite wisdom in mountains, rivers, and falls.

The Staubbach falls in the valley of Lauterbrunnen, called Switzerland's most picturesque district. Simond's description is quoted: ascending the valley beside the Lutschine torrent, among rock fragments torn from the heights. Smooth pastures of richest verdure carpet every interval of plain ground. Sonorous Alpine cow-bells sound among the precipices above the travellers' heads. Readers get a waterfall approached through philosophy first and a traveller's boots second.
the-phrenological-delineator-a-compendiu: D. P. Butler, a practical phrenologist, published The Phrenological Delineator at Boston in 1858. It is a compendium of phrenology, in a fourth edition entered in 1856. The scanned title page is badly garbled, but its claims can be read. The book includes recent findings on the brain and the temperaments. Other conditions of body that affect mentality are covered too. A chart of phrenological developments is promised. Only the digitizer's page and that title page are present here, so the compendium itself does not appear.
the-return-pg19158:
H. Beam Piper and John J. McGuire set their story in the air. A helicopter flies five hundred feet above a river. The river runs yellow-brown below the transparent nose. The text comes from a 1960 Holmes-themed collection. Copyright research found no renewal for that book. Pilot Altamont praises a meal in the opening scene. His companion Loudons improvised the dish.

Loudons explains the recipe with pride. Leftover smoked pork chops went into it. Aging rice, egg powder, and milk joined them. Bacon grease fried the mixed dish. A drink called caffchoc follows the meal. Domestic skill in a battered aircraft sets the world. Readers should not confuse this tale with another return. Walter de la Mare's novel shares its short title in the set.
the-way-to-bliss-in-three-books-1658: The surviving text of The Way to Bliss is garbled almost past reading. A title rendered The Way to Blifs in three books comes first, half buried in stray marks and broken words. After it, the pages dissolve into scrambled type that yields no sentences. One stray heading, The Contents, appears near the end, followed by more scrambled matter. Because the scan is this damaged, the book's teaching cannot be described. The record preserves a 1658 devotional title and the ruined remains of its pages, nothing more.
tob-0158:
Seventeen hymns stand at the oldest layer of the Avesta: the Gathas, sung in an archaic tongue and credited to Zoroaster himself. Kenneth Sylvan Guthrie translated them for English readers. No other part of the Zoroastrian scriptures carries the same weight, since the prophet's own voice is heard here.

The hymns praise Ahura Mazda, the Wise Lord, and urge hearers to choose good thoughts, good words, and good deeds against the Lie. Their monotheism is stark and early, from the dawn of recorded religious history. Verified from a pre-1930 edition, Guthrie's version lets the three-thousand-year-old songs speak plainly.
tob-4058:
The first volume of Isis Unveiled, from 1877, takes on the science of its day. Its subtitle claims a master key to the riddles of old and new science and faith. H. P. Blavatsky argues that a science of mere matter can not explain magnetism, trance cures, or the feats of the seance room. Old wisdom, she says, can.

Fierce, stuffed with quotes, and prone to wander, the book runs from the magic of Egypt to the lab tests of her own age. Some claims fall flat now, but the attack still bites. As the first shot of the Theosophic cause, the volume made its author famed at once.
tob-4158:
William James delivered the Gifford Lectures published in 1902 as The Varieties of Religious Experience: A Study in Human Nature. Under its full title, the classic approaches religion through the people who live it. Converts, mystics, and saints describe their experiences in their own words, quoted at generous length, and James asks what those states are worth.

Healthy-minded believers, sick souls, divided selves, and sudden conversions each receive a hearing before his pragmatic test: judge by fruits, not roots. The lectures founded the psychology of religion as a field. Philosophy here listens to life before theorizing about it, which is why the book still recruits readers across every belief and none.
tob-4161-70458:
Edward B. Tylor, often called the father of anthropology, published Primitive Culture in 1871. Volume one argues that culture develops in stages, much as living things were then said to evolve. Tylor studies tools, customs, language, and myths as evidence of that growth.

He treats myth as early man's honest attempt at science, an effort to explain dreams, death, and disease. Old customs that linger as mere habits, he calls survivals, and he tracks them like fossils. The book gave the young field its program and its name for its subject. Victorian readers met here a bold claim: all peoples share one mental history.
un-ga-res-2758:
On 25 October 1971 the UN General Assembly voted to seat the People's Republic of China in place of the Republic of China. Resolution 2758 says the Beijing government's team are the only lawful voice of China at the UN. It also confirms China as one of the five permanent members of the Security Council, with veto power.

The vote shut the door on the team of Chiang Kai-shek, which had held China's seat since 1945 from its base on Taiwan. From that day, Beijing took China's place in the Assembly, the Council, and all linked UN bodies. Few single votes have changed the UN more.
un-ga-res-a-69-58:
A rare high-level meeting on nuclear disarmament, held on 26 September 2013, is followed up in Resolution A/69/58, from the Assembly's sixty-ninth session. Strong support at that meeting for swift, real steps toward the total end of nuclear arms is stressed. The text voices deep concern at the ruinous toll any use of such arms would take on mankind.

The Assembly calls for fast heed of the legal duties states owe on disarmament. Wide support for a full pact on nuclear weapons is backed. Talks should start at once in the Conference on Disarmament on such a pact, one that bars the arms in all forms and provides for their destruction. A world meeting on the point is set for no later than 2018.
un-ga-res-china-s-position-paper-on-the-:
China's seat at the United Nations changed hands through General Assembly resolution 2758 in October 1971, and this position paper states Beijing's view of that vote. Before 1971 the seat was held by the government on Taiwan. The resolution gave the seat to the People's Republic of China instead.

The paper argues that the vote settled the question of who speaks for China. It backs the one-China line and rejects any claim of two Chinas or a separate Taiwan seat. The text matters because the 1971 vote is still cited in fights over Taiwan's status today.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 2758 (XXVI), adopted on 25 October 1971, settled who speaks for China at the United Nations. The Assembly held that restoring the lawful rights of the People's Republic of China was vital. It was vital to guard the Charter and the cause the United Nations serves. It held that its government's delegates were China's only lawful voice.

The decision restored all rights to the People's Republic of China. It named it one of the five permanent members of the Security Council. It ordered the prompt removal of the delegates who had held China's seat until then. They were to be removed from the United Nations and all bodies tied to it.

General Assembly resolution 69/58 (2014) follows up its high-level meeting on nuclear disarmament, held on 26 September 2013. It backs the wide support voiced there for a comprehensive convention on nuclear weapons. It calls for negotiations to begin in the Conference on Disarmament. The negotiations are on a convention banning the weapons and providing for their destruction. It recalls the decision to hold a United Nations conference on nuclear disarmament by 2018. It welcomes the naming of 26 September as the International Day for the Total Elimination of Nuclear Weapons.
un-sc-res-1358: For the year 2006, the catalog lists Resolution 1358 among the Security Council's formal decisions. The Council's fifteen members vote on draft texts, and adopted ones enter the record as numbered resolutions. The library holds the complete text in the form transcribed for English Wikisource from the official UN record. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-1458:
Liberia's sanctions panel was sent back to work in January 2003. The Council's next review of the Liberia measures was due by May. Fighting in Liberia and nearby Côte d'Ivoire caused deep concern. On 28 January 2003 the Council took note of the panel's October report. It said it would keep giving that report full attention. The panel had tracked how Liberia's government met the Council's demands.

The panel was re-established for three more months. Its new term had to start by 10 February 2003. It would run a follow-up mission to Liberia and nearby states. The mission would check compliance with the demands in resolution 1343. Those demands covered Liberia's support for rebels abroad. The panel's findings would guide the May review.
un-sc-res-1558:
Somalia's arms embargo needed fresh watchers in the summer of 2004. A monitoring group had reported that month on breaches of the ban. On 17 August 2004 the Security Council ordered the group rebuilt. The Secretary-General had thirty days to re-establish it. It would work for a further period with a fresh mandate. The 1992 embargo remained in force, and all states had to honor it.

The Council said it would study the group's findings with care. Better enforcement of the embargo was the goal. The Secretary-General also had to arrange the money for the work. Somalia's reconciliation process ran in parallel in Kenya. The monitors' reports fed the sanctions committee named for resolution 751.
un-sc-res-1658: Under the number 1658, the Security Council's formal decision is held in record wording transcribed by Wikisource. The members' method is visible on the page: establish the situation, invoke earlier action, then decide. For readers tracing UN practice, that method matters as much as any single outcome, and the full text shows both.
un-sc-res-1758:
Cyprus and its long division return in Resolution 1758 of the United Nations Security Council, adopted on 15 June 2007. The island stayed broadly calm, yet buffer zone violations had risen. A deal reached on 8 July 2006 still waited for action, and mine clearing had stalled.

The text extends the United Nations Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus, called UNFICYP, until 15 December 2007. It calls the frozen state of affairs flatly unacceptable. Both leaders are urged to start the agreed process at once and show real progress. The Council also asks the Turkish Cypriot side to let mine clearing resume in the buffer zone.
un-sc-res-1858: In 2009 the Security Council adopted Resolution 1858, and this collection keeps the official text through a Wikisource transcription. The act's preamble aligns fifteen governments on one description of a situation; its operative part aligns them on one response. Preserving both alignments, word for word, is the service performed by this entry.
un-sc-res-258: Year 1968 in the catalog holds Resolution 258, a formal Security Council decision of the United Nations. Voting in the Council requires support from its permanent members, so each adopted text marks a point of agreement. Readers will find the full wording here, taken from the English Wikisource transcription of the UN official record. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-358:
Cyprus's ceasefire was breaking down within weeks of the 1974 fighting. On 15 August 1974 the Security Council deplored the failure to obey its order of the day before. Resolution 357 had demanded that the shooting stop. Violence and bloodshed on the island went on. The Council's patience in the text is plainly thin. It had already passed four Cyprus resolutions in under a month.

The Council insists on full use of all those resolutions. Every party had to follow them. The ceasefire had to be observed at once and strictly. The demand covered resolutions 353, 354, 355, and 357. Together they called for a halt, talks, and respect for Cyprus's sovereignty.
un-sc-res-458: Acting formally, the Security Council produced the decision numbered 458, catalogued under 1979. Such texts can call for cease-fires, set up missions, impose duties, or settle points of UN procedure and membership. Its value lies in the primary wording: the decision as adopted, kept through the Wikisource transcription of the record. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-58:
Switzerland's path into the World Court's elections was set by the Security Council on 28 September 1948. Switzerland had joined the Statute of the International Court of Justice under conditions the General Assembly laid down in December 1946. It had even accepted the Court's compulsory jurisdiction. With judge elections due, the Council had to recommend terms for states in Switzerland's position.

The Council recommended that a state party to the Statute but not a United Nations member stand equal with members in nominating candidates. Such a state would vote in the General Assembly for judges in the same manner as members. One bar applied: a state behind on its payments to the Court's expenses, by two full years or more, could not vote. The Assembly could excuse arrears caused by events beyond the state's control. The formula let Switzerland and later others join the Court's system without membership.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci: Behind closed doors on 27 June 2001, the Council took up one short question: who should lead the United Nations next. Having considered the matter, it recommended to the General Assembly that Kofi Annan be appointed Secretary-General for a second term, running from 1 January 2002 to 31 December 2006. Under the Charter, the Council's recommendation comes first and the Assembly then makes the appointment, so this brief text is the formal step that set the second term in motion.

Liberia's file came back for a short, sharp look in 2003. A team of sleuths had probed the state's rule the past fall. Their word came on 25 October 2002. The charge was plain: did Monrovia obey the bans laid on it in 2001? War in next-door Côte d'Ivoire made the file burn hot. Resolution 1458 passed with no dissent on 28 January 2003.

The sleuth team was brought back for three months. It would start by 10 February at the late. Five sleuths at most would do the work. They would tour Liberia and the states round it. Old audits of state cash would get a fresh read. Rebel moves fell in their scope too. Their word was due by 16 April 2003. A full six-month check on the bans loomed in May.

Guns kept seeping into Somalia in 2004, twelve years into a ban. A UN watch team had just sent its first report, dated 11 August. Its finds were grim. Talks to rebuild a Somali state ran in parallel. Resolution 1558 passed with no dissent on 17 August 2004.

The watch team was brought back for six months. The chief had thirty days to set it up. Its chores were clear. Track the flow of arms in and out of Somalia. Keep a fresh list of ban-breakers and their backers. Send the sanctions group a mid-term and a last word. All states were told the ban still bound them in full. The team was urged to hone its list with care, for steps the Council might take later.

Senegal's path to this text ran through a failed federation. It had shared the short-lived Mali Federation with its neighbor. That union broke apart in August 1960. Senegal then applied for its own UN seat. Resolution 158 was adopted unanimously on 28 September 1960 at the 907th meeting.

The Council recommended that the General Assembly admit the Republic of Senegal. Admission came the same day in the Assembly, a rare same-day double. Senegal joined during the celebrated Year of Africa. Its first president, Léopold Senghor, became a leading voice of the new African bloc. The one-sentence resolution marks Senegal's formal entry onto the world stage.

Haiti had just held the first round of its elections on 7 February 2006, and on 14 February its stabilization mission, MINUSTAH, is extended until 15 August 2006. Haitians are congratulated on the successful vote. Municipal and local elections were still to come in April.

All Haitians are urged to keep taking part in the political process and accept its results peacefully. The mission's central role in supporting the remaining elections and Haiti's longer recovery is restated. The Secretary-General is asked to report soon on the situation, including how the mission should be shaped for the period after the new elected president took office.

A stalled settlement process shadows Resolution 1758 on Cyprus, adopted on 15 June 2007. The island stayed generally calm, though buffer-zone violations had risen. The 8 July 2006 Agreement, aiming at a bicommunal, bizonal federation with political equality, still had not been put into effect. Demining in the buffer zone had stalled, and housing for many UNFICYP troops was poor.

The Council extends the UN Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus, UNFICYP, until 15 December 2007. It says the status quo is unacceptable and time is not on the side of a settlement. It calls on both sides to engage at once, show measurable progress, and stop trading blame so full negotiations can begin. It asks the Turkish Cypriot side and Turkish forces to restore the earlier military position at Strovilia. Talks on the buffer zone, including the Ledra Street crossing, are urged. A report is due by 1 December 2007.

Burundi's integrated office, BINUB, is extended until 31 December 2009 on 22 December 2008. Heads of state of the Great Lakes region had met in Bujumbura on 4 December and agreed steps with the Palipehutu-FNL, the last rebel movement. Carrying out the 2006 ceasefire with that group was the main unfinished piece of Burundi's peace.

The government and the FNL are urged to carry out their December agreements before the end of 2008 and to settle the rest by dialogue, without any return to fighting. The FNL is called on to release child soldiers and join the disarmament process. BINUB would keep supporting peace consolidation, justice, and security reform while the final phase of the peace process closed.

Resolution 1958, passed on 15 December 2010, shuts down the last gears of Iraq's oil-for-food scheme. The scheme, born in 1995, was a stopgap under the bans on Iraq. It let Iraq sell oil to buy food and drugs for its people. It shut in form in 2003. Yet stray tasks dragged on for years: old credit notes with claims still live, as a UN note of that December set out in depth.

The Council told the UN chief to take all steps to end the scheme's last tasks for good. It noted that the stray credit notes had lapsed by their own terms. Two twin Iraq texts passed the same day. With them, the books closed on a huge relief plan, one later stained by fraud probes.

The situation in the Middle East kept getting worse after the 1967 war, and the Council spoke on 18 September 1968. Resolution 258 insisted that the cease-fire the Council had ordered must be strictly respected. It reaffirmed Resolution 242 of 1967, the landmark text on settling the conflict. That text called for Israeli withdrawal from occupied territories and for all states in the area to live in peace. All parties were urged to cooperate fully with the Secretary-General's special envoy, who was working to carry out that plan.

Cyprus was being torn apart in the summer of 1974. After a coup backed by Greece, Turkey had invaded, and fighting continued despite repeated Council demands to stop. Resolution 358, adopted unanimously on 15 August 1974, came one day after an earlier ceasefire order had been ignored, a failure the text openly deplores.

The members recalled their chain of Cyprus resolutions from July and August 1974 and insisted that all parties carry them out in full. Above all, they demanded immediate and strict respect for the ceasefire. The resolution is short, but its tone shows a Council losing patience with orders that were not being obeyed.

Cyprus's peacekeeping force was renewed once more on 14 December 1979, by Resolution 458. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 1 December, recommended six more months. The parties concerned agreed with the recommendation. Cyprus accepted that the force should stay beyond 15 December.

The Council extended the force's stationing to 15 June 1980. It voiced support for a ten-point agreement meant to restart the talks between the two communities. That agreement had been worked out at a high-level meeting in Nicosia in May 1979. The parties were urged to resume the talks without delay. The talks had to be steady and focused on results. The Secretary-General was to continue his mission of good offices and report by 31 May 1980.

Resolution 58, adopted on 28 September 1948, sorts out how Switzerland can help choose World Court judges without joining the UN. Switzerland had met the Assembly's conditions and become a party to the court's statute, even accepting the court's compulsory jurisdiction. Elections for the court were coming at the next Assembly session, and the statute required the Council to recommend the terms for such states.

The Council recommended that a state in Switzerland's position stand on an equal footing with UN members in nominating candidates. It would vote in the Assembly on the same terms as members. One limit applied: a state behind on its payments toward the court's expenses could not take part in electing judges.
